# 2 Dynamics: Forces and Newton's Laws

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Dynamics** is the study of **forces and their relationship to the motion of
objects**. Newton's laws of motion form the **cornerstone of classical mechanics**
and provide the framework for understanding how forces affect motion.

## Key formulas

**Newton's Second Law** — the net force acting on an object equals its mass
multiplied by its acceleration. The guide calls this **perhaps the most important
equation in classical mechanics**:

$$F_{\text{net}} = ma$$

**Weight** — the gravitational force exerted on an object by a massive body such
as Earth, equal to the product of mass and gravitational acceleration:

$$F_g = mg$$

**Friction** — the coefficient of friction multiplied by the normal force. This
applies to **both static and kinetic friction, though the coefficients differ**:

$$f = \mu N$$

## Other forces to understand conceptually

| Force | Description |
|---|---|
| **Tension** | Force transmitted through a string, rope, cable or wire |
| **Normal force** | The perpendicular force exerted by a surface |
| **Spring force** | The force exerted by a compressed or stretched spring |

## Method

When analysing physical systems it is crucial to **identify all forces acting on an
object**, **draw a free-body diagram**, and **apply Newton's Second Law** to
determine the resulting motion.

Remember that **forces are vector quantities**, having both magnitude and
direction — which is why the free-body diagram comes before the arithmetic.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Dynamics** | The study of forces and their relationship to the motion of objects |
| **Newton's Second Law** | $F_{\text{net}} = ma$; the net force equals mass times acceleration |
| **Weight** | The gravitational force on an object, $F_g = mg$ |
| **Friction** | $f = \mu N$, the coefficient of friction times the normal force |
| **Tension** | Force transmitted through a string, rope, cable or wire |
| **Normal force** | The perpendicular force exerted by a surface |
| **Free-body diagram** | A diagram identifying all forces acting on an object |

# 3 Circular Motion and Gravitation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Circular motion** describes the movement of objects along a circular path, while
**gravitation** deals with the attractive force between masses. The two are closely
related, because **gravitational forces often cause circular orbital motions**.

## Centripetal force

When an object moves in a circular path it **constantly changes direction**, which
means it is **accelerating toward the centre of the circle**. That acceleration
requires a force — the **centripetal force**:

$$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $F_c$ | The centripetal force |
| $m$ | The mass of the object |
| $v$ | The **tangential** velocity of the object |
| $r$ | The radius of the circular path |

The reasoning matters as much as the formula: changing direction *is* acceleration,
even at constant speed, and acceleration requires a force.

## Gravitational force

**Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation** states that **every mass attracts every
other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely
proportional to the square of the distance between them**:

$$F_g = G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $F_g$ | The gravitational force between the masses |
| $G$ | The gravitational constant, $6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg² |
| $m_1, m_2$ | The masses of the two objects |
| $r$ | The distance between the **centres** of the masses |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Centripetal force** | The force required to keep an object on a circular path, $F_c = mv^2/r$ |
| **Tangential velocity** | The velocity of an object along its circular path |
| **Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation** | Every mass attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance |
| **Gravitational constant ($G$)** | $6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg² |

# 4 Energy, Work and Power

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Energy** describes the **capacity to do work**. Understanding energy and its
various forms is crucial for analysing physical systems and their interactions.

## Kinetic energy

The energy an object possesses **due to its motion**:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$$

where $m$ is mass and $v$ is velocity. The equation shows that **kinetic energy
increases with the square of velocity**, making **speed much more significant than
mass** in determining an object's kinetic energy.

## Potential energy

**Potential energy** is **stored energy depending on an object's position or
configuration**. Two common forms:

**Gravitational potential energy** — the energy an object possesses due to its
height above a reference point:

$$PE = mgh$$

where $m$ is mass, $g$ gravitational acceleration and $h$ height.

**Elastic potential energy** — the energy stored in a stretched or compressed
spring:

$$PE_s = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$$

where $k$ is the spring constant and $x$ the displacement from equilibrium.

## Work and power

**Work** is the **energy transferred when a force moves an object**:

$$W = Fd\cos\theta$$

where $F$ is force, $d$ displacement, and $\theta$ the angle between the force and
displacement vectors.

**The work–energy theorem** — the net work done on an object equals its **change in
kinetic energy**:

$$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE$$

**Power** is the **rate at which work is done or energy is transferred**, measured
in **watts**:

$$P = \frac{W}{t} = Fv\cos\theta$$

Both forms of the power equation carry the same $\cos\theta$ as the work equation,
for the same reason: only the component of force along the motion does work.

## Conservation of energy

**Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to
another.** This principle is fundamental to solving many physics problems.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Energy** | The capacity to do work |
| **Kinetic energy** | Energy due to motion, $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ |
| **Potential energy** | Stored energy depending on position or configuration |
| **Gravitational potential energy** | $PE = mgh$, from height above a reference point |
| **Elastic potential energy** | $PE_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$, stored in a stretched or compressed spring |
| **Spring constant ($k$)** | The constant in the elastic potential energy formula |
| **Work** | Energy transferred when a force moves an object, $W = Fd\cos\theta$ |
| **Work–energy theorem** | Net work equals the change in kinetic energy |
| **Power** | The rate at which work is done, measured in watts |
| **Conservation of energy** | Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed |

# 5 Momentum

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Momentum** is a **vector quantity** representing the **product of an object's mass
and velocity**. It is **conserved in closed systems**, which makes it a powerful
tool for analysing collisions and interactions.

## Linear momentum

$$p = mv$$

Since velocity is a vector, **momentum is also a vector quantity** with both
magnitude and direction.

## Impulse

**Impulse** represents the **change in momentum**, equal to the force applied
multiplied by the time interval over which it acts:

$$J = Ft = \Delta p$$

This relationship, the **impulse–momentum theorem**, is particularly useful for
analysing collisions and impacts. It shows that **a small force applied for a long
time can produce the same change in momentum as a large force applied for a short
time**.

## Conservation of momentum

In a **closed system where no external forces act**, the total momentum before an
interaction equals the total momentum after it:

$$m_1v_1 + m_2v_2 = m_1v_1' + m_2v_2'$$

where the primed variables are the velocities after the interaction. This applies
to **collisions, explosions and other interactions** between objects.

Conservation of momentum **follows from Newton's laws of motion**, and it applies
**even where energy is not conserved** — as in **inelastic collisions**, where
kinetic energy is converted to other forms such as heat or sound.

That last point is what makes momentum more useful than energy for collision
problems: it holds in cases where an energy accounting would not close.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Momentum** | The vector product of an object's mass and velocity, $p = mv$ |
| **Impulse** | The change in momentum, $J = Ft = \Delta p$ |
| **Impulse–momentum theorem** | The relationship showing a small force over a long time equals a large force over a short time |
| **Conservation of momentum** | In a closed system with no external forces, total momentum is unchanged by an interaction |
| **Inelastic collision** | A collision in which kinetic energy is converted to heat or sound, though momentum is still conserved |

# 6 Rotational Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Rotational motion** deals with the movement of objects **around an axis**. Many
concepts from linear motion have **rotational analogues**, creating a parallel set
of equations and principles — which is the most efficient way to learn this topic.

| Linear | Rotational |
|---|---|
| Force $F$ | Torque $\tau$ |
| Mass $m$ | Rotational inertia $I$ |
| $F = ma$ | $\tau = I\alpha$ |
| $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ | $KE_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ |
| Momentum $p = mv$ | Angular momentum $L = I\omega$ |

## Torque

**Torque** is the **rotational equivalent of force**, causing objects to rotate:

$$\tau = rF\sin\theta$$

where $r$ is the distance from the rotation axis to the point where the force is
applied, $F$ is the force, and $\theta$ the angle between the force vector and the
position vector.

**Torque is maximised when the force is perpendicular to the position vector** —
that is, when $\sin\theta = 1$.

## Rotational inertia

**Rotational inertia ($I$)** is the **rotational equivalent of mass**, representing
an object's **resistance to changes in rotational motion**. Its value **depends on
the object's mass distribution relative to the axis of rotation** — which is the one
place the analogy with mass breaks down, since mass alone does not depend on where
you put the axis.

## Newton's Second Law for rotation

$$\tau = I\alpha$$

where $\tau$ is net torque, $I$ rotational inertia and $\alpha$ angular
acceleration.

## Rotational kinetic energy and angular momentum

**Rotational kinetic energy** — the energy of a rotating object, where $\omega$ is
angular velocity:

$$KE_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$

**Angular momentum** — a **conserved quantity in systems with no external
torques**:

$$L = I\omega$$

## Why it matters

Rotational motion is essential for analysing **wheels, gears, motors and celestial
bodies**. Conservation of angular momentum explains phenomena **from figure skating
spins to the stability of gyroscopes**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Torque ($\tau$)** | The rotational equivalent of force, $\tau = rF\sin\theta$, maximised when force is perpendicular to the position vector |
| **Rotational inertia ($I$)** | The rotational equivalent of mass, depending on mass distribution relative to the axis |
| **Angular acceleration ($\alpha$)** | The rotational analogue of acceleration, in $\tau = I\alpha$ |
| **Rotational kinetic energy** | $KE_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ |
| **Angular velocity ($\omega$)** | The rate of rotation |
| **Angular momentum ($L$)** | $L = I\omega$, conserved in systems with no external torques |

# 7 Fluid Dynamics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Fluid dynamics** studies the **behaviour of liquids and gases in motion**, with
applications in engineering, meteorology, oceanography and biology.

## Density and pressure

**Density** — the mass per unit volume of a substance, measured in kg/m³:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

**Pressure** — force per unit area, measured in **pascals**. In fluids, **pressure
acts in all directions**:

$$P = \frac{F}{A}$$

**Pressure at a depth** — the pressure at depth $h$ in a fluid, where $P_0$ is
typically atmospheric pressure, $\rho$ the fluid density and $g$ gravitational
acceleration:

$$P = P_0 + \rho gh$$

## Pascal's and Archimedes' principles

**Pascal's Principle** — in hydraulic systems, **pressure is transmitted equally
throughout a confined fluid**, allowing **force multiplication through area
differences**:

$$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$$

**Archimedes' Principle** — an object immersed in a fluid experiences an **upward
buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced**:

$$F_b = \rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$$

## Fluid flow

**The continuity equation** — for **incompressible fluids**, the product of
cross-sectional area and fluid velocity remains constant. This represents
**conservation of mass**:

$$A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$$

**Bernoulli's equation** — representing **conservation of energy in fluid flow**:

$$P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$$

The two flow equations are the two conservation laws applied to a moving fluid:
continuity conserves mass, Bernoulli conserves energy.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Density ($\rho$)** | Mass per unit volume, measured in kg/m³ |
| **Pressure ($P$)** | Force per unit area, measured in pascals; in fluids it acts in all directions |
| **Pressure at depth** | $P = P_0 + \rho gh$ |
| **Pascal's Principle** | Pressure is transmitted equally through a confined fluid, allowing force multiplication |
| **Archimedes' Principle** | An immersed object experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid displaced |
| **Buoyant force ($F_b$)** | $\rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$ |
| **Continuity equation** | $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$, representing conservation of mass in incompressible flow |
| **Bernoulli's equation** | $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$, representing conservation of energy in fluid flow |

markdown:
# 3.4 Linear Programming

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The four parts of a linear program

**Linear programming** is a mathematical model consisting of a **linear function to
be optimised** — maximised or minimised — **and a set of inequalities representing
the restrictions on resources**.

| Part | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Objective function** | The function to be maximised or minimised. It might represent amounts of money earned or spent, goods manufactured or delivered, or any of a variety of other quantities |
| **Constraints** | The linear inequalities |
| **Feasible region** | The solution of the system of linear inequalities |

The central fact, and the reason the method works at all: **if a linear program has
a solution, it will occur at a vertex — a corner point — of the feasible region.**
If there are multiple solutions, **at least one of them will occur at a vertex**.

That is what turns an infinite search into a finite one. The feasible region
contains infinitely many points, but only its corners need to be tested.

## Method

1. **Solve the system of linear inequalities.** Determine the coordinates of the
   vertices of the feasible region — that is, solve the system of equations
   consisting of the lines whose intersection is the vertex
2. **Evaluate the objective function** to be optimised at each vertex
3. **Identify the maximum or minimum value** of the objective function

## When two vertices tie

If **two vertices of the feasible region are both solutions** to a linear program,
then **every point on the line segment connecting the two vertices is also a
solution**.

This follows from the objective function being linear: if it takes the same value
at both ends of a segment, it takes that value all along it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Linear programming** | A model consisting of a linear function to be optimised and a set of inequalities representing restrictions on resources |
| **Objective function** | The function to be maximised or minimised in a linear program |
| **Constraints** | The linear inequalities of a linear program |
| **Feasible region** | The solution of the system of linear inequalities |
| **Vertex** | A corner point of the feasible region, where a solution will occur if one exists |

# 8.2 Sine and Cosine Curves

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three measurements of a sinusoid

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Frequency** | The number of cycles the graph completes in an interval of $2\pi$ radians |
| **Amplitude** | Half the difference between the function's maximum and minimum values |
| **Midline** | Determined by the average of the maximum and minimum values of the function |

Amplitude and midline are the two halves of the same calculation: the **half
difference** of the extremes gives the amplitude, and their **average** gives the
midline. Together they fix the vertical position and reach of the curve, which is
why 8.3 uses them as the route from a graph back to an equation.

## The four transformations

| Transformation | Form |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal dilation** | $y = \sin(bx)$ and $y = \cos(bx)$ |
| **Vertical dilation** | $y = a\sin x$ and $y = a\cos x$ |
| **Horizontal translation** | $y = \sin(x + c)$ and $y = \cos(x + c)$ |
| **Vertical translation** | $y = \sin x + d$ and $y = \cos x + d$ |

The guide also lists **reflecting a trigonometric function** as part of this
section, without giving its form.

Each constant acts on one measurement above: $b$ changes the frequency, $a$ the
amplitude, $d$ the midline, and $c$ shifts the curve horizontally without altering
any of the three.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Frequency** | The number of cycles a sinusoidal graph completes in an interval of $2\pi$ radians |
| **Amplitude** | Half the difference between a sinusoidal function's maximum and minimum values |
| **Midline** | The line determined by the average of the maximum and minimum values |
| **Horizontal dilation** | The transformation $y=\sin(bx)$ or $y=\cos(bx)$ |
| **Vertical dilation** | The transformation $y=a\sin x$ or $y=a\cos x$ |
| **Horizontal translation** | The transformation $y=\sin(x+c)$ or $y=\cos(x+c)$ |
| **Vertical translation** | The transformation $y=\sin x + d$ or $y=\cos x + d$ |

# 8.3 Modelling Periodic Behaviour

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Modelling runs in the opposite direction to 8.2: there, constants were given and
the curve followed; here the behaviour is observed and the constants must be
recovered from it.

## Recovering period and frequency

**The smallest interval of input values over which the maximum or minimum output
values start to repeat** can be used to determine or estimate the **period and
frequency** for a sinusoidal function model.

## Recovering amplitude and vertical shift

**The maximum and minimum output values** can be used to determine the
**amplitude and vertical shift** for a sinusoidal function model.

This is 8.2's amplitude and midline calculation used in reverse: the half
difference of the observed extremes gives the amplitude, and their average gives
the vertical shift.

## Choosing sine or cosine

**Flexibly select sine or cosine functions based on the situation**, making the
equation easier to calculate as well as promoting critical thinking.

The two curves differ only by a horizontal translation, so either can model the
same behaviour — but one will usually need a smaller phase shift than the other,
and that is the one worth choosing.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Period** | Determined from the smallest interval of input values over which the maximum or minimum output values start to repeat |
| **Vertical shift** | Determined, with the amplitude, from the maximum and minimum output values |

# 10.4 Solving Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide carries the syllabus's own sub-codes here, which are given alongside each
statement below.

## Equations

**Equivalent trigonometric forms may be useful in solving trigonometric
equations.**

**Because trigonometric functions are periodic, there are often infinitely many
solutions to trigonometric equations** (10.4.A.3). This is the fact everything else
in the section responds to — every method below is a way of cutting an infinite
solution set down to the ones being asked for.

**Algebraic and graphical methods are used to solve trigonometric equations in a
finite interval, including the use of trigonometric identities and factorisation**
(10.4.A.4).

**Inverse trigonometric functions are useful in solving equations involving
trigonometric functions, but solutions may need to be modified due to domain
restrictions.** An inverse returns one value where the equation has infinitely
many, so the others must be recovered by hand.

**In trigonometric equations arising from a contextual scenario, there is often a
domain restriction that can be implied from the context, which limits the number of
solutions** (10.4.A.6).

## Inequalities

The same three points carry over.

**Equivalent trigonometric forms may be useful in solving trigonometric
inequalities.**

**Inverse trigonometric functions are useful in solving inequalities involving
trigonometric functions, but solutions may need to be modified due to domain
restrictions** (10.4.B.2).

**In trigonometric inequalities arising from a contextual scenario, there is often a
domain restriction that can be implied from the context, which limits the number of
solutions** (10.4.B.3).

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Equivalent trigonometric forms** | Rewritings of an expression that may make an equation or inequality solvable |
| **Domain restriction** | A limit on the input values, either from an inverse function or implied by the context, which reduces the number of solutions |

# 11.1 Polar Coordinates and Graphs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The polar coordinate system

The **polar coordinate system** is an alternative to the Cartesian system of
rectangular coordinates for locating points in a plane.

The polar coordinates of a point $P$ consist of an **ordered pair** $(r,\theta)$:

- $r$ is the **directed distance from the pole** to $P$
- $\theta$ is the **measure of the angle from the polar axis to** $OP$

The polar coordinates of the pole $O$ are $(0,\theta)$ — the distance is zero
whatever the angle, so the pole has infinitely many representations.

The angle $\theta$ can be measured in **degrees or radians**, and **both $r$ and
$\theta$ can be either positive or negative**. That last point is what the two
rules below exist to settle.

## The sign of the angle

| Sign of $\theta$ | How the polar angle is obtained |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | Rotating $OP$ **counterclockwise** from the polar axis |
| **Negative** | Rotating $OP$ **clockwise** from the polar axis |

## The sign of the distance

| Sign of $r$ | Where the polar distance is measured |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | From $O$ **along the terminal side** of the angle $\theta$ |
| **Negative** | From $O$ **on the ray opposite** the terminal side of the angle $\theta$ |

A negative $r$ therefore places the point on the far side of the pole from where
the angle points — which is why the same point has more than one set of polar
coordinates.

## Naming the plane

A plane is called an **$r\theta$-plane** when polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ are
used to identify its points.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polar coordinate system** | An alternative to the Cartesian system for locating points in a plane |
| **Polar coordinates** | The ordered pair $(r,\theta)$ giving a point's directed distance from the pole and the angle from the polar axis |
| **Pole** | The origin $O$ of the polar system, with coordinates $(0,\theta)$ |
| **Polar axis** | The reference ray from which the angle $\theta$ is measured |
| **Terminal side** | The side of the angle along which a positive polar distance is measured |
| **$r\theta$-plane** | A plane whose points are identified by polar coordinates |

# S1M-1 Chapter 1 - Linear and Quadratic Functions

## Chapter 1 - Linear and Quadratic Functions

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Pre-calculus AP review guide (PA). Writers: Justin Lee 10-4. Editor: Calvin 10-9. Range: Ch 1-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**1.2 Slopes of Lines & 1.3 Finding Equations of Line & 1.4 Linear Functions and Models**

Slope: $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}=\frac{y2-y1}{x2-x1}$ (Linear functions have constant rate of change)

Parallel Lines: the slopes of two lines are equal

Perpendicular Lines: the slopes of two lines are negative reciprocals

Different forms of Lines

- Slope-intercept form: $y=mx+k$
- General form: $Ax+By=C$
- Point-slope form: $y-y1=m(x-x1)$
- Intercept form: $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1$

## 1.5 The Complex Numbers

The imaginary unit: $i=\surd -1$

Complex number: $a+bi$ (a: real part; b: imaginary part)

Complex conjugates: $z=a+bi$ and $z̄=a-bi$

$${i}^{1}=i, {i}^{2}=-1, {i}^{3}=-i, {i}^{4}=1$$

$${i}^{4n+1}=i, {i}^{4n+2}=-1, {i}^{4n+3}=-i, {i}^{4n+4}=1$$

## 1.6 Solving Quadratic Equations & 1.7 Quadratic Functions and Their Graphs

Quadratic Equation

- Standard form: $a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0, a\ne 0 \text{ and } a,b,c\in \mathbb{R}$

Method for solving quadratic equations:

- Factoring
  - Only works when the equation has rational roots
- Completing the square
  - Use when the equation has the form ${x}^{2}+(\text{ even } \text{ number })x+\text{ constant }=0$
- Quadratic formula
  - $x=\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$

Discriminant: $D={b}^{2}-4ac$

- If D>0, the equation has 2 real solutions
- If D=0, the equation has one real solution
- If D<0, the equation has no real solutions

**ALWAYS CHECK for losing/gaining a root**

- Losing a root; eg: solve (2x-5)(x+6) = 7(x+6)
- Gaining a root; eg: solve √(3x+6)=2x+1

Quadratic Function ($f(x)=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ or $f(x)=a(x-ℎ{)}^{2}+k$)

- Axis of symmetry: $-\frac{b}{2a}$
- Vertex: $(-\frac{b}{2a},c-\frac{{b}^{2}}{4a})$
- Opening: if a>0, the vertex is the function’s minimum; if a<0, the vertex is the function’s maximum

Average rate of change between two points of a quadratic function is equivalent to finding the slope of the secant between those points

- The instantaneous rate of change at a point can be approximated by the average rates of change of the function over small intervals containing that point

Slope and concavity:

- Slope sign → tells you if the function is going up or down
- Concavity → tells you which way the curve bends (up = ∪, down = ∩)
- Positive rate of change→graph is increasing
- Increasing rate of change→concave up
- Decreasing rate of change→concave down

**given a data chart, it is quadratic if and only if the second differences (the differences of consecutive average rates of change) are constant**

# S1M-2 Chapter 2 - Polynomial Functions

## Chapter 2 - Polynomial Functions

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Pre-calculus AP review guide (PA). Writers: Justin Lee 10-4. Editor: Calvin 10-9. Range: Ch 1-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 2.1 Polynomials

Polynomial function of degree n: $f(x)={a}_{n}{x}^{n}+{a}_{n-1}{x}^{n-1}+{a}_{n-2}{x}^{n-2}+…+{a}_{1}x+{a}_{0}$

- aₙ, aₙ₋₁, aₙ₋₂, …, a₀ are real numbers (n is a nonnegative integer, aₙ ≠ 0)
- The degree of a polynomial is the degree of the term of highest degree
- Leading Term: the term containing the highest power of x
- Leading coefficient: coefficient of the leading term

Degree

Name

Example

## 0

constant

f(x)=2

## 1

linear

f(x)=x

## 2

quadratic

f(x)=x^2

## 3

cubic

f(x)=x^3

## 4

quartic

f(x)=x^4

## 5

quintic

f(x)=x^5

## 2.2 Long Division; The Remainder & Factor Theorems

Example of long division:

Dividend: $2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-6x-8$; Divisor: $x-2$; Quotient: $2{x}^{2}+5x+4$ ; Remainder: 0

Dividing a polynomial with a divisor of degree n always produces a remainder whose degree is at most n-1

- Remainder Theorem: When polynomial P(x) is divided by x-a, the remainder is P(a)
- Factor Theorem: A number a is a solution of the polynomial equation f(x)=0 if and only if x-a is a factor of f(x)

## 2.3 Graphing Polynomial Functions

Fundamental shapes of polynomial functions:

**Steps to Graphing Polynomial Functions**

1. Determine the end behavior — look at the leading term ${a}_{n}{x}^{n}$: if $n$ is even and ${a}_{n}>0$, both ends go up; even and ${a}_{n}<0$, both ends go down; odd and ${a}_{n}>0$, left down/right up; odd and ${a}_{n}<0$, left up/right down.

- Use limit notation to describe end behavior: eg: $\lim_{x\to \infty }f(x)=\infty$

2. Find the y-intercept— set $x=0$ and evaluate $f(0)$; plot the point $(0,f(0))$.

3. Find the x-intercepts (zeros) — set $f(x)=0$ and solve (factor, use the quadratic formula, etc.); plot each real root on the x-axis.

4. Determine multiplicity at each zero — if the factor $(x-r{)}^{m}$: odd $m$ → graph crosses the axis; even $m$ → graph touches and turns around; larger $m$ → flatter near the root.

5. Find turning points — a polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n-1$ turning points

6. Make a sign table / test intervals — pick test points between the zeros to determine whether the graph is above or below the x-axis in each interval.

7. Sketch the curve — connect the points smoothly, respecting end behavior, intercepts, multiplicity, and turning points (no sharp corners).

8. Label key features — mark intercepts, turning points, and note the end behavior arrows.

**Important Theorems/Principles**

**Local Extrema Theorem**: a polynomial function of degree n has at most n-1 relative extrema

**Extreme Value Theorem**: if a polynomial function f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f has both a maximum and a minimum value on [a,b]

**Intermediate Value Theorem**: if P(x) is a polynomial function such that a<b and P(a)≠P(b), then P(x) takes on every value between P(a) and P(b) in the interval [a,b]

**Location Principle**: if P(x) is a polynomial function with real coefficients, and a and b are real numbers such that P(a) is positive and P(b) is negative, then P(x) has at least one zero between a and b

**Rational Root Theorem**: if qx-p is a factor of a polynomial, then q must divide the leading coefficient, and p must divide the constant term

**The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra**: if P(x) is a polynomial of degree n, then the equation of P(x) has exactly n roots, including complex solutions (provided a double root is counted as 2 roots, a triple root is counted as 3 roots, and so on)

**Complex Conjugates Theorem**: if P(x) is a polynomial with real coefficients, and a+bi is an imaginary root of the equation P(x)=0, then a-bi is also a root

**Theorem 3**: suppose P(x) is a polynomial with rational coefficients, and a and b are rational numbers such that √b is irrational; if a+√b is a root of the equation P(x)=0, then a-√b is also a root

**Theorem 4**: if P(x) is a polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients, then the equation P(x)=0 has at least one real root

# S1M-4 Chapter 4 - Functions

## Chapter 4 - Functions

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Pre-calculus AP review guide (PA). Writers: Justin Lee 10-4. Editor: Calvin 10-9. Range: Ch 1-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 4.1 Functions

Function: a correspondence or rule that assigns to every element in a set D exactly one element in a set R

- It is a subset of the more general class of correspondences called relations
  - Relation: any correspondence/rule that pairs the members of two sets
  - ${y}^{2}=4x$ is a relation but not a function
  - The **vertical-line test**: if no vertical line intersects a given graph in more than one point, then the graph is a graph of a function

Domain: the set of x-coordinates of points on the graph

Range: the set of y-coordinates of points of the graph

Zeros: the x-intercepts of the graph

Special Functions:

- Greatest integer function (floor function)
- Its output is the greatest integer less than or equal to the number
- Notation: y=⌊x⌋
- Least integer function (ceiling function)
- Its output is the least integer greater than or equal to the number
- Notation: y=⌈x⌉
- Equal functions
- Two functions f and g are equal functions if
  - The domains of the two functions are equal
  - For all x in the domain, f(x)=g(x)

## 4.2 Operations on Functions

**the DOMAIN of each resulting function consists of those values of x common to the domains of f and g**

Composite Functions: the combination of functions in which functions are successively applied in a specific order

- $f∘g$ or $f(g(x))$is the operation of applying g and then f
- The input x must be in the domain of the inner function, AND the inner function's output must be in the domain of the outer function.

## 4.3 Reflecting graphs; Symmetry

Reflection: reflection in line t is the congruent graph symmetric to the original graph with respect to t; it is the mirror image of the graph where line t is the mirror of the reflection

- Reflection in the x-axis: y=f(x) → y=-f(x)
- Reflection in the y-axis: y=f(x) → y=f(-x)
- Reflection in the line y=x: equivalent to interchanging x and y in the equation
  - Eg: $y=3x+2$ → $x=3y+2$ → $y=\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{2}{3}$

Symmetry:

- A line $l$ is called an axis of symmetry if it is possible to pair the points of the graph in such a way that $l$ is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each pair
- A point $O$ is called a point of symmetry of a graph if it is possible to pair the points of the graph in such a way that $O$ is the midpoint of the segment joining each pair

Tests for the symmetry of a graph:

- X-axis: replace (x,y) by (x,-y)
- Y-axis: replace (x,y) by (-x,y)
- y=x: replace (x,y) by (y,x)
- Origin: replace (x,y) by (-x,-y)

Even function: function that satisfies f(-x)=f(x) x$\in$D

Odd function: function that satisfies f(-x)=-f(x) x$\in$D

In a given interval:

Increasing: x1>x2, f(x1)≥f(x2)

Decreasing: x1>x2, f(x1)≤f(x2)

Strictly Increasing: x1>x2, f(x1)>f(x2)

Strictly Decreasing: x1>x2, f(x1)<f(x2)

## 4.4 Periodic Functions; Stretching and Translating

Periodic Functions

- A function f is periodic if there is a positive number p, called a period of f, such that f(x+p)=f(x) for all x in the domain of f
- Fundamental period: the smallest period of a periodic function
- If a periodic function has maximum value M and minimum value m, the amplitude of the function is given by ½(M-m)

Stretching and Shrinking Graphs

- Vertical stretching/shrinking of a graph can be expressed by y=cf(x) where c is positive
  - If c>1 → vertical stretch
  - If 0<c<1 → vertical shrink
  - The amplitude of the function changes to $cA$
- Horizontal stretching/shrinking of a graph can be expressed by y=f(cx) where c is positive
  - If c>1 → horizontal shrink
  - If 0<c<1 → horizontal stretch
  - The period of the function changes to $\frac{p}{c}$

Translating Graphs

- The graph of y-k=f(x-h) is obtained by translating the graph of y=f(x) horizontally h units and vertically k units

## 4.5 Inverse Functions

Inverse Function: two functions whose composition give the identity function h(x)=x

A function f has an inverse function g if and only if

- f(g(x))=x for all x in the domain of g(x) **and**
- g(f(x))=x for all the x in the domain of f(x)

Notation: inverse function of $f$ is denoted as ${f}^{-1}$ (NOTE: ${f}^{-1}$ does not mean the reciprocal of f)

If f and g are inverse functions, they are symmetric with respect to the line y=x, **so you can find the inverse function by simply switching y and x and solving for y**

Horizontal-Line test: if the graph of function y=f(x) is such that no horizontal line intersects the graph in more than one point, then f is one-to-one and has an inverse function

## 4.8 Radical Functions

Definition: A radical function is a function in which the variable appears inside a radical (root) symbol — most commonly a square root.

General form: $f(x) = \sqrt[n]{g(x)}$ where g ( x ) is some expression involving x and n ≥ 2 is an integer

Domain Rule:

- Even index (n is even): solve g ( x ) ≥ 0
- Odd index (n is odd): domain is all real numbers (unless g ( x ) itself has restrictions)

Graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$

Partial fraction: $\frac{2}{x-3}+\frac{5}{x+1}$ (Single fraction: $\frac{7x-13}{{x}^{2}-2x-3}$)

Steps to decompose a fraction with denominators that can be factored into linear factors and the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator

- Factor the denominator
- Express two fractions using A and B for the numerators
- Multiply by the least common denominator
- Solve for A and B
- Express with partial fractions

Rational Function: eg:$\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x+2}{3{x}^{2}+3x+1}$

Limit of a function: $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=L$

- This means that when x is getting closer to c, f(x) approaches a fixed number L

Left-hand limit: x approaches c from the left $\lim_{x\to {c}^{-}}f(x)$

Right-hand limit: x approaches c from the right $\lim_{x\to {c}^{+}}f(x)$

Continuity

- A function f (x) is continuous at a point x = a if all three of the following conditions hold:
- f (a) is defined
- $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists
- $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)$

A function is continuous at a point if you can draw the graph through that point without lifting your pencil, meaning that there are no holes, jumps, or vertical asymptotes

- 3 basic kinds of discontinuity at a point
- Point
- Jump
- Infinite

Horizontal asymptote

- if$\lim_{x\to \pm \infty }f(x)=b$ then line y=b is a horizontal asymptote of f(x)

Vertical asymptote

- if$\lim_{x\to {a}^{\pm }}f(x)=\pm \infty$ then line x=a is a vertical asymptote of f(x)

# S1M-1 Unit 0: Introduction to Psychological Research Methods

## Unit 0: Introduction to Psychological Research Methods

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 1.1 The Scientific Attitude

Critical thinking in psychology rests on three habits working together: curiosity, skepticism, and humility. Together they let you examine assumptions, appraise sources, discern hidden biases, and weigh evidence against conclusions. Three biases constantly get in the way: hindsight bias (the "I knew it all along" effect), overconfidence in our own judgments, and the tendency to perceive order in genuinely random events.

## 1.2 Key Concepts

- **Falsifiability.** A scientific claim must be testable. The classic non-falsifiable example: the existence of God.
- **Operational definition.** A precise, measurable definition of a research procedure or concept.

- **Hypothesis vs. theory.** A hypothesis is a testable prediction; a theory is an organized explanation. A hypothesis is often implied by a theory.

## 1.3 Non-Experimental Methods

- **Case study.** In-depth analysis of one individual or group.
- **Naturalistic observation.** Observing behavior without interfering.

- **Survey.** Self-report via questions.
- **Correlational study.** Measuring the association between two variables.

**Exam note.** Know the three survey biases: wording effect, social desirability bias, and self-report bias (people report their own behavior inaccurately).

- **Random sampling.** Everyone in the population has an EQUAL CHANCE of being selected.

**Exam note.** On the exam, write "equal chance" — the phrase "random" alone does not earn the point.

Population refers to ALL those studied; the sample is the SOME who represent the population.

## 1.4 Correlation

A correlation is a linear association between two variables, summarized by the correlation coefficient r, which ranges from −1.00 to +1.00. Correlational data are displayed in scatterplots — the only graph type you need to know for the exam. Two related pitfalls: an illusory correlation is perceiving a relationship that is not actually there (similar to confirmation bias), and regression toward the mean describes how extreme scores drift toward the average on retest.

**Exam note.** r is NOT the slope. The sign of r only tells you the direction of the relationship.

**Exam note.** Illusory correlation, lurking variables, and "correlation ≠ causation" are three distinct concepts — do not blur them together.

![Scatterplots: r = +0.9, r = −0.9, and r = 0. The coefficient's sign gives direction only — it is not the slope.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-01.png)

*Figure 1. Scatterplots: r = +0.9, r = −0.9, and r = 0. The coefficient's sign gives direction only — it is not the slope.*

## 1.5 Experimentation

An experiment compares an experimental group against a control group. Random assignment equalizes pre-existing differences between the groups. In a single-blind study participants are blind to the treatment; in a double-blind study participants AND researchers are blind. Key vocabulary: the placebo effect (improvement from expectation alone), confounding variables (factors that may influence the dependent variable), and experimenter bias (researcher expectations skewing results). The independent variable is what the researcher manipulates; the dependent variable is what is measured.

| **Validity** | **Reliability** |
|---|---|
| Does the experiment measure what it is supposed to measure? | Can the results be consistently replicated? |

**Exam note.** Reliability cannot be inferred from the name alone — memorize the definition: consistently replicated.

## 1.6 Other Research Methods and Ethics

- **Developmental designs.** Twin studies (identical vs. fraternal twins), cross-sectional, and longitudinal studies.
- **Data types.** Quantitative vs. qualitative (categorical) research.

- **Ethics.** Informed consent — informed ASSENT for minors — debriefing, protection from greater-than-usual harm, and confidentiality.
- **Guidelines.** Issued by the APA and BPS; animal studies are governed by common sense.

## 1.7 Statistics

Descriptive statistics measure and describe characteristics (in AP Psychology, histograms are basically bar charts). Inferential statistics ask whether results can generalize to the larger population. Better studies have representative rather than biased samples, bigger rather than smaller samples, more estimates rather than fewer, and may pool findings in a meta-analysis.

| **Mode** | **Median** | **Mean** |
|---|---|---|
| Most frequent value. Bimodal = two peaks (textbook-tested, not covered in class). | Middle value. | Average — pulled toward the tail in skewed data. |

Measures of variation include the range and the standard deviation (skip the IQR).

**Exam note.** Define standard deviation as the AVERAGE distance of all data points from the mean.

Skew: look at the tail. A tail trailing right = right (positive) skew, and the mean is HIGHEST in positive skew — the reverse for negative skew.

![Distributions in negative skew (mean lowest), normal (mean = median), and positive skew (mean highest). Always read the tail.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-02.png)

*Figure 2. Distributions in negative skew (mean lowest), normal (mean = median), and positive skew (mean highest). Always read the tail.*

The normal curve is bell-shaped, and the 68-95-99.7 rule gives the percentage of scores within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean.

![The normal curve: 68% of scores fall within ±1 SD, 95% within ±2 SD, and 99.7% within ±3 SD of the mean.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-03.png)

*Figure 3. The normal curve: 68% of scores fall within ±1 SD, 95% within ±2 SD, and 99.7% within ±3 SD of the mean.*

## 1.8 Statistical Significance

A p-value tells you how likely the result occurred by chance, assuming there is no difference in the population.

**Exam note.** In AP Psychology, p < 0.05 AND p = 0.05 both mean "no difference" (no significant effect).

Statistical significance is not the same as practical significance; the effect size tells you the strength of the relationship between two variables.

# S1M-2 Unit 1: Biological Bases of Behavior

## Unit 1: Biological Bases of Behavior

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 2.1 Nature vs. Nurture

Nature covers natural selection and evolutionary psychology; nurture covers environment and heredity.

**Exam note.** "50% genetic" means 50% of the INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES in the trait — not 50% of your height.

Identical vs. fraternal twins form the basis of twin studies.

## 2.2 The Nervous System

| **Part** | **Contents** |
|---|---|
| CNS (central) | Brain + spinal cord. Bundles of axons = TRACTS; clusters of soma = NUCLEI. |
| PNS (peripheral) | Everything outside the CNS. Bundles = NERVES; clusters = GANGLIA. |
| PNS branches | Somatic = voluntary. Autonomic = automatic: sympathetic (arousal) vs. parasympathetic (calm). |

**Exam note.** CNS terms are tracts and nuclei; PNS terms are nerves and ganglia. Exam questions may use them without defining them (the optic nerve is a named exception).

Sensory neurons carry input; motor neurons carry output. The reflex arc runs: sensory neuron → INTERNeuron → motor neuron.

## 2.3 The Neuron

Know the parts: soma, dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, node of Ranvier, axon hillock, and axon terminal. Glial cells support neurons; Schwann cells produce myelin in the PNS.

**Exam note.** If you are labeling a CNS neuron, do NOT write "Schwann cell" — write "glial cell" (oligodendrocyte earns bonus-level credit).

The action potential: resting potential −70 mV, threshold −55 mV; the response is all-or-none, followed by a refractory period. The sequence is depolarization → repolarization → hyperpolarization.

![The action potential: resting potential −70 mV, threshold −55 mV, all-or-none firing, refractory period.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-04.png)

*Figure 4. The action potential: resting potential −70 mV, threshold −55 mV, all-or-none firing, refractory period.*

## 2.4 Neural Communication

At the synaptic cleft, neurotransmitters are released from the pre-synaptic axon terminal...

**Exam note.** ...and they BIND receptors on the post-synaptic neuron. Never write that neurotransmitters GO INTO the post-synaptic neuron.

Signals are excitatory or inhibitory; reuptake recycles neurotransmitters back into the sending neuron.

## 2.5 Neurotransmitters

| **Neurotransmitter** | **Role** | **Linked to** |
|---|---|---|
| Acetylcholine (ACh) | Muscle action, learning, memory | Alzheimer's disease |
| Dopamine | Movement, learning, attention, emotion | Schizophrenia, Parkinson's |
| Serotonin | Mood, hunger, sleep, arousal | Depression |
| Norepinephrine | Alertness, arousal, mood | — |
| GABA | MAJOR inhibitory | Undersupply: seizures, tremors, insomnia |
| Glutamate | MAJOR excitatory; memory | Migraines, seizures |
| Endorphins | Pain & pleasure perception | — |
| Substance P | Pain perception, immune response | — |

**Exam note.** If the question says adrenaline or noradrenaline, it means the HORMONE. Norepinephrine is the neurotransmitter.

Agonists enhance a neurotransmitter's activity; antagonists block it. Reuptake inhibitors such as SSRIs act as agonists.

## 2.6 The Endocrine System and Drugs

Hormones travel via glands — know the adrenal gland and pituitary gland, and the hormone oxytocin.

| **Class** | **Examples** |
|---|---|
| Depressants | Alcohol, barbiturates, opioids |
| Stimulants | Nicotine, cocaine, methamphetamine, MDMA (ecstasy) |
| Hallucinogens | LSD, MDMA, marijuana |

Substance use disorder: addiction vs. tolerance (needing more of the drug for the same effect).

## 2.7 Studying the Brain

- **Approaches.** Biopsychosocial approach (at most 1 MCQ); neuroplasticity; lesion studies.
- **Imaging.** Structural: MRI, CT. Functional: EEG, MEG, PET, fMRI.

## 2.8 Brain Structures and Functions

| **Structure** | **Function** |
|---|---|
| Brainstem (medulla + pons + midbrain) | Life-support basics; the medulla and pons are parts OF the brainstem, not separate from it. |
| Reticular formation | Arousal |
| Thalamus | Sensory relay to cortex |
| Hypothalamus | Homeostasis; talks to the endocrine system via the pituitary; reward center |
| Cerebellum | Balance, coordination |
| Amygdala | Emotion (fear) |
| Hippocampus | Memory |
| Cerebral cortex | Outer grey matter OF the cerebrum |

## 2.9 The Cerebral Cortex

Four lobes: frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal. The motor cortex sits at the rear of the frontal lobe; the somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe; association areas fill the rest. One odd fact: the right temporal lobe also handles facial recognition.

- **Language.** Broca's area (production) and Wernicke's area (comprehension) — BOTH on the LEFT hemisphere.
- **Contralateral organization.** Each side of the brain connects to the body's opposite side.

- **Hemisphere specialties.** Left: language, logic, analytical. Right: music & art, visual-spatial, creativity.

## 2.10 Classic Case Studies

- **Phineas Gage.** Frontal lobe damage → personality change.
- **Neurogenesis.** Forming new neurons.

- **Split-brain.** Corpus callosum severed. Right visual field → the person can SAY what they saw; left visual field → the LEFT HAND picks the object (contralateral processing).

**Exam note.** If you can explain split-brain studies, you understand how the brain works — a top exam favorite.

# S1M-3 Module 1.5: Consciousness and Sleep

## Module 1.5: Consciousness and Sleep

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 3.1 Consciousness and Dual Processing

Consciousness is being aware of yourself and your surroundings; it has multiple states — awake, asleep, dreaming. Cognitive neuroscience studies how brain activity connects to mental processes.

Thinking, knowing, remembering, and communicating happen on two levels at the same time: the conscious track is slow, deliberate, and step-by-step (like long division), while the unconscious track is fast, automatic, and effortless (like catching a ball).

- **Blindsight.** The eyes work but the part of the brain that makes you "aware" of seeing is damaged — a person responds to visual things without being consciously aware of them. Lawrence Weiskrantz walked a blindsight patient down a cluttered hallway; told it was empty, the patient had no idea obstacles existed — yet weaved around every one.
- **Parallel processing.** The brain handles many parts of a stimulus at once (recognizing a friend's face = color + shape + movement together).

- **Sequential processing.** Handling one part at a time, step by step — used for new or difficult problems.

## 3.2 Sleep and the Circadian Rhythm

Sleep is a natural, repeating loss of consciousness — NOT the same as a coma, general anesthesia (drugs that make you unconscious for surgery), or hibernation.

- **Circadian rhythm.** Your internal biological clock on a roughly 24-hour cycle ("about a day" in Latin), controlling sleep, body temperature, alertness, and hunger.
- **The master clock.** The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN): light → SCN decreases melatonin (the "sleepy hormone") → you wake up.

- **Desynchronization.** Internal clock vs. outside world out of sync (jet lag).

![The circadian rhythm over 24 hours: body temperature, alertness, and melatonin, set by the suprachiasmatic nucleus.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-05.png)

*Figure 5. The circadian rhythm over 24 hours: body temperature, alertness, and melatonin, set by the suprachiasmatic nucleus.*

## 3.3 The Stages of Sleep

Brain wave signatures follow a sequence: beta (alert) → alpha (relaxed) → theta (Stage 1) → delta (Stage 3 deep) → REM (rapid, irregular).

![Brain wave signatures: beta, alpha, theta, delta, and REM.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-06.png)

*Figure 6. Brain wave signatures: beta, alpha, theta, delta, and REM.*

| **Stage** | **Brain activity** | **Key facts** |
|---|---|---|
| Awake (relaxed) | Alpha waves — slow, big waves | Drowsy, calm |
| Awake (alert) | Beta waves — fast, small waves | Thinking, focused |
| NREM-1 | Theta waves | Hallucinations (seeing/hearing things that aren't there); hypnagogic sensations = hallucinations right as you fall asleep (the falling feeling) |
| NREM-2 | Sleep spindles (short bursts of fast brain activity) | Spindles help process and store memories |
| NREM-3 (deep) | Delta waves — large, slow waves | Hardest to wake; the body restores itself |
| REM | Rapid, irregular waves (like Stage 1) BUT heart rate rises, breathing fast & irregular | Dreams happen here; paradoxical sleep (brain active, body paralyzed); REM rebound = extra REM after deprivation |

Across a night of sleep, deep sleep dominates early and REM periods grow longer toward morning.

![A night of sleep in young vs. older adults: deep sleep early, lengthening REM periods toward morning.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-07.png)

*Figure 7. A night of sleep in young vs. older adults: deep sleep early, lengthening REM periods toward morning.*

## 3.4 Why We Sleep

Six reasons: (1) protects — kept ancestors safe from nighttime dangers; (2) restores — repairs body and brain; (3) consolidates memory — files away what you learned; (4) feeds creative thinking — the brain connects ideas; (5) supports growth — growth hormone is released; (6) conserves energy.

Sleep deprivation causes: fatigue, irritability, poor concentration, weak memory, depression, obesity, joint inflammation, slowed performance, and a weakened immune system.

## 3.5 Sleep Disorders

- **Insomnia (in- = not; somnus = sleep).** Trouble falling or staying asleep.
- **Narcolepsy (narco = sleep).** Sudden, uncontrollable sleep attacks during the day.

- **Sleep apnea (apnea = "no breathing").** Repeatedly stopping breathing during sleep.

## 3.6 Why Do We Dream? (Four Theories)

- **1. Information processing.** Dreams sort and file memories.
- **2. Physiological function.** Dreams exercise brain circuits.

- **3. Neural activation.** Random brain firing turned into stories.
- **4. Cognitive development.** Dreaming helps the brain develop.

markdown:
# S1M-4 Module 1.6: Sensation

## Module 1.6: Sensation

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 4.1 Foundations

- **Sensation.** Detecting raw information from the environment (light, sound, pressure).
- **Sensory receptor.** A cell that detects a specific type of energy (light, sound waves, chemicals).

- **Transduction (trans- = across; ducere = to lead).** Converting sensory energy into neural signals the brain can read. Three steps: receive → transform → deliver.
- **Bottom-up processing.** The brain builds perception from raw sensory data, starting with the senses.

- **Top-down processing.** Interpreting sensations using expectations and memory, starting with what you already know.
- **Psychophysics.** The study of how physical stimuli relate to what we mentally experience.

## 4.2 Thresholds and Key Terms

| **Concept** | **Meaning** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute threshold | Smallest amount of a stimulus you can detect 50% of the time | A candle flame seen 30 miles away on a dark night |
| Difference threshold (JND) | Smallest difference between two stimuli you can detect | Noticing your phone got slightly heavier with a new case |
| Weber's Law | JND is a constant percentage of the original stimulus | +1 candle is obvious with 10 candles, invisible with 100 |
| Signal detection theory | Detection depends on signal strength AND your expectations/alertness | A sleepy parent hears the baby; a partygoer doesn't |
| Subliminal | Too weak for conscious awareness | An image flashed too briefly to "see" |
| Sensory adaptation | Receptors get used to a constant stimulus — you stop noticing it | You stop smelling your own house |

![Weber's Law: the just-noticeable difference grows in constant proportion to the stimulus.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-08.png)

*Figure 8. Weber's Law: the just-noticeable difference grows in constant proportion to the stimulus.*

## 4.3 Vision

Light is energy. Wavelength determines hue (the color you see); amplitude determines intensity (brightness).

Light path through the eye: cornea → pupil → lens → retina → optic nerve. The lens changes shape to focus (accommodation).

![Anatomy of the eye: cornea, pupil, iris, lens, retina, fovea, blind spot, and optic nerve.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-09.png)

*Figure 9. Anatomy of the eye: cornea, pupil, iris, lens, retina, fovea, blind spot, and optic nerve.*

|  | **Rods** | **Cones** |
|---|---|---|
| Detect | Black/white, dim light | Color and fine detail |
| Where | Edges of the retina | Clustered at the fovea (center) |
| Signal path | Photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells → optic nerve | Same; fibers cross at the optic chiasm |

![Retinal processing: light triggers rods and cones, which activate bipolar cells, then ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-10.png)

*Figure 10. Retinal processing: light triggers rods and cones, which activate bipolar cells, then ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.*

- **Blind spot.** Where the optic nerve exits — no receptors there, so you can't see it (your brain paints over it).
- **Trichromatic theory (tri = three).** Three cone types (red, green, blue) mix to make all colors.

- **Opponent-process theory.** Cells work in opposing pairs (red vs. green, blue vs. yellow) — explains afterimages.

Both color theories are correct: they describe different stages of processing.

![Trichromatic theory (three cone types mix) vs. opponent-process theory (opposing cell pairs).](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-11.png)

*Figure 11. Trichromatic theory (three cone types mix) vs. opponent-process theory (opposing cell pairs).*

- **Feature detectors.** Brain cells that fire only for specific features (edges, lines, movement); the brain combines them with parallel processing.

## 4.4 Audition (Hearing)

Frequency (waves per second) determines pitch (how high or low); amplitude determines loudness, measured in decibels (dB).

![Frequency → pitch; amplitude → loudness.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-12.png)

*Figure 12. Frequency → pitch; amplitude → loudness.*

Sound path: pinna → eardrum → hammer/anvil/stirrup → oval window → cochlea → hair cells bend → auditory nerve.

![Anatomy of the ear: outer, middle (ossicles), and inner ear (cochlea, hair cells, auditory nerve).](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-13.png)

*Figure 13. Anatomy of the ear: outer, middle (ossicles), and inner ear (cochlea, hair cells, auditory nerve).*

| **Conductive hearing loss** | **Sensorineural hearing loss** |
|---|---|
| Problem in the mechanical parts (eardrum, ossicles) — sound can't get through | Damage to the cochlea or auditory nerve — the signal never becomes neural (loud noise kills hair cells; causes tinnitus) |

- **Place theory.** Explains high pitches — different spots on the basilar membrane vibrate.
- **Frequency theory.** Explains low pitches — hair cells fire at the same rate as the wave.

- **Loudness.** How many hair cells fire.
- **Stereophonic hearing (stereo = 3D).** Comparing the ears to locate sound.

Decibels are logarithmic: each +10 dB is roughly 10× the intensity.

![The decibel scale is logarithmic: each +10 dB represents a tenfold increase in intensity.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-14.png)

*Figure 14. The decibel scale is logarithmic: each +10 dB represents a tenfold increase in intensity.*

## 4.5 Touch and Pain

Skin detects pressure, warmth, cold, and pain — with separate receptors for each. Nociceptors (noci = harm) are pain receptors.

- **Gate-control theory.** Rubbing an injury floods the spinal "gate" with touch signals, so the pain signal is blocked. Endorphins are the body's own painkillers.
- **Phantom limb sensation.** Feeling an itch or pain in a missing limb — the brain generates the feeling.

- **Tinnitus.** Ringing in the ears with no external sound.

Pain can be controlled by placebos (fake treatments that work because you believe), distraction, and social/cultural factors — pain is part perception.

![Gate-control theory: touch signals (rubbing) close the spinal gate on pain signals; endorphins also close the gate.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-15.png)

*Figure 15. Gate-control theory: touch signals (rubbing) close the spinal gate on pain signals; endorphins also close the gate.*

## 4.6 Taste and Smell

| **Taste (gustation)** | **Smell (olfaction)** |
|---|---|
| 6 basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami (savory), oleogustus (fatty) | Path: odor → receptor cells in the olfactory membrane → olfactory bulb → olfactory nerve → brain |
| Taster types: supertasters (many taste buds — find veggies bitter), medium, non-tasters | The only sense that skips the thalamus — it goes straight to emotion & memory areas (why smells trigger vivid memories) |
|  | Pheromones = airborne chemical signals between members of a species |

## 4.7 Body Senses and Interaction

| **Sense** | **What it is** | **Receptor** |
|---|---|---|
| Kinesthesis (kine = movement) | Knowing where body parts are without looking | Proprioceptors in joints, tendons, muscles |
| Vestibular sense | Balance and head position | Semicircular canals + vestibular sacs (fluid in the inner ear) |

- **Sensory interaction.** Senses influence each other. McGurk effect: watch lips say "ga" while hearing "ba" → you hear "da".
- **Embodied cognition.** The body influences the mind: sit on a hard chair → judge criminals as "hard on crime."

- **Synesthesia (syn = together).** Senses cross-wired — some people see music as colors or taste words.

# S1M-5 Module 2.1: Perception

## Module 2.1: Perception

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 5.1 Attention

Perception is the brain organizing and interpreting sensory information. Attention selects what gets processed.

- **Selective attention.** Focusing on one thing while ignoring everything else.
- **Cocktail party effect.** Tuning out a noisy room but instantly hearing your name.

- **Inattentional blindness.** Missing something obvious because attention is elsewhere (the invisible gorilla experiment).
- **Change blindness.** Failing to notice a change in a scene (the person you're talking to gets swapped).

- **Perceptual set.** Expectations shape what you perceive (top-down) — expect danger, and a stick looks like a snake.

## 5.2 Gestalt Organization

Gestalt (German for "shape/form") means the whole is more than the sum of its parts — the brain auto-organizes what it sees.

Grouping principles: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity.

- **Figure-ground.** Separating the object (figure) from the background (ground) — the vase/faces illusion.

![Gestalt grouping principles: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-16.png)

*Figure 16. Gestalt grouping principles: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity.*

## 5.3 Depth Perception

Depth perception is seeing in 3D. The visual cliff experiment showed babies avoid the "deep" side of a glass table — depth perception is partly innate.

- **Binocular cues (need both eyes).** Retinal disparity & convergence.

![Binocular cues: retinal disparity (near objects produce a bigger difference between the two eyes' images) and convergence (eyes angle inward for near objects).](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-17.png)

*Figure 17. Binocular cues: retinal disparity (near objects produce a bigger difference between the two eyes' images) and convergence (eyes angle inward for near objects).*

- **Monocular cues (one eye is enough).** Linear perspective, interposition, texture gradient.

![Monocular depth cues: relative clarity, relative size, texture gradient, linear perspective, and interposition.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-18.png)

*Figure 18. Monocular depth cues: relative clarity, relative size, texture gradient, linear perspective, and interposition.*

## 5.4 Motion Perception

| **Illusion** | **What tricks you** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| Stroboscopic movement | Rapid still frames read as motion | Movies, animation (24 frames/sec) |
| Phi phenomenon | Lights blinking in sequence = one light moving | Neon signs, runway lights |
| Autokinetic effect | A stationary dot in the dark appears to drift | Staring at a single star |

## 5.5 Perceptual Constancy

Perceptual constancy means perceiving objects as stable even as the raw image changes.

- **Color/brightness constancy.** White looks white in sun or candlelight, judged by relative luminance (light reflected compared to surroundings).
- **Shape constancy.** A door still looks rectangular when its image is a trapezoid.

- **Size constancy.** Friends don't shrink as they walk away.

The moon illusion: the horizon moon and the overhead moon have the same retinal size, but context cues near the horizon trick size constancy.

![The moon illusion: context cues near the horizon make the moon look huge; it is the same size overhead.](/media/pa-guides/ap-psychology/s1m-fig-19.png)

*Figure 19. The moon illusion: context cues near the horizon make the moon look huge; it is the same size overhead.*

## 5.6 Critical Period and Perceptual Adaptation

- **Critical period.** An early window when the brain must receive sensory input or perception never develops properly (restored-vision adults can't learn to see faces well).
- **Perceptual adaptation.** The brain adjusts to changed input (upside-down goggles start looking normal after days).

Bottom line: your brain CONSTRUCTS your perceptions.

# S1M-6 Module 2.2: Thinking, Problem-Solving, and Creativity

## Module 2.2: Thinking, Problem-Solving, and Creativity

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 6.1 Concepts and Schemas

- **Concept.** A mental category of similar things ("bird," "furniture").
- **Prototype.** The most typical example of a concept (a robin is a better "bird" than a penguin).

- **Schema.** A mental framework that organizes knowledge.
- **Assimilate.** Fit new info into an existing schema (wolf → "big dog!").

- **Accommodate.** Change the schema itself (learning wolves are their own category).
- **Metacognition (meta = about).** Thinking about your own thinking.

## 6.2 Creativity

Creativity produces ideas that are both new and valuable.

| **Convergent thinking** | **Divergent thinking** |
|---|---|
| Narrows to one correct answer (standard tests) | Expands to many possible answers ("uses for a brick?") |

Five components of creativity: Expertise, Imaginative thinking, a Venturesome personality, Intrinsic motivation (doing it for its own sake), and a creative Environment. Mnemonic: "Every Idea Ventures If Encouraged."

Obstacles: fixation (getting stuck on one approach) and functional fixedness (only seeing an object's usual use — the candle box as a shelf).

## 6.3 Problem-Solving

| **Strategy** | **How it works** | **Trade-off** |
|---|---|---|
| Algorithm | Step-by-step rule that guarantees the answer | Slow but certain |
| Heuristic | Mental shortcut, rule of thumb | Fast but can mislead |
| Executive functions | The brain's "CEO" — planning, focusing, switching | Fatigues without sleep |
| Insight | Sudden "Aha!" — the answer clicks at once | Can't be forced |

Classic insight puzzle: connect 9 dots with 4 straight lines — impossible until the lines go outside the box ("think outside the box").

## 6.4 Decision Traps

| **Bias** | **Definition** | **Everyday example** |
|---|---|---|
| Confirmation bias | Seek only evidence that supports your belief | Only reading news that agrees with you |
| Mental set | Solve problems the same old way | Restarting the router the same way every time |
| Representativeness heuristic | Judge by stereotypes, ignoring real odds | "Poetry lover = librarian" (salespeople vastly outnumber librarians) |
| Availability heuristic | Judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind | Fearing planes after one crash story |
| Overconfidence | Overestimate how right you are | "I'm 99% sure I'll finish Friday" |
| Belief perseverance | Cling to beliefs even after they're disproven | Still believing a debunked rumor |
| Framing | Same facts, different wording → different choice | "90% survival" vs "10% mortality" |
| Anchoring bias | First number heard skews your estimate | "Was Gandhi older than 114?" — guess creeps up |

In short: heuristics make us fast; biases make us wrong.

# S1M-7 Exam Pitfalls and Rapid Self-Check

## Exam Pitfalls and Rapid Self-Check

> From the AP Psychology Midterm review guide. Range: Unit 0 (Research Methods), Unit 1 (Biological Bases of Behavior), Modules 1.5 Consciousness & Sleep, 1.6 Sensation, 2.1 Perception, 2.2 Thinking, Problem-Solving & Creativity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## Appendix A — Consolidated Exam Pitfalls

The traps below are the ones most likely to cost points. Each is phrased the way you should remember it for the exam.

| **Topic** | **The trap** |
|---|---|
| Random sampling | Write "equal chance," not just "random". |
| Correlation coefficient | Sign = direction only, NOT the slope (range −1.00 to +1.00). |
| Illusory correlation | Not the same as lurking variables or "correlation ≠ causation" — three separate concepts. |
| p-value | p < 0.05 AND p = 0.05 both mean "no difference" in AP Psychology. |
| Significance | Statistical ≠ practical significance — add effect size. |
| Skew | Look at the TAIL; the mean is highest in positive (right) skew. |
| Nervous system terms | CNS = tracts & nuclei; PNS = nerves & ganglia. |
| Myelin | CNS myelin = glial cell (oligodendrocyte), NOT Schwann cell. |
| Neurotransmitters | They BIND receptors — they do NOT enter the post-synaptic neuron. |
| Adrenaline | In a question, adrenaline/noradrenaline = the HORMONE; norepinephrine = neurotransmitter. |
| Brainstem | Medulla + pons + midbrain. |
| Cortex vs. cerebrum | Cortex = outer layer OF the cerebrum; cerebrum = the whole structure. |
| "50% genetic" | Refers to individual differences, not your trait. |
| Bimodal | Two peaks (textbook concept, may not be covered in class). |
| Standard deviation | AVERAGE distance of all data points from the mean. |
| Reliability | Consistently replicated — memorize it; the name misleads. |
| Consent | Informed consent → informed ASSENT for minors. |
| MDMA | Appears under BOTH stimulants and hallucinogens. |

## Appendix B — Rapid Self-Check

| **Question** | **Answer** |
|---|---|
| Stage with sleep spindles? | NREM-2 |
| Sense that skips the thalamus? | Smell |
| "Gorilla" experiment? | Inattentional blindness |
| Weber's Law = constant ____? | percentage |
| Sudden "Aha!"? | Insight |
| Updating a schema itself? | Accommodation |
| Blindsight patient walking the hallway? | Eyes work, awareness blind (dual processing) |
| Brain wave of deep sleep? | Delta |
| Extra REM after deprivation? | REM rebound |
| Rubbing an injury hurts less? | Gate-control theory |
| Seeing a green after-image? | Opponent-process theory |
| High pitches? Low pitches? | Place theory · Frequency theory |
| Lights blinking in sequence? | Phi phenomenon |
| Movies / animation? | Stroboscopic movement |
| Range of the correlation coefficient? | −1.00 to +1.00 |

# 8.1 Setting the Stage for the Cold War and Decolonisation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

*Governance.*

## Technological gains of the victorious allies

The **United States and the USSR** were the most important Allied powers.
Wartime government investment produced advances that all had **post-war
application and benefits**:

- **Nuclear energy** — the US created the atomic bomb in **1945**, the USSR in **1949**
- **Computing** — for example Colossus in the United Kingdom
- **Jet propulsion and rocketry**

## Economic gains

**The United States.** Significant government investment in wartime
manufacturing, the **arsenal of democracy**, expanded industrial capacity during
the war. The United States ended it as **50% of global GDP**.

**The USSR.** Despite a **10% population loss**, the five-year plans of
**1928–1941** and wartime industrial expansion, together with an **expansion of
resources and territory** through control of eastern Europe and eastern Germany.

The contrast matters for everything that follows: both powers emerged stronger
than they began, while the states between them did not.

## Shifts in the global power structure

The **destructiveness of the Second World War** exceeded that of the First. Japan
and Germany were in ruins, and there was widespread devastation in France, Britain
and other European nations.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Arsenal of democracy** | The US wartime manufacturing effort that expanded its industrial capacity |
| **Five-year plans** | The Soviet economic programmes of 1928–1941 |
