# 13.2 Ribosomes and Protein Synthesis

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Translation

**Translation** **makes a polypeptide chain using the genetic code on the mRNA**. It
is carried out **by the ribosome, in the cytoplasm**.

## Proteins

A **polypeptide** is a **long chain of amino acids**, containing a combination of
**only 20 amino acids**. The **sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide determines
the properties, shape and function of the protein** — which is why translating the
mRNA in the right order matters so much, and why changing a single amino acid can
change what the protein does.

Proteins have **four levels of organisation**:

| Level | What it is |
|---|---|
| **1** | The **sequence** of amino acids in the chain |
| **2** | The **folding or coiling** of the chain |
| **3** | The complete **3D arrangement** — held by ionic bonds, covalent bonds, van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds |
| **4** | **More than one chain** together |

## The genetic code

A **codon** is **three consecutive nucleotide bases on the mRNA** — a triplet — and it
**codes for a single amino acid**.

- **Start codon:** **AUG**, which codes for **methionine**
- **Stop codons:** **UAA**, **UAG**, **UGA**

Some amino acids are **universal** and **can be coded for by more than one codon**.

## The steps of translation

**1. mRNA.** The mRNA is **transcribed in the nucleus and enters the cytoplasm**, and
the **ribosome attaches to the mRNA in the cytoplasm**.

**2. tRNA.** **Translation begins at the start codon, AUG.** **tRNA brings the proper
amino acids into the ribosome**, and the **ribosome attaches those amino acids to the
growing chain**.

**3. The polypeptide "assembly line".** The **bond between an amino acid and its RNA
is unbound**, the **amino acids are joined together by peptide bonds**, and the
**ribosome moves along, binding new tRNA and amino acids**.

**4. Completing the polypeptide.** The ribosome comes to a **stop codon (UAA, UAG or
UGA)** and **releases the newly formed polypeptide and the mRNA**. **Translation
ends.**

## The role of rRNA

The rRNA in the ribosome **helps hold the ribosomal proteins in place** and **helps
locate the beginning of the mRNA message**, and it **may even carry out the chemical
reaction that joins the amino acids together**.

## The molecular basis of heredity

The **central dogma of molecular biology** is that **genetic information is
transferred from DNA to RNA to protein**.

**Genes contain the instructions for making proteins**, and proteins are what a cell
actually runs on:

- **Enzymes catalyse and regulate chemical reactions**
- Proteins **build and operate living cells**

This is what ties the whole unit together. DNA is the store, RNA is the working copy,
protein is the product — and because protein does the work of the cell, a change
anywhere along that path shows up as a change in the organism.

## Worked examples

**Transcribe the DNA template 3′-TAC GTA CTT GCA-5′ into mRNA and translate it,
given AUG = methionine, CAU = histidine, GAA = glutamic acid, CGU = arginine.**

Transcription matches opposite bases, with **U in place of T**:

| DNA template | 3′- | TAC | GTA | CTT | GCA | -5′ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **mRNA** | 5′- | **AUG** | **CAU** | **GAA** | **CGU** | -3′ |
| **Amino acid** | | Methionine | Histidine | Glutamic acid | Arginine | |

The chain is **methionine – histidine – glutamic acid – arginine**. Note that it opens
with AUG, the start codon, which is where translation begins.

**Which mRNA codon does a tRNA with the anticodon AUU pair with?**
**None.** Matching opposite bases gives UAA, and UAA is a **stop codon** — it codes
for no amino acid, so no tRNA carries one for it. The other options can be ruled out
faster still: ATG contains thymine, which does not occur in mRNA.

**How do retroviruses violate the central dogma?**
By going **RNA → DNA**, the reverse of the DNA → RNA step the central dogma sets out.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Translation** | Making a polypeptide chain using the genetic code on mRNA, carried out by the ribosome in the cytoplasm |
| **Polypeptide** | A long chain of amino acids, containing a combination of only 20 amino acids |
| **Codon** | Three consecutive nucleotide bases on mRNA, coding for a single amino acid |
| **Start codon** | AUG, which codes for methionine and is where translation begins |
| **Stop codon** | UAA, UAG or UGA, at which the polypeptide and mRNA are released and translation ends |
| **Peptide bond** | The bond by which amino acids are joined together in the growing chain |
| **Central dogma of molecular biology** | Genetic information is transferred from DNA to RNA to protein |

# 13.3 Mutations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Mutations and mutagens

**Mutations** are **heritable changes in genetic information**. Because they are
heritable, they are changes to the DNA itself rather than damage to a protein — the
alteration is copied on to every descendant cell.

**Mutagens** are **chemical or physical agents in the environment that cause
mutations**: **pesticides, tobacco smoke, pollutants, X-rays and UV light**.

## The two types

| Type | Scale of the change |
|---|---|
| **Gene mutation** | Changes in **one gene** |
| **Chromosomal mutation** | Changes in a **whole chromosome** |

## Gene mutations

A **point mutation** is a **change in one nucleotide**, and there are three kinds:

1. **Single base substitution** — one nucleotide base is **replaced** with another
2. **Single base insertion** — one nucleotide base is **added**
3. **Single base deletion** — one nucleotide is **removed**

Their consequences are not equally serious, and the reason is the triplet code.

- A **single base substitution affects no more than one amino acid.** Changing one
  base changes at most the one codon it sits in, so the rest of the chain is read
  exactly as before.
- A **single base insertion or deletion is more dramatic**: it **changes every amino
  acid following the mutation point**. Adding or removing a base shifts where every
  subsequent triplet begins, so the **altered protein is unable to perform its normal
  functions**. This is the case the practice set calls a **frameshift**.

The practice set also names two kinds of substitution by their effect on the protein:

| Name | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Missense** | The substituted base changes one amino acid into a different one |
| **Nonsense** | The substituted base creates a **stop codon**, cutting the chain short and leaving a **non-functional protein** |

## Chromosomal mutations

### Changes of structure

| Mutation | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Duplication** | Produces **extra copies** of parts of a chromosome |
| **Inversion** | **Reverses the direction** of part of a chromosome |
| **Translocation** | Part of a chromosome **breaks off and attaches to another** |
| **Deletion** | **Loss of part or all** of a chromosome |

### Changes of number

**Aneuploidy** is having **one fewer or one extra chromosome (2n + 1, 2n − 1)**.
**Down syndrome** is the example: **47 chromosomes**, **trisomy 21** — three copies of
chromosome 21.

**Polyploidy** is having **three or more sets of each type of chromosome** —
**triploid (3n)**, **tetraploid (4n)**. It arises when **chromosomes fail to separate
in meiosis**. **Polyploid plants are usually larger and stronger than diploid
plants.**

## The effects of mutations

**Many mutations are neutral** — they have **little or no effect on gene expression**,
which is to say on protein function.

**Beneficial mutations** **produce proteins with new activities useful to the
organism**. **Insects resisting pesticides** and **bacteria resisting antibiotics**
are the examples, and this is the reason mutation matters beyond disease: it is the
**source of the genetic variation** on which evolution works.

**Harmful mutations** include:

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **Progeria** | Causes children to age quickly |
| **Sickle cell disease** | A **point mutation** |
| **Marfan syndrome** | |
| **Albinism** | |
| **Red-green colour blindness** | |
| **Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)** | Causes the nerves that control muscle to stop working |

## Worked examples

**Sickle cell anaemia's Glu → Val mutation is which type?**
**Missense.** One amino acid has been replaced by another and the rest of the chain is
intact, which is the signature of a single base substitution — not a frameshift,
which would have altered every amino acid after the mutation point, and not a
nonsense mutation, which would have produced a stop codon instead of valine.

**A mutation changes the DNA of 3′-TAC GTA CTT GCA-5′ to 3′-TAC GTA CTT CCA-5′.
Identify the mutation type and compare the original and mutated amino acid
sequences.**
The mutation type is a **substitution** — one base has been swapped, with none added
or removed. Only the **fourth codon** is affected: the first three amino acids stay
**methionine – histidine – glutamic acid**, and the fourth changes from **arginine
(CGU)** to **proline (CCA)**. The answer key reads the mutated codon CCA straight off
the DNA strand rather than transcribing it as part (a) does, but either way the
examinable point holds: one substituted base changes one amino acid and leaves the
rest of the chain untouched.

**How does a translocation cause chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML)?**
By **activating a gene that drives uncontrolled cell division**. The chromosome
material is moved rather than lost, so the damage comes from a gene switched on in
the wrong place, not from deletion.

**How does polyploidy benefit plants, and how does its impact differ in animals?**
In **plants** it is **beneficial** — polyploid plants are **larger and stronger**. In
**animals** it is **lethal**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Mutation** | A heritable change in genetic information |
| **Mutagen** | A chemical or physical agent in the environment that causes mutations |
| **Gene mutation** | A change in one gene |
| **Chromosomal mutation** | A change in a whole chromosome |
| **Point mutation** | A change in one nucleotide |
| **Single base substitution** | One nucleotide base replaced with another; affects no more than one amino acid |
| **Single base insertion** | One nucleotide base added |
| **Single base deletion** | One nucleotide removed |
| **Frameshift** | An insertion or deletion that changes every amino acid following the mutation point |
| **Missense mutation** | A substitution that changes one amino acid into a different one |
| **Nonsense mutation** | A substitution that creates a stop codon, giving a non-functional protein |
| **Duplication** | A chromosomal mutation producing extra copies of parts of a chromosome |
| **Inversion** | A chromosomal mutation reversing the direction of part of a chromosome |
| **Translocation** | A chromosomal mutation in which part of a chromosome breaks off and attaches to another |
| **Deletion (chromosomal)** | Loss of part or all of a chromosome |
| **Aneuploidy** | Having one fewer or one extra chromosome (2n + 1, 2n − 1) |
| **Trisomy 21** | Down syndrome: 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21 |
| **Polyploidy** | Having three or more sets of each type of chromosome, such as triploid (3n) or tetraploid (4n), arising when chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis |
| **Neutral mutation** | A mutation with little or no effect on gene expression |
| **Beneficial mutation** | A mutation producing proteins with new activities useful to the organism, and a source of genetic variation |

title: Gene Regulation and Expression
summary: In prokaryotes, DNA binding proteins regulate genes by controlling transcription — the switch is thrown before any RNA is made at all. The genes themselves are organised into operons: groups of genes
markdown:
# 13.4 Gene Regulation and Expression

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Prokaryotic gene regulation

In prokaryotes, **DNA binding proteins regulate genes by controlling transcription**
— the switch is thrown before any RNA is made at all.

The genes themselves are organised into **operons**: **groups of genes that are
regulated together**. The example is the **lac operon in *E. coli***, which
**contains three lactose genes**. Those three genes **need to be expressed together**
so that the proteins they code for are all present and the bacterium can **digest
lactose as food** — there is no use in producing one enzyme of a pathway without the
others, which is precisely why they share a single switch.

### Operon structure

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Promoter** | The **RNA polymerase binding site** |
| **Operator** | The **repressor protein binding site** |
| **Genes** | A **cluster of functionally related genes** — for instance the lactose metabolism genes in *E. coli* |

## Eukaryotic gene regulation

### RNA interference (RNAi)

The mechanism runs as follows:

1. **Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs / miRNAs) form hairpin loops.**
2. These are **diced by the Dicer enzyme into 20-base-pair fragments.**
3. The fragments **load into a silencing complex**, which **binds complementary
   mRNA** and **blocks translation or degrades the mRNA.**

Note where in the sequence this acts: the mRNA has already been transcribed, so RNAi
regulates a gene after the fact rather than at the promoter.

**Discovery (Fire and Mello, 1998).** **Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) injections caused
gene silencing** — the ***unc-22* gene in *C. elegans***, whose silencing made the
worms twitch. **Single-stranded RNA had no effect**, which is what identified
double-strandedness as the trigger.

**Significance.** RNAi is a **universal regulatory tool across life forms**, and it
has **medical potential**: **silencing viral or cancer genes** using RNAi technology.

## Cell specialisation and differentiation

**Differentiation** is the process by which **cells become specialised** — a liver
cell as against a nerve cell — **via selective gene expression**.

**The challenge this answers:** **all cells share identical DNA.** Since the
instruction set is the same everywhere, the difference between one cell type and
another cannot lie in the genes present; it is **regulation that enables the
diversity**.

## Genetic control of development

### Homeotic genes

**Homeotic genes** are **master switches determining body part identity** — whether a
fruit fly structure develops as a leg or as an antenna.

**When they mutate**, the result is **body part misplacement**: a leg growing from
the head.

### Homeobox and Hox genes

The **homeobox** is a **180-base-pair DNA sequence coding for transcription factors
that activate developmental genes**.

**Hox genes** are a **subgroup of homeobox genes**, **arranged in clusters** whose
**order correlates with the body axis, head to tail**. Their **role** is to **define
segment identity** — a Hox mutation alters the position of an organ.

**Evolutionary conservation:** **identical clusters appear in fruit flies, mice and
humans**, controlling, for example, limb and fin development.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Operon** | A group of genes that are regulated together |
| **lac operon** | The operon in *E. coli* containing three lactose genes, expressed together so the bacterium can digest lactose as food |
| **Promoter (operon)** | The RNA polymerase binding site |
| **Operator** | The repressor protein binding site |
| **RNA interference (RNAi)** | Regulation in which small RNAs are diced into fragments that load into a silencing complex and bind complementary mRNA, blocking translation or degrading the mRNA |
| **siRNA / miRNA** | Small interfering RNAs that form hairpin loops and are diced into 20-base-pair fragments |
| **Dicer** | The enzyme that dices small RNAs into 20-base-pair fragments |
| **Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)** | The form of RNA whose injection caused gene silencing in Fire and Mello's 1998 experiment; single-stranded RNA had no effect |
| **Differentiation** | Cells becoming specialised via selective gene expression |
| **Homeotic genes** | Master switches determining body part identity; mutation causes body part misplacement |
| **Homeobox** | A 180-base-pair DNA sequence coding for transcription factors that activate developmental genes |
| **Hox genes** | A subgroup of homeobox genes, arranged in clusters whose order correlates with the body axis from head to tail, defining segment identity |

# S1M-1 2.3 Carbon Compounds

## 2.3 Carbon Compounds

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Biology H review guide (PA). Writers: Tiffany Cheah, Elisa Lau. Editor: Chloe Yu. Range: mostly 7.1, 7.2, 7.3, 8.1, 8.2, 8.3; 1.3, 2.3, 2.4 may be tested a little. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

#### 1.3 Studying Life

Biology: The study of life

Big ideas in biology

- The cellular basis of life
- Information and heredity
- Matter and energy
- Growth, development, and reproduction
- Homeostasis
- Evolution
- Structure and function
- Unity and diversity of life
- Interdependence in nature
  - Biosphere: Living planet
- Science as a way of knowing

Fields of Biology

- Biotech
- Molecular bio
- Genetics
- Cellular bio
- Ecology

Science as a way of knowing

- Scientific method
- Measurement system
  - Metric system
    - Decimal system of measurement
    - Multiples of 10
    - Used by scientists
  - SI system

Characteristics of living things

- Made up of units called cells
  - Cells
    - Collection of living matter enclosed by a barrier
    - Smallest unit considered fully alive
    - Grow, respond, and reproduce
    - Complex, highly organized
  - Unicellular organisms
    - Only one cell
    - Ex: Bacteria, yeast
  - Multicellular organisms
    - Contain many cells
    - Ex: Plants, animals
- Reproduce
  - Sexual reproduction
    - Two parents
    - Unique offspring
  - Asexual reproduction
    - Single parent
    - Identical offspring
    - e.g. Binary fission
- Based on a universal genetic code
  - DNA
    - Carry directions of inheritance
    - Determine the inherited traits
- Grow & develop
  - Life cycle: Particular pattern of growth and change
  - Growth: Increase in size
  - Development: Cells increase in number and become different (Differentiate)
- Obtain and use materials & energy
  - Metabolism
    - Combination of chemical reactions
    - An organism builds up or breaks down materials
  - Photosynthesis
    - Autotrophs convert light energy into chemical energy
    - Chemical energy is stored in sugar
  - Heterotrophs
    - Eat autotrophs or other heterotrophs to obtain energy
  - Decomposers
    - Obtain energy from remains
- Respond to environment
  - Organisms respond to changes in their own ways
  - Stimulus
    - Signal to which an organism responds
- Maintain a stable internal environment
  - Homeostasis
    - The process by which organisms keep their internal conditions relatively stable
- Change over time (taken as a group)
  - Evolution
    - Populations change over time

The chemistry of Carbon

- Carbon Atom
  - Has 4 valence electrons → forms at most four covalent bonds
  - Bonds with other elements (HOPSN: H, O, P, S, N)
  - Bonds with other carbon atoms
    - Can form chains, rings, or complex structures
    - Can form single, double, or triple bonds
- Macromolecules
  - Giant molecules
  - Polymer = macromolecule made of repeating similar building blocks (monomers)
    - Formed by polymerization
  - Polymers in living things:
    - Synthesis → dehydration → releases H2O
    - Breakdown → hydrolysis → requires H2O
- Macromolecules in Living Things
  - Carbohydrates
    - Made of CHO in a ratio of 1:2:1
    - Monosaccharides = single sugar molecules (sugar monomers)
      - Glucose: main source of energy
      - Fructose: in fruit
      - Galactose: in milk and blood
    - Disaccharides = formed by 2 monosaccharides
      - Sucrose = glucose + fructose → common table sugar
      - Lactose = glucose + galactose → major sugar in milk
      - Maltose = glucose + glucose → product of starch digestion
    - Polysaccharides = many monosaccharides joined together
      - Function: store excess sugar
      - Glycogen (animals) → many glucose connected together
      - Starch (plants)
      - Function: structural support
      - Cellulose → plant cell wall
      - Chitin → fungal cell wall, arthropod exoskeleton
  - Lipids
    - Not soluble in water
    - Made mostly from C and H
    - Include fats, oils, waxes, steroids
    - Not polymers
    - Fats = glycerol molecule + fatty acids
      - Saturated fats
      - Only single bonds between carbons in fatty acids
      - Linear shape → easier to stack
      - Contain max possible number of H atoms (saturated)
      - Solid at room temperature (e.g., butter)
      - Unsaturated fats
      - At least one C=C double bond in fatty acid
      - Causes a bending shape
      - Liquid at room temperature (e.g., olive oil)
    - Functions:
      - Store energy
      - Parts of biological membranes and waterproof coverings
      - Chemical messengers
  - Nucleic Acids
    - Contain NCHOP
    - Monomer = nucleotide
    - Structure
      - 5-carbon sugar
      - Phosphate group
      - Nitrogen base
    - Nucleotides joined by covalent bonds → polynucleotides (nucleic acid)
    - Function: store and transmit genetic information
      - DNA code → transcription → RNA code → read by ribosome → translation → protein
    - DNA
      - Deoxyribonucleic acid
      - Sugar: deoxyribose (one fewer OH)
      - Bases: A, T, C, G
      - Double-stranded
    - RNA
      - Ribonucleic acid
      - Sugar: ribose (has an OH)
      - Bases: A, U, C, G
      - Single-stranded
  - Proteins
    - Contain NCHO, sometimes S
    - Monomer = amino acid
    - Structure
      - Central carbon
      - Hydrogen
      - Amino group (NH₂)
      - Carboxyl group (COOH)
      - R group → different for different amino acids
      - Some Functional groups:
      - methyl (CH₃)
      - hydroxyl (OH)
      - amino (NH₂/NH₃⁺)
      - carboxyl (COOH/COO⁻)
      - phosphate (PO₃⁻)
      - sulfhydryl (SH)
      - Chemical property of R group determines chemical property of amino acid
    - Formed by bonding amino group to carboxyl group
      - Bonded by covalent bond (peptide bond)
      - Dehydration occurs between carboxyl and amino groups
    - Functions:
      - Some control rate of reactions and regulate cell processes
      - Some form bones and muscles
      - Others transport substances or help fight disease
    - Four levels of organization
      - Primary structure: sequence of amino acids (linear chain)
      - Secondary structure: folding or coiling of polypeptide chain
      - Formed by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms (C, H, NH₂, COOH)
      - Easily broken by high temperature/pH change
      - Apha helix or Beta sheet
      - Tertiary structure: secondary structure itself coiled or folded
      - Precise 3D shape
      - Formed by all kinds of bonds between R groups
      - Quaternary structure: association of different polypeptide chains
      - Does not occur in all proteins

## 2.4 Chemical Reactions and Enzymes

Chemical Reactions

- A process that changes one set of chemicals into another set
- Reactants: elements or compounds that enter into a reaction
- Products: elements or compounds produced by a reaction
- Involve
  - Breaking of bonds in reactants
  - Formation of new bonds in products
- Energy in Reactions
  - Energy is released or absorbed whenever chemical bonds are formed or broken
  - Energy-releasing reactions
    - Occur spontaneously
  - Energy-absorbing reactions
    - Will not occur without an energy source
    - Energy source:
      - Autotroph: sunlight
      - Heterotroph: food
  - Use energy:
    - All life processes
    - Metabolism
  - Activation energy: energy needed to get a reaction started

Enzymes

- Act as biological catalysts
  - Speed up the chemical reaction
  - Reduce the activation energy
- Naming: part of name derived from catalyzed reaction, many end in -ase
- Most enzymes are proteins
- Process
  - Enzymes provide an active site for substrates to bond together and react
    - Substrates: reactants of enzyme-catalyzed reactions
  - Induced fit: shape of active site is changed slightly to accommodate the shape of substrates
  - Enzyme-substrate complex forms
    - Enzymes are specific → catalyze only one chemical reaction
    - Shape and charge of substrate must be compatible with the active site of the enzyme for catalyzing to occur
  - Products released
  - Enzyme is free again
- Regulation of Enzyme Activity
  - Temperature, pH, and regulator molecules can affect enzyme activity
  - Enzymes work better under optimal conditions
    - Different enzymes have different optimal conditions
  - Inhibitors can bind to enzymes and reduce enzyme activity
    - Competitive inhibition
      - Blocks the active site
      - Substrate cannot bind
    - Non-competitive inhibition
      - Binds to a location other than the active site → allosteric site
      - Enzyme shape changed → inactivated

markdown:
# S1M-2 7.1 Life is Cellular

## 7.1 Life is Cellular

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Biology H review guide (PA). Writers: Tiffany Cheah, Elisa Lau. Editor: Chloe Yu. Range: mostly 7.1, 7.2, 7.3, 8.1, 8.2, 8.3; 1.3, 2.3, 2.4 may be tested a little. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

Cell: The common structure that makes up living things.

Resolution: the shortest distance between two points that can be distinguished

Calculation of Magnification:

- Method 1: eyepiece lens x objective lens
- Method 2: size of image / actual size of specimen
- Method 3: measured length of scale bar (image) / actual value scale bar represents (real size units)

Microscopes: Produce magnified images of structures that are too small to see with the unaided eye.

**Light Microscope:**

- Use glass lenses to focus light and magnify an object
- Magnification < 1000x
- Compound light microscope has two lenses
- Scientists can use fluorescent dyes to show structures inside the cells

**Electron Microscopes:**

- Focus beams of electrons with magnetic fields instead of light
- Higher magnification (1 billionth of a meter in size)
- Samples are dried out (vacuumed)
- Therefore electron microscopes cannot view living cells; only dead, prepared specimens
- **Types of Electron Microscopes:**
- **Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM):**
- **Shine beams of electrons through thin slices of cells**
- **2D image**
- **Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM):**
- **Electrons scan back and forth through surface**
- **3D image**

**The Cell Theory Timeline:**

- Robert Hooke
- First to observe dead cells from a thin slice of cork (1665)

Defined “cell”

- Auton Van Leeuwenhoek
- First to observe living cells in a drop of water (1674)
- Matthias Schleiden
- Proposed that all plants are made of cells (1838)
- Theodor Schwann
- Proposed that all animals are made from cells (1839)
- Rudoff Virchow
- Proposed that all cells come from existing cells (1855)

**The Cell Theory**

- All living things are composed of cells
- Cells are the basic units of structure and function in living things
- New cells are produced from existing cells

**Prokaryotes vs. Eukaryotes**

Eukaryote: an organism whose cells contain a nucleus

- Contain nuclei, cell membrane & cytoplasm
- Contain membrane bound organelles
- Carry out all life activities inside specialized organelles
- e.g. plants, animals, protists, fungi…
- DNA associated with protein (chromosomes)

Prokaryote: a unicellular organism that lacks a nucleus

- Smaller & simpler than Eukaryotes
- DNA is circular, naked
- Have cell membrane & cytoplasm
- no internal membrane (membrane-bound organelles)
- carry out all life processes in one cell
- e.g. bacteria

## 7.2 Cell Structures

**Cell Organization:**

- Eukaryotic cell:
- Nucleus
- Cytoplasm
- Cell membrane
- …
- Prokaryotic cells:
- Cell wall
- Plasma membrane
- Cytoplasm
- Ribosomes
- Nucleoid (Region containing naked DNA)
- Some have flagella or pili (hair-like protection for attachment and conjugation)

**Nucleus:**

- Control cell processes and contain heredity information of DNA
- Coded instruction to make protein and other molecules
- Chromatin:
- Material of eukaryotic chromosomes (coiled condensed to form chromosomes)
- DNA bound to histone proteins
- Chromosomes:
- Condense chromatin during cell division
- Distinct threadlike structures visible under a microscope
- Carry genetic information
- Nucleolus – small dense region in nucleus where the assembly of ribosomes begins
- Nuclear Envelope – double membrane surrounding the nucleus; nuclear pores allow materials to move through, such as RNA and other molecules

**Vacuoles:**

- Saclike, membrane enclosed structure to store water, salts, proteins, carbohydrates, etc.
- Plants:
- Large central vacuole
- Can support heavy structures such as leaves & flowers
- Can be found in some unicellular organisms
- e.g. contractile vacuole that pumps excess water out of cell

**Vesicles:**

- Smaller vacuoles involve in storing and transporting substances between organelles/ to and from the outside of the cell
- Nealy all eukaryotic cells have vesicles

**Lysosomes:**

- Small organelles filled with enzymes
- Break down food materials
- Break down outlived organelles
- Removing “junk” that might otherwise pile up in the cell

**Cytoskeleton:**

- Prefix “cyto-” means cell
- Network of protein filaments
- Help cell maintain shape
- Facilitate cell movement

e.g.:

Microfilament

- Long fibers made of actin
- Movement & support

Microtubules

- Hollow tubes made of tubulin
- Maintain cell shape
- Tracks that organelles are moved along
- Help separate chromosomes during cell division

Centrioles

  - Found in pairs
  - Organize microtubules
  - Play a key role in cell division
  - Only in animal cell

Cilia & Flagella

  - Hair-like projections formed from cell surface
  - Produce force to help move
  - “9+2” microtubules structure
- Functions: structure & support/ intracellular transport/ contractility & motility/ spatial organization

**Ribosomes:**

- Small particles made of RNA & proteins
- Make protein according to instructions from nucleus

**Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER):**

- Rough ER
- Has bound ribosomes on the surface
- Modify proteins made by ribosomes (membrane proteins/ secretory proteins)
- Receive proteins from ribosomes
- Some proteins made on the rough ER will leave the cell; others are membrane proteins and proteins that go to lysosomes and other specialized locations inside the cell
- Smooth ER
- No ribosomes on surface
- Synthesis of lipids & detoxification

**Golgi Apparatus/ Golgi Body:**

- Stacks of membrane to modify, sort, package protein & other materials
- Pathway of proteins: Ribosomes -> rough ER -> vesicle -> Golgi Body -> vesicle -> destination

**Chloroplasts:**

- Exist in plants
- Use solar energy to make energy-rich food molecules by photosynthesis
- 2 envelope membranes
- Large stacks of photosynthetic membranes containing chlorophyll

**Mitochondria:**

- Use chemical energy from food to make high-energy compounds (ATP)
- 2 envelope membranes
- Inner membrane is much larger than the outer one
- Inner membrane is highly folded to increase surface area (more enzymes can react)
- In nearly all eukaryotic cells

**Organelle DNA:**

- Chloroplast & mitochondria contain DNA
- Mitochondria DNA inherited from cytoplasm of ovum (egg)
- Mitochondria come from mother
- Circular strand DNA
- In mitochondria
- Similar in those in prokaryotes
- Evidence for endosymbiotic theory

**Cell Wall:**

- Plants, algae, fungi, most prokaryotes
- Not in animal cells
- Lie outside the cell membrane
- Porous: allow substances pass through
- Provide support & protection
- Made from fibers of carbohydrates & protein
- Plant cell wall (made of mainly cellulose)
- Fungus cell wall (made of mainly chitin)
- Bacteria cell wall (made of peptidoglycan)

**Cell Membrane:**

- Boundary of cell
- Regulate what enters and leaves the cell
- Provide protection & support
- Structure: fluid mosaic model
- Selectively permeable
- Only some substances can pass through
- Structure: Phospholipid bilayer
- Form barrier between cell and surroundings
- Lipids are large molecules made mostly from carbon and hydrogen atoms
- Composed of a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail
- Compose of 1 glycerol + 2 fatty acid + 1 phosphate group
- Tail (Fatty acid portion): hydrophobic
- Head (glycerol with phosphate): hydrophilic
- In water, fatty acid tails cluster together to form bilayers
- Membrane proteins:
- Provide many functions
- Integral proteins embedded in membrane:
- Cytoplasmic/extracellular side: hydrophilic
- Cone: hydrophobic
- Typically, transmembrane
- Peripheral protein
- Most attached to surface of integral proteins
- Carbohydrates
- Attached to some membrane proteins
- Cell-to-cell identification
- Cholesterol (only in animal cells)
- Located in the hydrophobic region (fatty acid tails)
- Regulate membrane fluidity

## 7.3 Cell Transport

- Solution (e.g. cytoplasm)
- Liquid mixture of at least 2 substances
- Solute dissolve in solvent
- Concentration
- Mass/volume
- Mole/liter

**Types of Cell Transport:**

**Passive Transport:** Does not require energy (ATP)

- **Diffusion**
- Molecules tend to move from high concentration to lower concentration (reach equilibrium)
- Equilibrium
- Concentration on both side is the same
- No further change in concentration
- Solutes continue to move in both directions in equal numbers (no net movement)
- Substances move across membrane
- e.g. carbon dioxide, oxygen can be carried by diffusion
- properties of these substances include:
- non-polar
- small (so they can directly cross the membrane)
- Factors that influence the rate of reaction:
- Temperature (higher temperature means faster rate)
- Concentration Difference (greater concentration difference, faster rate)
- **Facilitated Diffusion**
- Movement of specific molecules across cell membrane through transport proteins
- From high to low concentration
- e.g. water, glucose
- property: polar, large
- Channel protein
- shape will not be changed
- Carrier protein
- Shape will change
- Factors that influence the rate of reaction:
- Temperature (if temperature is too high, the proteins will be distorted and stop working)
- Concentration difference
- The number of specific carrier or channel proteins in membrane
- **Osmosis**
- Involve only the diffusion of H2O access a selectively permeable membrane
- Selectively permeable membrane
- Only some substances can pass through
- Biological membranes
- Aquaporins
- Many cells contain water channel proteins named aquaporins
- allow water to pass faster through cell membrane
- water moves from high water concentration to low water concentration
- water moves from low solute concentration to high solute concentration to dilute the concentrated solution
- water moves from more free water to less free water
- Isotonic solution:
- Concentration of water & solute are the same both sides
- Hypertonic solution:
- High concentration of solute
- Cell shrinks
- Hypotonic solution:
- Lower concentration of solute
- Cell swells
- Water moves from hypotonic solution to hypertonic solution
- Osmotic Pressure
- It is the pressure exerted by osmosis on the hypertonic side of selectively permeable membrane (force produced by the difference in concentration)
- The pressure can cause the movement of water out of or into a cell through osmosis
- Osmotic pressure can cause cell in hypotonic solution to swell and eventually burst
- Plants & Bacteria have cell wall to prevent cells from expanding
- Contractile vacuole: will excrete excess water to prevent bursting

**Active Transport:** Requires energy (ATP)

Two forms:

- Protein pump:
- Moves materials against a concentration difference (from low to high concentration)
- e.g. Sodium ion and potassium ion pump
- use to maintain the resting potential
- 3 Na+ moving out of the cell and 2 K+ in
- Cause electrical concentration difference
- Bulk Transport:
- Transport larger molecules or a large number of molecules/ions by movements of cell membrane
- Include exocytosis & endocytosis
- Endocytosis
- Process of taking material into the cell by infoldings, or pockets of the cell membrane
- Form a vesicle entering the cytoplasm
- e.g.
- Amoebas use this method to take in food
- White blood cells use endocytosis to engulf damaged cells
- Phagocytosis:
- The process of large particles (solid) is taken into the cell by endocytosis
- Pinocytosis
- The process of solutions (liquid) is taken into the cell by endocytosis
- Exocytosis
- Removal of large amounts of materials from cell
- Membrane of vesicles fuses with the cell membrane
- Steps (reverse of endocytosis):
- Proteins (made by ribosomes) enters the ER
- Protein exists ER, entering Golgi apparatus by a vesicle
- Protein is modified and exists on the trans face of Golgi apparatus inside a vesicle
- Vesicle with the modified protein moves to and fuses with the plasma membrane
- Cells use exocytosis to get rid of wastes and give off chemical signals

# S1M-3 8.1 Energy of Life

## 8.1 Energy of Life

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Biology H review guide (PA). Writers: Tiffany Cheah, Elisa Lau. Editor: Chloe Yu. Range: mostly 7.1, 7.2, 7.3, 8.1, 8.2, 8.3; 1.3, 2.3, 2.4 may be tested a little. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

Forms of Energy

- Include light, heat, electricity and chemical energy
- Living things use chemical energy as fuels

ATP and ADP

- Energy can be stored in chemical compounds such as ATP
- Storing energy:
  - Cells can store small amounts of energy by adding a phosphate group to ADP
    - ADP + Pi → ATP
  - ATP is used by all types of cells as basic energy source
- Released energy:
  - ATP → ADP + Pi
  - Subtract 3rd phosphate group
    - Energy released
- Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)
  - Adenine (containing-nitrogen)
  - Ribose (5-carbon sugar)
  - Three phosphate groups
- Adenosine diphosphate (ADP)
  - Adenine (containing-nitrogen)
  - Ribose (5-carbon sugar)
  - Two phosphate groups

Using Biochemical Energy

- Active transport
  - Sodium-potassium pump
    - Move Na+ out and K+ in
    - Energy provided by one ATP molecule
      - 3Na+ out, 2K+ in
- Movement within the cell
  - Motor protein moves organelles along microtubules
  - Energy source: ATP
- ATP also powers other events
  - Protein synthesis
  - Responses to chemical signals at cell surface
  - Produces light

ATP and Glucose

- ATP can only store small amount of energy
- Glucose can store 90 times more energy than ATP
- Cell regenerates ATP from ADP by using energy in food (e.g. glucose, protein, lipid)

Autotrophs and Heterotrophs

- Autotrophs
  - Make own food
  - Plants and some other organisms use light energy to produce food by photosynthesis
  - Some organisms use chemical energy to produce food
- Heterotrophs
  - Obtain energy from foods they consume

8.2 & 8.3 Photosynthesis

Discovery of Photosynthesis

- Jan Van Helmont
  - Watered the plant for 5 years and measured the mass of soil
  - Since only water was added, he concluded the mass came from water
  - Soil was not the main source for plant's growth
- Joseph Priestley
  - Used a candle, a jar and mint plant
  - Mint released oxygen gas
- Jan Ingenhousz
  - Light is necessary for plants to produce oxygen gas

The Photosynthesis Equation

- In the presence of light, plants transform carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates and release oxygen
  - 6CO2 + 6H2O --light--> C6H12O6 + 6O2
  - Remember: light is not a reactant

Location

- Chloroplasts
  - Outer and inner membranes
  - Thylakoids
    - Saclike photosynthetic membrane containing chlorophyll
  - Stroma
    - Fluid portion, outside of thylakoids
  - Grana (sig. granum)
    - Stacks of thylakoid membrane

Light and Pigments

- The "white" sunlight is a mixture of different colors
  - The visible sunlight makes up the visible spectrum
- Photosynthesis requires light and pigments, molecules in chloroplasts
- Pigment
  - Light-absorbing molecules of plants
  - Chlorophyll (principal pigment)
    - Chlorophyll a
    - Chlorophyll b
- Chlorophyll absorbs well in violet-blue & red regions, but not well in green region
- Carotenoids
  - Red, orange and yellow pigment
  - Absorb light in violet and blue-green region
- As temperature drops, chlorophyll breaks down first, leaving carotenoid pigments to see in the autumn

Energy Collection

- Chlorophyll absorbs the light
  - Energy level of electrons in chlorophyll raised
- High-energy electrons make photosynthesis work

Electron Carriers

- A compound that can accept a pair of high energy electrons and transfer them to another molecule
  - E.g. NADP+
  - NADP+ + 2 high energy e- + H+ → NADPH
- A substance loses electrons, or is oxidized
- A substance gains electrons, or is reduced

Two Sets of Reactions

- Light-dependent reactions
  - In thylakoid membrane
  - Need light and water
  - Photosystems (PSII and PSI)
    - Clusters of chlorophyll and proteins on thylakoid membrane
    - Contain light-harvesting complex
      - Accessory pigment
      - A matrix of protein
    - Contain reaction-center complex
      - A pair of chlorophyll α
      - A matrix of protein
      - A primary electron acceptor
  - Use solar energy to produce O2 and convert ADP & NADP+ into energy carriers ATP & NADPH
    - 2H2O + ADP + Pi + NADP+ + 2e- + H+ --light--> O2 + ATP + NADPH
  - 1. PS II
    - Electrons (P680) are excited after absorbing energy from light
    - Electrons in chlorophyll are resupplied via photolysis (splits water into protons, electrons, and oxygen)
  - 2. Electron transport chain
    - Carrier proteins move high energy electrons from PS II to PS I
    - Use energy from electrons to pump protons from stroma into thylakoid lumen
    - PQ, Cytochrome complex (pumps protons), PC
  - 3. PS I
    - Electrons (P700) are reenergized
    - Electrons pass down another electron transport chain to protein Fd
    - NADP+ picks up electrons and becomes NADPH (reaction catalyzed by NADP+ reductase
  - ATP formation
    - Because of the concentration difference of protons between the two sides of the thylakoid membrane, protons diffuse from lumen into stroma
    - As protons pass through ATP synthase, potential energy causes ATP synthase to rotate and synthesize ATP from ADP and Pi
      - Chemiosmosis
- Light Independent (Calvin Cycle)
  - Creates high energy carbohydrates that can be stored for a long time
  - 1. Carbon dioxide enters cycle
    - Enzyme in stroma combines carbon dioxide with 5-carbon compounds already present, producing 3-carbon compounds that continue in cycle
    - Other enzymes convert 3-carbon compounds into high energy compounds (energy comes from ATP and NADPH)
    - At midcycle, two of twelve 3-carbon compounds are removed from the cycle
      - They become the building blocks for sugars, lipids, and amino acids
    - Remaining ten molecules converted back into 5 carbon compounds that cycle back to begin next cycle

Factors affecting photosynthesis

- Temperature
  - Enzymes involved work best between 0 to 35 degrees Celsius
- Light
  - High light intensity increases rate of photosynthesis up to a certain point
- Water
  - Plants living in dry conditions have adaptations to minimize water loss

Photosynthesis under extreme conditions

- Plants living in bright, hot conditions have special forms of photosynthesis:
- C4 photosynthesis
  - Can capture extremely low levels of CO2
  - C4: first compound formed in the pathway has four carbon atoms (most plants are C3)
  - Requires extra ATP to function
  - Ex: corn, sugar cane, etc.
- CAM plants (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism)
  - Members of the family Crassulacae
  - Minimizes water loss by opening stomata only at night
  - Carbon dioxide is absorbed at night and stored for photosynthesis next day
  - Ex: pineapple trees, many desert cacti, etc.

# S1M-1 7.1 Life Is Cellular

## 7.1 Life Is Cellular

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Biology S review guide (PA). Writers: Sophia 10-5. Editor: Angelina 10-1. Range: 7.1～8.3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**The Discovery of the Cell**

The invention of the microscope(1600s)enabled researchers to see cells for the first time.

-Robert Hook

- English

- used an early microscope to look at thin slices of cork(1665)

- first to observe dead cells

- defined ‘cell’

-Anton Van Leeuwenhoek

- Dutch lens maker

- first to observe living cells in a drop of water(1674)

-Matthias Schleiden

- all plants are made of cells(1838)

-Theodor Schwann

- all animals are made of cells(1839)

-Rudolf Virchow

- all cells come from existing cells(1855)

**CELL THEORY**

by Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow(German)

-All living things are made of cells.

-Cells are the basic units of structure and function in living things.

-New cells are produced from existing cells.

**Exploring the Cell**

Scientists use **light microscopes** and **electron microscopes** to explore the structure of cells.

**Compound light microscopes**

-have lenses that focus light

-magnify objects by up to 1000 times

-chemical stains and fluorescent dyes make cell structures easier to see

**Electron microscopes**

-use beams of electrons focused by magnetic fields

-offer much higher resolution than light microscopes

-two main types of electron microscopes：transmission and scanning

-transmission electron microscope

- Use beams of electrons to examine thin slices of materials

- 2D range(inner structure

-scanning electron microscope

- Use beams of electrons to view the surface of a specimen

- 3D range(cell surface

Scientists use computers to add color to electron micrographs, which are photos of objects seen through a microscope.

**Prokaryotes & Eukaryotes**

-cell vary in shapes & sizes

- smallest: DNA 2nm

- biggest: egg

-basic cell parts

- cell membrane: thin, flexible barrier around cell

- cytoplasm: material inside cell membrane(except the nucleus), contain important structures

-nucleus

- contain cell’s genetic material

- control cell activities

- not all cells have it

- prokaryotic cell-no nucleus

- smaller&simpler than eukaryotes

- most are unicellular

- no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles

- have a circular stranded chromosome

-eukaryotic cell-have nucleus

- can be both unicellular and multicellular

## 7.2 Cell Structure

**-Major parts of eukaryotic cells**

- nucleus

- cytoplasm

- between the nucleus and the cell membrane

- contains organelles (specialized structures to perform cellular functions)

- cell membrane

**Nucleus**

-Structure

- Double nuclear envelope

- Inside: Chromatin / chromosome

- Inside: nucleolus

-Function

- control most cell processes

- contain DNA

**Chromatin and condensed chromosome structure**

-Chromosomes

- Condensed chromatin during cell division

- Distinct threadlike structures visible under a microscope

-Chromatin

- DNA packed by protein

**Nucleolus**

-Structure: small dense region in nucleus

-Composition: rich in DNA

-Function: make ribosomes

**Nuclear envelope**

-Structure: double membrane with nuclear pores

-Function: allow material to move in or out of the nucleus

-Additional: RNA and other informative molecules are sent out

**Vacuoles and vesicles**

- Vacuoles

-Structure: saclike membrane-enclosed

-Function: store water, salts, proteins and carbohydrates

-Examples:

-Central vacuole in plant cell

- A single large one filled with liquid

- Increase rigidity, support heavy structures

-Contractile vacuoles in some unicellular organisms

- Pump excess water out of the cell

- Vesicles

-Structure: smaller membrane-enclosed sac

-Function: store and move materials between organelles and to and from the cell surface

**Lysosomes**

-Structure: small organelles filled with enzymes

-Function: break down lipids, carbohydrates, and proteins / wornout organelles

**Cytoskeleton**

-Structure: network of thin protein fibers

- Two types: Microtubules and microfilaments

-Function:

- maintain cell shape

- transport materials in cell

- help many forms of cell movement

-Microfilaments

- Structure: threadlike, made up of protein actin

- Function: movement and support of the cell

-Microtubules

- Structure:

- hollow tubes

- made up of protein tubulin

- Function:

- maintain cell shape

- serve as "tracks" to move vesicles (with materials)

- Examples:

- spindles

- centrioles

- Flagellum and cilia

**Cytoplasm**

**Ribosomes**

-Structure: small particles made of RNA and proteins

-Function: make proteins

-Attached ribosomes:

- proteins that are to be released or secreted out of the cell

- membrane proteins

- proteins destined for lysosomes and other specialized locations within the cell

-Free ribosomes:

- make other proteins to be used within the cell

**Endoplasmic reticulum**

-Structure：internal membrane system

-Function：

- Rough ER：

- with ribosomes attached

- protein synthesis

- Smooth ER

- no ribosomes attached

- synthesis of membrane lipids

- detoxification of drugs

- Liver cells have lots of smooth ER

**Golgi apparatus**

-Structure: stack of flattened membranes

-Function: modify, sort and package proteins

**Chloroplast**

-Structure: double membrane

-inside:

- large stacks of photosynthetic membranes containing chlorophyll

- found in plants and some other organisms like algae

-Function:

- use solar energy to make energyrich food molecules by photosynthesis

**Mitochondria**

-Structure: double membrane

- smooth outer membrane

- folded inner membrane

-Function:

- use energy from food to make highenergy compounds (ATP)

- site of cellular respiration

**Organelle DNA**

-chloroplasts and mitochondria contain their own DNA

-supposed to be descended from independent prokaryotic microorganisms

-supposed to be descended from independent microorganisms (endosymbiotic theory)

-Mitochondrial DNA inherited only from the mother

**Cell wall**

-plant, algae, fungi, most prokaryotes all have cell wall

-not in animal cells

-lie outside the cell membrane

-Structure: porous wall, allows many substances to pass through easily

- Plant cell wall: Cellulose

- Fungi cell wall: Chitin

- Bacterial cell wall: Peptidoglycan

-Function: support, shape and protect the cell

**Cell membrane**

-Function

- selectively permeable, regulate what enters and leaves the cell

- protects and supports the cell

-Fluid mosaic model of cell membrane

- The proteins embedded in the lipid bilayer can move around and float among the lipids.

- Many kinds of molecules make up the cell membrane.

## 7.3 Cell Transport

**Passive Transport**

-the movement of materials across the cell membrane without using cellular energy

**Diffusion**

-the process by which particles move from an area of high concentration to an area of lower concentration.

**Facilitated diffusion**

-the process by which molecules that cannot directly diffuse across the membrane pass through special protein channels.

**-Osmosis**

- the net facilitated diffusion of water through a selectively permeable membrane

- **Aquaporins**

- water channel proteins that allow water to pass through cell membranes

- **isotonic** solutions

- two adjacent solutions have the same concentrations of solute

- water molecule still move across the membrane in both direction, no net movement of water

- have a higher concentration of solute compared to another solution

- **Hypotonic** solutions

- have a lower concentration of solute compared to another solution

**-Osmotic pressure**

- the force caused by the net movement of water by osmosis.

**Active Transport**

-The movement of materials against a concentration difference

-requires energy.

- Transport proteins that act like pumps use energy to move small molecules and ions across cell membranes.

- The bulk transport of large molecules and clumps of materials into and out of cells occurs by movements of the cell membrane, which require energy.

# S1M-2 8.1 Energy and Life

## 8.1 Energy and Life

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Biology S review guide (PA). Writers: Sophia 10-5. Editor: Angelina 10-1. Range: 7.1～8.3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Chemical Energy and ATP**

-Energy is the ability to do work

-Organisms need energy to stay alive.

**Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)**

-a chemical compound cells use to store and release energy

- An ATP molecule consists of adenine, the sugar ribose, and three phosphate groups.

- Cells store energy by adding a phosphate group to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) molecules. (energy is stored in its high energy phosphate bonds)

- Cells release energy from ATP molecules by subtracting a phosphate group.

- Energy provided by ATP is used in active transport, to contract muscles, to make proteins, and in many other ways.

- Cells contain only a small amount of ATP at any one time. They regenerate it from ADP as they need it, using energy stored in food.

**Heterotrophs and Autotrophs**

- The energy to make ATP from ADP comes from food.

- Organisms get food in one of two ways.

**-Heterotrophs**

- Cannot make their own food.

- Obtains food by feeding on others.

- Animals, fungi, etc.

**-Autotrophs**

- Make their own food

- Photosynthesis comes from the Greek words, photo means "light", and synthesis means "putting together".

- Plants, algae, some bacteria

**-Photosynthesis**

- the process that uses light energy to produce food molecules.

## 8.2 Photosynthesis: an overview

**-Visible light**

**·**The wavelength of light determines its color

**-Pigment**

**·**Light-absorbing molecules

**·**Found in chloroplasts

**-Chlorophyll**

**·**Chlorophyll a

**·**Chlorophyll b

**·**Absorb blue and red light well

**·**Reflect green light

**-Carotene**

**·**Red and orange pigment

**·**Absorb light in other regions of spectrum

### Chlorophyll and Chloroplasts

-In eukaryotes, photosynthesis occurs in organelles called chloroplasts. Chloroplasts house light-absorbing chemicals.

-light

- Light is a form of energy.

- Sunlight is a mixture of all the different colors of visible light.

-Light-absorbing molecules called pigments capture the sun’s energy.

-Chlorophyll

- the principal pigment in photosynthetic organisms

- absorbs blue-violet and red light but reflects green light.

-Chloroplasts have a complex internal structure that includes:

- thylakoids:

- saclike photosynthetic membranes that contain chlorophyll and other pigments and are arranged in stacks called grana.

- stroma:

- the fluid portion outside of the thylakoids.

### High-Energy Electrons

The energy in light raises some of the electrons in chlorophyll to higher energy levels. These high-energy electrons are used in photosynthesis.

-Electron carriers are used to transport the electrons from chlorophyll to other molecules during photosynthesis.

-NADP⁺

- a compound that can accept and hold 2 high-energy electrons and 1 hydrogen ion

- This process converts NADP⁺ into NADPH.

### Overview of Photosynthesis

-The light-dependent reactions

- require light, light-absorbing pigments, and water

- form NADPH, ATP, and oxygen.

-The light-independent reactions

- do not use light energy

- use carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, NADPH, and ATP

- make energy-rich carbon compounds

## 8.3 The Process of Photosynthesis

**Light-dependent reaction**

- **On thylakoid membrane there are:**

- Photosystems: clusters of chlorophyll and proteins

- Electron transport chain: series of electron carrier proteins that shuttle highenergy electrons

- ATP synthase: enzyme that synthesizes ATP->H⁺ ions flow down their concentration gradient through ATP synthase, providing energy to produce ATP (chemiosmosis)

- **Photosystems**

- clusters of chlorophyll and proteins contained by thylakoids

- Photosystems absorb sunlight and generate highenergy electrons

- Highenergy electrons are then passed to a series of electron carriers embedded in the thylakoid membrane

Water is split by sunlight to form oxygen, protons while the electrons are grabbed by chlorophyll

**A. Photosystem II**

- Light energy absorbed by PS II produces highenergy e⁻

- highenergy e⁻ pass to the electron transport chain

- water is split to replace those electrons, releasing H⁺ and oxygen

- PSII happens before PSI

**B. Electron transport chain (ETC)**

- highenergy e⁻ move from PSII to PSI through the ETC

- e⁻ causes pumping of H⁺ from stroma to the thylakoid space (active transport)

**C. Photosystem I**

- e⁻ passed to PSI are reenergized

- Highenergy e⁻ then pass to the secondary electron transport chain

- NADP⁺ picks up the H⁺ and e⁻ at the end of the ETC

- NADP⁺ + 2e⁻ + H⁺ → NADPH

# 2.2 Properties of Water

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Polarity

Water's **polarity** means there is a **greater probability of finding its shared electrons closer to its oxygen atom**.

**Polar molecules have unevenly distributed charges** — **oxygen is slightly negative, hydrogen slightly positive**.

## Hydrogen bonding

A **hydrogen bond** is a **weak intermolecular attraction between hydrogen on one molecule and oxygen on another**.

## Cohesion, adhesion, and capillary action

| Property | Definition | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Cohesion** | Attraction between molecules of the **same** substance | Causes **surface tension** |
| **Adhesion** | Attraction between molecules of **different** substances | Causes **menisci** to form |

**Capillary action** works by both at once: **cohesion holds the continuous column of water together as adhesion causes it to rise**. This is what **draws water out of roots into stems**.

## Solutions

Water's polarity lets it **dissolve ionic compounds and other polar molecules**.

- **Solute** — the substance that is dissolved
- **Solvent** — the substance in which the solute dissolves

## The pH scale

The **pH scale** measures the **concentration of H⁺ ions** in a solution, ranging from **0 (very acidic) to 14 (very basic)**.

| pH | Condition | Relationship |
|---|---|---|
| **< 7** | Acidic | [H⁺] > [OH⁻] |
| **= 7** | Neutral | [H⁺] = [OH⁻] |
| **> 7** | Basic | [H⁺] < [OH⁻] |

$$\text{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H^+}], \qquad [\mathrm{H^+}] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$$

Because the scale is **logarithmic**, each whole step is a **tenfold** change in H⁺ concentration — pH 4 is ten times more acidic than pH 5, not slightly more.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polarity** | The greater probability of finding water's shared electrons closer to its oxygen atom |
| **Polar molecule** | A molecule with unevenly distributed charges |
| **Hydrogen bond** | A weak intermolecular attraction between hydrogen on one molecule and oxygen on another |
| **Cohesion** | Attraction between molecules of the same substance, causing surface tension |
| **Adhesion** | Attraction between molecules of different substances, causing menisci |
| **Capillary action** | Cohesion holding a water column together while adhesion causes it to rise |
| **Solute** | The substance that is dissolved |
| **Solvent** | The substance in which the solute dissolves |
| **pH scale** | A logarithmic measure of H⁺ concentration, from 0 (very acidic) to 14 (very basic) |

# 3.1 What Is Ecology?

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The basics

The **biosphere** consists of **all life and all parts of the Earth with life**.

**Ecology** is the **scientific study of interactions among organisms, and between organisms and their physical environment**.

The Greek root is **oikos**, meaning *house*:

- **Ecology** — the study of nature's "houses" and the inhabitants of those houses
- **Economics** — the study of human "houses" and interactions involving money and trade

The shared root is not a coincidence, and it is a useful reminder of what ecology studies: not organisms alone but the **household they run**.

## Levels of organisation

From least to most inclusive:

| Level | Definition |
|---|---|
| **1. Individual organism** | A single living thing |
| **2. Population** | A group of individuals of **one species** living in the **same area**. A **species** is a group of similar organisms that can produce **fertile offspring** |
| **3. Community** | **All the different populations** that live together in an area |
| **4. Ecosystem** | All organisms in an area **together with their physical environment** |
| **5. Biome** | A group of ecosystems sharing **similar climates and organisms** |
| **6. Biosphere** | Our entire planet |

## Environmental factors

The **environment** is **all the conditions and factors surrounding an organism**.

| Factor | Nature | Definition | Example (for a bullfrog) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Biotic** | Biological | Any **living** part of the environment an organism might interact with | Insects and herons |
| **Abiotic** | Physical | Any **nonliving** part of the environment | Water availability and temperature |

**Both types of factor can influence the other**, shaping an environment with their dynamic mix.

## Ecological methods

- **Observation**
- **Experimentation** — can be used to **test hypotheses**
- **Modelling** — helps understand events that happen over **long periods of time or large distances**, using **formulas based on data from observation and experimentation**

Note why modelling exists as a third method: some ecological questions span centuries or continents, where neither watching nor experimenting is possible.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Biosphere** | All life and all parts of the Earth with life |
| **Ecology** | The scientific study of interactions among organisms and with their physical environment |
| **Population** | A group of individuals of one species living in the same area |
| **Species** | Similar organisms that can produce fertile offspring |
| **Community** | All the different populations living together in an area |
| **Ecosystem** | All organisms in an area together with their physical environment |
| **Biome** | A group of ecosystems sharing similar climates and organisms |
| **Environment** | All conditions and factors surrounding an organism |
| **Biotic factor** | Any living part of the environment an organism might interact with |
| **Abiotic factor** | Any nonliving part of the environment |
| **Modelling** | Using formulas based on observational and experimental data to understand events over long times or distances |

# 3.2 Energy, Producers, and Consumers

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Producers

**Autotrophs** are organisms that **use solar or chemical energy to produce "food" (glucose)**.

They are also called **primary producers**, because they are the **first producers of energy-rich compounds** later used by other organisms, and they are **essential to energy flow in the biosphere**.

The Greek roots are **auto** (by itself) and **trophikos** (to feed).

### Photosynthesis

A process in which **light energy powers reactions to produce carbohydrates**, converting **carbon dioxide and water into oxygen and energy-rich sugars and starches**.

Performed by:

- **Plants**, on land
- **Algae**, in freshwater and the upper layers of the ocean
- **Bacteria** (commonly **cyanobacteria**), in tidal flats and salt marshes

### Chemosynthesis

A process in which **chemical energy is used to produce carbohydrates**. **Chemosynthetic bacteria power ecosystems** at deep-sea volcanic vents, hot springs, and coastal tidal marshes.

## Consumers

**Heterotrophs** must **acquire energy and nutrients from other organisms**.

| Type | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Carnivores** | Kill and eat other animals | Snakes, dogs, cats |
| **Herbivores** | Eat plant leaves, roots, seeds, or fruits | Cows, caterpillars, deer |
| **Omnivores** | Diets include both plants and animals | Humans, bears, pigs |
| **Scavengers** | Consume carcasses of animals killed by other predators or dead by other means | Vultures, flies |
| **Decomposers (saprotrophs)** | Release digestive enzymes to break down organic matter **externally**, producing **detritus** | Fungi, bacteria |
| **Detritivores** | Feed on **detritus particles**, chewing and grinding them into smaller pieces; commonly digest the decomposers living on or in those particles | Mites, snails, shrimp, crabs |

**Detritus** is small pieces of dead and decaying plant and animal remains.

Note the trade-off in carnivory: **catching and killing prey requires energy**, but meat is generally **rich in nutrients and energy and easily digested**.

## Beyond the consumer categories

**Strict categories do not represent the full complexity.**

- **Plant leaves are much less nutritious and harder to digest than seeds or fruits**, so herbivores that eat different parts differ in how they obtain and digest food. **Most birds do not have the digestive systems to digest leaves**
- **Hyenas**, though classified as carnivores, **will scavenge**
- **Aquatic animals** eat a mixture of algae, bits of animal carcasses, and detritus
- **Carnivorous plants and euglenoids are mixotrophic** — both heterotrophic and autotrophic

This is the section's real point: the categories are a useful first pass, and almost every organism examined closely violates them somewhere.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Autotroph** | An organism using solar or chemical energy to produce food (glucose) |
| **Primary producer** | Another name for an autotroph — the first producer of energy-rich compounds |
| **Photosynthesis** | Light energy powering reactions that convert CO₂ and water into oxygen and sugars |
| **Chemosynthesis** | Chemical energy being used to produce carbohydrates |
| **Heterotroph** | An organism that must acquire energy and nutrients from other organisms |
| **Carnivore** | A consumer that kills and eats other animals |
| **Herbivore** | A consumer that eats plant leaves, roots, seeds, or fruits |
| **Omnivore** | A consumer whose diet includes both plants and animals |
| **Scavenger** | A consumer of carcasses killed by others or dead by other means |
| **Decomposer (saprotroph)** | An organism releasing digestive enzymes to break down organic matter externally |
| **Detritus** | Small pieces of dead and decaying plant and animal remains |
| **Detritivore** | An organism feeding on detritus particles, grinding them smaller |
| **Mixotroph** | An organism that is both heterotrophic and autotrophic |

# 3.3 Energy Flow in Ecosystems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Food chains and food webs

A **food chain** is **a series of steps in which organisms transfer energy by eating and being eaten**. **Energy flows through an ecosystem in a one-way stream.**

An example, four steps from producer to top predator:

$$\text{algae (phytoplankton)} \rightarrow \text{krill (zooplankton)} \rightarrow \text{penguin} \rightarrow \text{seal} \rightarrow \text{orca}$$

**Plankton** are small aquatic floating organisms. The **orca** is the top predator here, **four steps removed from the producer**.

A **food web** is **a network of feeding interactions, representing interconnected food chains** — necessary because **many animals eat more than one kind of food**.

**Decomposers in food webs recycle nutrients**, releasing them for primary producers to use. **A change in the population of one species can disturb other organisms in the web.**

## Ecological pyramids

A **trophic level** is **each step in a food chain or food web** — primary producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, tertiary consumer.

**Ecological pyramids** show the **relative amount of certain things at each trophic level** in an ecosystem.

### Pyramid of energy

Shows the **relative amount of energy available at each level**, in **kJ · m⁻² · y⁻¹**.

**About 10 percent of the energy in one trophic level is transferred to the next.** The other **90 percent is lost** as heat, and as non-ingested or non-digested parts.

### Pyramid of biomass

Shows the **relative amount of living organic matter at each level**, in **g · m⁻²**.

**It can be an inverted triangle when:**

- **In winter**, producers die or lose leaf mass while consumers retain stored mass
- **In the deep sea**, with huge top predators (whales, giant squid) and producers that come and go quickly

### Pyramid of numbers

Shows the **relative number of living organisms at each level**.

**It can be inverted when consumers are much less massive than their food sources** — thousands of insects grazing on a single tree.

The inversions are the point worth holding onto. **A pyramid of energy can never be inverted**, because energy is always lost between levels; biomass and numbers can invert, because they measure standing stock at one moment rather than flow.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Food chain** | A series of steps in which organisms transfer energy by eating and being eaten |
| **Plankton** | Small aquatic floating organisms |
| **Food web** | A network of feeding interactions representing interconnected food chains |
| **Trophic level** | Each step in a food chain or food web |
| **Ecological pyramid** | A diagram showing the relative amount of something at each trophic level |
| **Pyramid of energy** | Shows relative energy available at each level (kJ · m⁻² · y⁻¹) |
| **Pyramid of biomass** | Shows relative living organic matter at each level (g · m⁻²); can be inverted |
| **Pyramid of numbers** | Shows the relative number of organisms at each level; can be inverted |

# 3.4 Cycles of Matter

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Recycling in the biosphere

**Unlike the one-way flow of energy, matter is recycled within and between ecosystems.** Elements combine to form the building blocks of organisms.

**Biogeochemical cycles** are the **biological, chemical, and physical processes that transfer elements**. They are **powered by the flow of energy**.

Though not classified as a cycle, **human activity is influential as well** — deforestation, for instance.

## The water cycle

Water **continuously moves between the oceans, the atmosphere, land, and living organisms**.

| Process | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Evaporation** | Liquid water becomes water vapour |
| **Transpiration** | Evaporation from plant leaves |
| **Condensation** | Cooling water vapour condenses into droplets around dust particles |
| **Precipitation** | Water falls from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail |
| **Runoff** | Flow of water on the surface |
| **Groundwater** | Water absorbed into the soil |
| **Percolation** | Gradual filtering through a porous structure |

**Forms of water:** water vapour, clouds, oceans, rivers and lakes, plants, groundwater, and underground reservoirs.

## Nutrients

A **nutrient** is **a chemical substance that an organism must obtain from its environment to sustain life** — carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus. **Oxygen combines with these elements** and cycles through parts of their journeys.

## The carbon cycle

**Forms of carbon:**

- **Carbon compounds** in living organisms — carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids
- **CO₂** in the atmosphere and **dissolved CO₂** in the hydrosphere
- **Carbonate rocks (CaCO₃)**, **fossil fuels** (oil, coal), and **natural gas (CH₄)**

**Processes:** photosynthesis, cellular respiration, feeding, decomposition, fossilisation, combustion, dissolution, deposition.

## The nitrogen cycle

Organisms require nitrogen to make **amino acids**, used to build **proteins and nucleic acids** (which make up DNA and RNA).

**Forms of nitrogen:**

- **Nitrogen gas (N₂)** in the atmosphere
- **Ammonia (NH₃), ammonium (NH₄⁺), nitrate ions (NO₃⁻), and nitrite ions (NO₂⁻)** in soil, waste, and dead or decaying organic matter
- Dissolved nitrogen in several forms in large water bodies

**The processes:**

| Process | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Nitrogen fixation** | Bacteria in soil and on **legume roots** convert N₂ into NH₃/NH₄⁺. **Lightning** also converts N₂ into usable forms — atmospheric nitrogen fixation |
| **Nitrification** | Soil bacteria convert NH₃/NH₄⁺ into NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻, usable by producers |
| **Assimilation** | Plants absorb NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻ from the soil and convert these **inorganic** compounds into **organic** proteins and nucleic acids |
| **Feeding** | Consumers eat producers and assimilate the organic compounds |
| **Decomposition / ammonification** | Decomposers release nitrogen from waste and dead organisms as ammonia, nitrates, and nitrites |
| **Denitrification** | Other soil bacteria convert NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻ back to **N₂** in the air |

**Human factors:** **excess fertiliser is carried into surface water or groundwater by precipitation.**

Note that assimilation is the step where nitrogen crosses from **inorganic to organic** — the boundary between the geochemical and the biological halves of the cycle.

## The phosphorus cycle

**Phosphorus forms part of DNA and RNA, but is not abundant in the biosphere.**

**Forms of phosphorus:**

- **Inorganic phosphate (PO₄³⁻)** — rock and soil minerals on land; dissolved or as sediment in the ocean
- **Organic phosphorus compounds** in living things

**Weathering and erosion of rocks gradually release phosphate.** Phosphate then cycles between **soil, producers, and consumers**, while **marine organisms incorporate dissolved phosphate** into compounds.

Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus has **no atmospheric form** — which is why its supply depends on slow rock weathering and why it is so often limiting.

## Nutrient limitation

**The availability of nutrients can limit the primary productivity of an ecosystem** that has ample sunlight and water.

- **Primary productivity** — the rate at which primary producers create organic material such as carbohydrates
- **Limiting nutrient** — the nutrient whose supply limits productivity

**Fertiliser solves the problem of nutrient limitation in soil.**

**Aquatic ecosystems** are often nutrient-poor, with **nitrogen limiting in saltwater** and **phosphorus limiting in freshwater**.

**Large inputs of a limiting nutrient** — runoff from heavily fertilised fields — can produce an **algal bloom**, which can **cover the water's surface and disrupt the ecosystem**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Biogeochemical cycle** | Biological, chemical, and physical processes that transfer elements, powered by energy flow |
| **Evaporation** | Liquid water becoming water vapour |
| **Transpiration** | Evaporation from plant leaves |
| **Condensation** | Cooling water vapour condensing into droplets around dust particles |
| **Precipitation** | Water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail |
| **Runoff** | Flow of water on the surface |
| **Groundwater** | Water absorbed into the soil |
| **Percolation** | Gradual filtering through a porous structure |
| **Nutrient** | A chemical substance an organism must obtain from its environment to sustain life |
| **Nitrogen fixation** | Bacteria or lightning converting N₂ into NH₃/NH₄⁺ |
| **Nitrification** | Soil bacteria converting NH₃/NH₄⁺ into NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻ |
| **Assimilation** | Plants converting inorganic nitrogen compounds into organic proteins and nucleic acids |
| **Ammonification** | Decomposers releasing nitrogen from waste and dead organisms |
| **Denitrification** | Soil bacteria converting NO₃⁻/NO₂⁻ back to N₂ |
| **Primary productivity** | The rate at which primary producers create organic material |
| **Limiting nutrient** | The nutrient whose supply limits productivity |
| **Algal bloom** | Rapid algal growth from a large input of a limiting nutrient, disrupting the ecosystem |

# 4.1 Climate

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Weather, climate, and microclimates

- **Weather** — the **day-to-day** condition of Earth's atmosphere
- **Climate** — **year-after-year** patterns of temperature and precipitation
- **Microclimates** are created because **environmental conditions can vary over small distances**

## Factors affecting climate

1. **Solar energy trapped in the biosphere**
2. **Latitude**
3. **The transport of heat by winds and ocean currents**

## The greenhouse effect

1. **Solar energy (sunlight) strikes Earth's surface**
2. Some is **reflected into space**; some is **absorbed and converted into heat (infrared radiation)**
3. Some heat **radiates into space**; some is **trapped by atmospheric gases** — mainly **carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapour**

**This phenomenon maintains Earth's average temperature.**

- **More greenhouse gases** → more heat trapped → **Earth warms**
- **Fewer greenhouse gases** → less heat trapped → **Earth cools**

Note the change of form in step 2: sunlight arrives as visible light, which the atmosphere lets through, and leaves as **infrared**, which greenhouse gases absorb. That asymmetry is the whole mechanism.

## Latitude and solar energy

**Solar energy is intense near the equator**, where rays are **concentrated**, while **polar areas receive less intense solar energy**, where rays are **spread out**.

This **unequal distribution creates the tropical, temperate, and polar climate zones**.

## Heat transport in the biosphere

**Warm air** — such as air near the equator — is **less dense and rises**, expanding and spreading north and south, **losing heat along the way**, and **sinking as it cools**.

**Cool air** — such as air near the poles — is **denser and sinks** toward the surface, **pushing surface air outward** and **warming as it travels**, then **rising as it warms**.

**Earth's rotation** makes winds blow **from west to east over temperate zones** and **east to west over the tropics and poles**.

**Ocean currents:** **warm currents add moisture and heat to air**, while **cool currents cool air**. **Deep ocean currents are caused by cold water near the poles sinking**, and that water **rises in warmer regions through upwelling**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Weather** | The day-to-day condition of Earth's atmosphere |
| **Climate** | Year-after-year patterns of temperature and precipitation |
| **Microclimate** | Local variation in environmental conditions over small distances |
| **Greenhouse effect** | Atmospheric gases trapping heat radiated from Earth's surface, maintaining average temperature |
| **Greenhouse gases** | Mainly carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapour |
| **Climate zones** | Tropical, temperate, and polar, created by unequal solar distribution |
| **Upwelling** | The rising of deep cold water in warmer regions |
