# 15.2 Homogeneous Aqueous Systems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A homogeneous aqueous system is one in which the solute has been dispersed so finely that the mixture is uniform throughout — a true solution. This section covers what such a solution is made of, which solutes conduct electricity in it, and what happens when water is built into a crystal rather than dissolved in it.

## Solutions

An **aqueous solution** is a solution with water as the solvent.

Deciding which component is the **solute** is normally settled one of two ways: it is the component whose original state is different from the state of the solution, or it is the one present in a small amount. The first test is the more reliable of the two, because it does not depend on proportions — a solid dissolved in a liquid is the solute however much of it there is.

**Solvation** is the process of surrounding solute particles with solvent particles to form a solution.

## Electrolytes and nonelectrolytes

An **electrolyte** is a compound that conducts an electric current when it is in an aqueous solution or in the molten state. Examples include all ionic compounds and some molecular compounds — most acids or bases, and water.

A **nonelectrolyte** is a compound that does not conduct an electric current in either an aqueous solution or the molten state.

Note that the definitions are tied to a state, not to the substance in the abstract. Some polar molecular compounds are nonelectrolytes in the pure state but become electrolytes when they dissolve in water: ammonia, $\mathrm{NH_3(g)}$, is not an electrolyte in the pure state. Asking "is this compound an electrolyte?" without saying in what state is therefore not a well-formed question.

## Hydrates

A **hydrate** is a compound that contains $\mathrm{H_2O}$ units within its crystal structure. The water is easily lost and regained, which is what makes the hydrate family behave as it does — the same compound can shed water to the air or take it back from the air depending on conditions.

The chart of hydrates is required material, and it has to be memorised.

**Efflorescence** (风化) is the process in which a hydrate loses its water of hydration.

The traffic runs the other way as well. Hydrated ionic compounds that have low vapour pressure remove water from moist air to form higher hydrates. **Hygroscopic hydrates** are hydrates and other compounds that remove moisture from air, and a **desiccant** is a substance used to absorb moisture from the air and create a dry atmosphere — a hygroscopic compound put to work.

**Deliquescent** (易潮解的) compounds are the extreme case: some compounds are so hygroscopic that they remove sufficient water from the air to dissolve completely and form solutions.

The three terms line up as a single scale of affinity for water. An efflorescent compound gives its water up to the air; a hygroscopic one takes water from the air; a deliquescent one takes so much that it ends up as a solution.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Aqueous solution** | A solution with water as the solvent |
| **Solute** | Normally the component whose original state is different from the state of the solution, or the one present in a small amount |
| **Solvation** | The process of surrounding solute particles with solvent particles to form a solution |
| **Electrolyte** | A compound that conducts an electric current when it is in an aqueous solution or in the molten state |
| **Nonelectrolyte** | A compound that does not conduct an electric current in either an aqueous solution or the molten state |
| **Hydrate** | A compound that contains $\mathrm{H_2O}$ units within its crystal structure |
| **Efflorescence** (风化) | The process in which a hydrate loses its water of hydration |
| **Hygroscopic hydrates** | Hydrates and other compounds that remove moisture from air |
| **Desiccant** | A substance used to absorb moisture from the air and create a dry atmosphere |
| **Deliquescent compounds** | Compounds so hygroscopic that they remove sufficient water from the air to dissolve completely and form solutions |

# 15.3 Heterogeneous Aqueous Systems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Not every mixture with water is a solution. Where the dispersed particles are large enough to be seen as a separate phase, the mixture is heterogeneous, and **particle size** is the quantity that sorts these mixtures out. Every other property in this section — settling, filtration, the scattering of light — follows from it.

## Suspensions

A **suspension** is a mixture from which particles settle out upon standing.

- Particle size: greater than 1000 nm
- Type of mixture: heterogeneous — the two substances can be clearly identified
- Filtration: the particles can be separated by filtration

A mixture of sand and water is a suspension, because the sand particles are large enough to be separated by filtration.

## Colloids

A **colloid** is a heterogeneous mixture containing particles ranging from 1 nm to 1000 nm. The **dispersion medium** may be solid, liquid or gas.

Colloidal particles are intermediate in size, and that intermediate size gives colloids their characteristic behaviour: the particles cannot be filtered, and they do not settle over time.

Two effects follow from the particles nonetheless being large enough to interact with light and with the surrounding molecules:

**Tyndall effect** — the scattering of visible light by colloidal particles, as when a beam of light passes through fog or mist.

**Brownian motion** — the chaotic movement of colloidal particles caused by collisions with molecules in the dispersion medium.

**Coagulation** is what happens when a colloid is destabilised. Colloidal particles adsorb ions from the medium, gaining charge, which prevents aggregation; adding electrolytes neutralises the charge, causing the particles to clump together and settle out. So the stability of a colloid is not simply a matter of particle size — it depends on a charge the particles have picked up, and removing that charge turns a colloid into something that behaves like a suspension.

## Suspension against solution

| | Suspension | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| Particle size | > 1000 nm | $\approx 1$ nm |
| Mixture type | Heterogeneous | Homogeneous |
| Separation by filtration | Can be separated | Cannot be separated |

## Emulsions

An **emulsion** is a colloidal dispersion of a liquid in a liquid.

An **emulsifying agent** is essential for the formation and stability of an emulsion; soap or detergent is the standard example. Soap molecules have a polar end, attracted to water, and a nonpolar end, attracted to oil or grease. A single molecule that both liquids will accept is exactly what is needed to hold together two liquids that otherwise separate.

Examples of emulsions: oil and water with soap, and mayonnaise.

## Examples of colloidal systems

| System type | Dispersed phase | Dispersion medium | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gas in liquid | Gas | Liquid | Whipped cream |
| Gas in solid | Gas | Solid | Marshmallow |
| Liquid in liquid | Liquid | Liquid | Milk, mayonnaise |
| Liquid in gas | Liquid | Gas | Fog, aerosol |
| Solid in gas | Solid | Gas | Smoke, dust in air |
| Solid in liquid | Solid | Liquid | Paint, blood, starch in water |

## Properties of solutions, colloids and suspensions

| Property | Solution | Colloid | Suspension |
|---|---|---|---|
| Particle type | Ions, atoms, small molecules | Large molecules or particles | Large particles or aggregates |
| Particle size | 0.1–1 nm | 1–1000 nm | 1000 nm and larger |
| Effect of light | No scattering | Exhibits Tyndall effect | Exhibits Tyndall effect |
| Effect of gravity | Stable, does not separate | Stable, does not separate | Unstable, sediment forms |
| Filtration | Particles not retained on filter | Particles not retained on filter | Particles retained on filter |
| Uniformity | Homogeneous | Heterogeneous | Heterogeneous |

Read down the columns and the useful distinctions appear. A colloid and a solution agree on filtration and on gravity, so neither test separates them — the Tyndall effect is what does. A colloid and a suspension agree on the Tyndall effect, so light does not separate *them* — settling and filtration do.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Suspension** | A mixture from which particles settle out upon standing |
| **Colloid** | A heterogeneous mixture containing particles ranging from 1 nm to 1000 nm |
| **Dispersion medium** | The solid, liquid or gas in which the colloidal particles are dispersed |
| **Tyndall effect** | The scattering of visible light by colloidal particles |
| **Brownian motion** | The chaotic movement of colloidal particles caused by collisions with molecules in the dispersion medium |
| **Coagulation** | Colloidal particles adsorb ions from the medium, gaining charge, which prevents aggregation; adding electrolytes neutralises the charge, causing the particles to clump together and settle out |
| **Emulsion** | A colloidal dispersion of a liquid in a liquid |
| **Emulsifying agent** | The substance essential for the formation and stability of an emulsion, such as soap or detergent |

# 16.1 Properties of Solutions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Two questions are easy to confuse in this topic: how *fast* a substance dissolves, and how *much* of it will dissolve. They have separate answers and separate lists of factors, and one factor — temperature — appears on both lists for different reasons.

## Solution formation: how fast a substance dissolves

Three factors affect how fast a substance dissolves.

**Agitation (stirring).** Dissolving occurs at the surface of the solute particles. Stirring brings the solvent — water, for example — into contact with the solute's surface, speeding up the dissolving process. Note that agitation does **not** influence the amount of solute that will dissolve.

**Temperature.** Higher temperatures increase the kinetic energy of the water molecules, causing them to move faster. This increases the frequency of collisions between solvent molecules and solute particles.

**Particle size of the solute.** Smaller particles — granulated sugar rather than a lump — have a greater surface area exposed to the solvent, which increases the rate of dissolving.

All three act on the same thing: the amount and frequency of solvent contact at the solute surface. That is why none of them can change the final amount dissolved. They change how quickly a solution reaches its limit, not where the limit lies.

## Solubility

A **saturated solution** contains the maximum amount of solute for a given quantity of solvent at a constant temperature and pressure. A **dynamic equilibrium** exists between the dissolved solute and any undissolved solute — the mixture stops changing in appearance, but dissolving and coming out of solution both carry on.

Solubility is expressed as grams of solute per 100 g of solvent ($\mathrm{g}/100\ \mathrm{g\ H_2O}$).

An **unsaturated solution** contains less solute than a saturated solution; additional solute can dissolve until saturation is reached.

**Miscible liquids** are liquids that dissolve in each other in all proportions — water and ethanol. **Immiscible liquids** do not dissolve in each other — oil and water.

## Factors affecting solubility

### Temperature

The direction of the effect depends on the state of the solute, so the state has to be identified before any prediction is made.

| Solute | Effect of increasing temperature |
|---|---|
| Solids | Solubility generally **increases** |
| Gases | Solubility **decreases** |

The gas case is the one worth remembering, because it runs against the intuition built from the solids case: carbonated beverages go flat more quickly at room temperature than when cold.

Note also that temperature raises the *rate* of dissolving in every case, but raises the *amount* dissolved only for solids. The two roles of temperature are independent.

### Pressure (Henry's law)

Pressure acts on gaseous solutes:

- Higher pressure increases gas solubility.
- Lower pressure decreases gas solubility.

## Supersaturated solutions

A **supersaturated solution** contains more solute than it can theoretically hold at a given temperature. It is holding solute past the saturation limit, so it is unstable: crystallisation can be triggered by adding a small seed crystal of the solute, at which point the excess comes out of solution.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Saturated solution** | A solution containing the maximum amount of solute for a given quantity of solvent at a constant temperature and pressure |
| **Solubility** | The amount of solute that dissolves, expressed as grams of solute per 100 g of solvent |
| **Unsaturated solution** | A solution containing less solute than a saturated solution, so that additional solute can dissolve until saturation is reached |
| **Supersaturated solution** | A solution containing more solute than it can theoretically hold at a given temperature |
| **Miscible liquids** | Liquids that dissolve in each other in all proportions |
| **Immiscible liquids** | Liquids that do not dissolve in each other |
| **Henry's law** | The name given to the effect of pressure on gas solubility: higher pressure increases gas solubility, lower pressure decreases it |

# 16.2 Concentrations of Solutions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The **concentration** of a solution is a measure of the amount of solute dissolved in a given quantity of solvent. A **dilute solution** contains a relatively small amount of solute; a **concentrated solution** contains a large amount. Those two words are only comparative, and the rest of this section replaces them with numbers.

## Molarity

**Molarity (M)**, also known as molar concentration, is the number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of solution:

$$M = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{litres of solution}}$$

The denominator is the volume of the **solution**, not of the solvent. That is the detail most often lost, and it matters because the solute takes up volume of its own once dissolved.

## Making dilutions

**Dilution** means reducing the number of moles of solute per unit volume by adding solvent, while the total number of moles of solute remains unchanged.

Both halves of that definition carry weight. Adding solvent raises the volume, so the moles per litre fall; but nothing has been added to or taken from the solute itself, so the moles of solute on either side of the operation are the same number. Since molarity multiplied by volume is precisely the moles of solute, that one conserved quantity is what links the concentration and volume before dilution to the concentration and volume after:

$$M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2$$

## Percent solutions

Concentration can also be given as a percentage, in either of two ways.

**Percent by volume** of a solution is the ratio of the volume of solute to the volume of solution:

$$\%(v/v) = \frac{\text{volume of solute}}{\text{volume of solution}} \times 100\%$$

**Percent by mass** of a solution is the ratio of the mass of the solute to the mass of the solution:

$$\%(m/m) = \frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}} \times 100\%$$

## Summary: three ways to calculate solution concentration

| Unit | Definition |
|---|---|
| Molarity (M) | Moles of solute per litre of solution |
| Percent by volume, $\%(v/v)$ | Volume of solute per volume of solution $\times\ 100\%$ |
| Percent by mass, $\%(m/m)$ | Mass of solute per mass of solution $\times\ 100\%$ |

Every one of the three is a ratio of solute to **solution**, which is what makes them a set. A fourth unit, molality, measures solute against *solvent* instead; it belongs with the colligative-property calculations in 16.4, where the reason for the difference becomes clear.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Concentration** | A measure of the amount of solute dissolved in a given quantity of solvent |
| **Dilute solution** | A solution that contains a relatively small amount of solute |
| **Concentrated solution** | A solution that contains a large amount of solute |
| **Molarity (M)** | The number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of solution; also known as molar concentration |
| **Dilution** | Reducing the number of moles of solute per unit volume by adding solvent, while the total number of moles of solute remains unchanged |
| **Percent by volume** | The ratio of the volume of solute to the volume of solution |
| **Percent by mass** | The ratio of the mass of the solute to the mass of the solution |

# 16.3 Colligative Properties of Solutions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Colligative properties** are properties of solutions that depend only on the *number* of solute particles, not on their identity. That single sentence controls everything in this section: whenever a colligative property is in question, the chemistry of the solute is irrelevant and the count of particles is everything.

There are three important colligative properties:

- Vapour-pressure lowering
- Freezing-point depression
- Boiling-point elevation

## Vapour-pressure lowering

Solute particles reduce the number of solvent particles able to escape into the vapour. Fewer escapes means equilibrium is established at a lower vapour pressure.

## Ionic against molecular solutes

Because only the count matters, ionic solutes that dissociate have a greater effect on vapour pressure than nondissociating solutes — one mole of a dissociating solute puts more than one mole of particles into the solution.

Take 3 moles of solute dissolved in water:

| Solute | Behaviour | Moles of particles |
|---|---|---|
| Glucose | Does not dissociate | 3 |
| $\mathrm{NaCl}$ | Dissociates into 2 ions | 6 |
| $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ | Dissociates into 3 ions | 9 |

The decrease in vapour pressure is proportional to the number of solute particles, so the three solutes above lower the vapour pressure in the ratio 3 : 6 : 9 even though equal amounts of each were added. Converting moles of solute into moles of particles is therefore the first step of any colligative problem, and it is the step most often skipped.

## Freezing-point depression

When a substance freezes, its particles form an orderly pattern. A solute disrupts the formation of that solid pattern, so more kinetic energy must be withdrawn before the solution will solidify. The freezing point of a solution is therefore lower than the freezing point of the pure solvent.

The magnitude of the freezing-point depression is proportional to the number of solute particles dissolved, not their identity.

## Boiling-point elevation

The **boiling point** is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid equals atmospheric pressure. That definition is what connects this property to the first one.

Adding a nonvolatile solute decreases the solvent's vapour pressure. More kinetic energy is then required to raise the vapour pressure back up to atmospheric, which increases the boiling point. The boiling point of a solution is therefore higher than the boiling point of the pure solvent, and the elevation is again proportional to the number of solute particles.

So boiling-point elevation is not an independent phenomenon; it is vapour-pressure lowering seen from the other side. The two always appear together, and both scale with particle count for the same reason.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Colligative properties** | Properties of solutions that depend only on the number of solute particles, not their identity |
| **Vapour-pressure lowering** | The reduction in vapour pressure caused by solute particles reducing the number of solvent particles able to escape into the vapour, so that equilibrium is established at a lower vapour pressure |
| **Freezing-point depression** | The lowering of a solution's freezing point below that of the pure solvent, because the solute disrupts the formation of the solid pattern and more kinetic energy must be withdrawn for the solution to solidify |
| **Boiling point** | The temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid equals atmospheric pressure |
| **Boiling-point elevation** | The raising of a solution's boiling point above that of the pure solvent, because a nonvolatile solute decreases the vapour pressure and more kinetic energy is required to raise it to atmospheric pressure |

# 16.4 Calculations Involving Colligative Properties

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

16.3 established that the freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation are proportional to the number of solute particles. This section supplies the concentration unit that counts particles per fixed amount of solvent, and the two formulas that turn that count into a temperature change.

## Molality and mole fraction

**Molality** is the number of moles of solute dissolved in 1 kilogram (1000 grams) of solvent. It is also known as molal concentration.

$$m = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{kilograms of solvent}}$$

Molality is the unit these calculations use rather than molarity, and the difference is in the denominator: molality is per kilogram of **solvent**, where molarity is per litre of **solution**.

The **mole fraction (X)** of a solute in a solution is the ratio of moles of the solute to the total number of moles of solvent and solute:

$$X_A = \frac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}, \qquad X_B = \frac{n_B}{n_A + n_B}$$

where $X_A$ is the mole fraction of solute A and $X_B$ the mole fraction of solvent B, $n_A$ is the moles of solute and $n_B$ the moles of solvent.

## Freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation

**Freezing-point depression ($\Delta T_f$)** is the difference between the freezing point of the solution and the freezing point of the pure solvent:

$$\Delta T_f = K_f \times m$$

where $K_f$ is the molal freezing-point depression constant and $m$ is the molality.

**Boiling-point elevation ($\Delta T_b$)** is the difference between the boiling point of the solution and the boiling point of the pure solvent:

$$\Delta T_b = K_b \times m$$

where $K_b$ is the molal boiling-point elevation constant.

Both formulas give a *difference*, not a temperature. The answer to a question asking for the freezing or boiling point of the solution is the pure solvent's value with $\Delta T$ applied — subtracted in the freezing case, added in the boiling case, because 16.3 fixes the direction each way. For water, an elevation of 1.54 °C gives:

$$100.00\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} + 1.54\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} = 101.54\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$$

## The constants

| Solvent | $K_f$ (°C/m) | $K_b$ (°C/m) |
|---|---|---|
| Acetic acid | 3.90 | 3.07 |
| Benzene | 5.12 | 2.53 |
| Camphor | 37.7 | 5.95 |
| Cyclohexane | 20.2 | 2.79 |
| Ethanol | 1.99 | 1.19 |
| Nitrobenzene | 7.00 | 5.24 |
| Phenol | 7.40 | 3.56 |
| Water | 1.86 | 0.512 |

The table is indexed by **solvent**. No solute appears in it, which is the definition of a colligative property expressed as a table: the size of the effect per unit molality is a property of the solvent alone.

## Order of working

Putting 16.3 and this section together gives the sequence a calculation follows.

1. Find the moles of solute.
2. Multiply by the number of particles the solute dissociates into — 1 for a solute that does not dissociate, 2 for $\mathrm{NaCl}$, 3 for $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$.
3. Divide by the kilograms of solvent to obtain the molality.
4. Multiply by $K_f$ or $K_b$ for the solvent to obtain $\Delta T_f$ or $\Delta T_b$.
5. Subtract $\Delta T_f$ from the pure solvent's freezing point, or add $\Delta T_b$ to its boiling point.

Step 2 is the one the formulas do not remind you about, and step 5 is where the sign goes wrong. Freezing point moves down, boiling point moves up.

## Solution concentration units

Solution concentration can be expressed in four ways in all.

| Unit | Definition |
|---|---|
| Molarity (M) | Moles of solute per litre of solution |
| Molality (m) | Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent |
| Percent by volume | (Volume of solute / volume of solution) $\times\ 100\%$ |
| Percent by mass | (Mass of solute / mass of solution) $\times\ 100\%$ |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Molality (m)** | The number of moles of solute dissolved in 1 kilogram (1000 grams) of solvent; also known as molal concentration |
| **Mole fraction (X)** | The ratio of moles of the solute to the total number of moles of solvent and solute |
| **Freezing-point depression ($\Delta T_f$)** | The difference between the freezing point of the solution and the freezing point of the pure solvent |
| **Boiling-point elevation ($\Delta T_b$)** | The difference between the boiling point of the solution and the boiling point of the pure solvent |
| **$K_f$** | The molal freezing-point depression constant |
| **$K_b$** | The molal boiling-point elevation constant |

# S1M-1 Semester 1 Midterm review: Intermolecular forces, Chapter 11, Chapter 3, Investigation 1

## Semester 1 Midterm review: Intermolecular forces, Chapter 11, Chapter 3, Investigation 1

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Chemistry H review guide (PA). Writers: Lorenzo Huang 10-3, Amy Li 10-8. Editor: Aiden Chen 10-12, Erica Zhang 10-7. Range: Intermolecular forces, Chapter 11, Chapter 3, Investigation 1. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

Review: Molecular Geometry and Polarity, Naming

Molecular Shape and Polarity

Polar vs Nonpolar molecule:

- Polar molecule: A molecule that has one end with a positive charge and the other end with a negative charge

- Non-polar molecule: a molecule that does not have positive or negative ends
- Having a polar bond (electrons being shared unevenly between two atoms) doesn’t guarantee the molecule is polar
- Polarity dependent on both bond polarity and molecular geometry
- Nonpolar: if molecular shape if symmetrical, it is a nonpolar molecule (polar bonds can cancel out)

- Polar: if shape is asymmetrical, then bond polarities cannot cancel each other out and there must be at least 1 polar bond to make it polar (thus there will be an overall dipole moment)

- Exception: Ozone (O3) has nonpolar bonds but is a polar molecule overall

Naming and Formulas

- Ionic compounds: Compounds with electrostatic attraction between cation and anion

- Neutral compounds, so charges must balance (crisscross method and swap numbers to form ratios)

-Formula unit: smallest whole number unit, represents the

ratio of the two ions

Naming ionic compounds:

- name of cation followed by anion (-ide)

Monatomic ions:

- cations formed from metal atoms have the same name as the metal, but anions are named by replacing the ending of the name with “-ide”

Polyatomic ions:

- some specific ones such as ammonium or hydroxide

Oxyanions: polyatomic ions composed of an element bonded to one or more oxygen atoms

- more O atoms, “-ate” (chlorate)

- less O atoms, “-ite” (chlorite)

- most number of O atoms, per-…-ate (e.g. perchlorate)

- least number of O atoms, hypo-…-ite (e.g. hypochlorite)

Naming molecules — Binary Molecular Compounds

- first element (entire name) + second element (root of element + ide), but difference with ionic compounds is that prefixes are used to indicate the number of atoms of each type (e.g. CO = Carbon Monoxide)

- if first element is 1, then no need for prefix

mono

Naming Acids:

- acid is a compound that contains one or more hydrogen atoms and produces hydrogen ions when dissolved in water (e.g. HCl -> Cl- and H+)

- if the anion is “ide”, then acid is “hydro-…-ic acid”

- if anion is “ate”, then acid is “..-ic acid”

- if anion is “-ite”, then acid is “—-ous acid”

Naming Bases:

- a base is compound that produces hydroxide ions when dissolved in water (generally is an ionic compound)

- rule: name of cation s followed by name of anion (e.g. KOH = Potassium Hydroxide)

Intermolecular forces

- Intramolecular forces: forces that exist inside the molecules (only covalent bonds)

- Intermolecular forces: forces that exist between neighboring molecules

- Intermolecular forces are much weaker than intramolecular forces

3 Types of Intermolecular forces: Dispersion, Dipole-dipole, and Hydrogen Bonds

- Melting and boiling involve overcoming intermolecular forces, not breaking covalent bonds.
- Stronger intermolecular forces generally result in higher boiling points.

1. Dispersion forces

-Caused by temporary and induced dipoles (temporary positive or negative charges on atoms).

-Present in all atoms and molecules.

- The only intermolecular force in noble gases and nonpolar molecules such as H₂ .

- Increase in strength with increasing molecular or atomic size and mass.

- Example: Dispersion force strength and boiling point: Br₂ > F₂ > H₂ .

2. Dipole–dipole forces

-Attractions between opposite partial charges of neighboring polar molecules.

-Occur between molecules with permanent dipoles.

-Examples of polar molecules: HCl and H₂O.

-Examples of nonpolar molecules: Cl₂ and CO₂.

-Molecular polarity depends on bond polarity and molecular geometry.

- Polar bonds can cancel out if the molecule is symmetrical

3. Hydrogen bonding

-A particularly strong type of dipole–dipole attraction, the strongest intermolecular force

-Occurs when H is covalently bonded to N, O, or F and is thus attracted to N, O, or F in another molecule.

-Examples: H₂O, HF, and NH₃ .

-Explains the unusually high boiling points of H₂O, HF, and NH₃. .

Intermolecular Forces and Boiling Points

- Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome, meaning higher boiling points.

-Larger molecules generally have stronger dispersion forces, meaning higher boiling points.

- Noble gas boiling points increase with atomic size and mass.

-Hydrogen bonding can produce unusually high boiling points.

Intermolecular forces and organic chemistry

Hydrocarbons

-Molecules made of only carbon and hydrogen

- General formula representation: C       H

- Carbon typically forms four covalent bonds

- Hydrocarbons are generally nonpolar, and Dispersion forces are their main intermolecular forces.

-Alkanes: Hydrocarbons with n carbon atoms and 2n+2 hydrogen atoms

Homologous Series

-A series of closely related organic compounds.

-Members have the same general formula, similar chemical properties but changing physical properties

- As the number of carbon atoms increases, molecular mass and dispersion forces generally increase

Molecular and Structural Formulae

-Empirical formula: Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.

-Molecular formula: Actual number of each type of atom. --

-Full structural formula: Shows all atoms and bonds.

-Condensed structural formula: Groups atoms together and omits most bonds.

-Skeletal formula: Shows the carbon backbone; carbon atoms are assumed at line ends and intersections.

-To obtain an empirical formula, divide all subscripts by their greatest common factor.

Example 1: C4H8 has the empirical formula CH₂ .

Example 2: C3H8 cannot be simplified, so its empirical formula is also C₃H₈ .

Structural Isomerism

-Isomers have the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms.

- Structural isomers can have different physical properties.

- Chain isomerism: Different arrangements of the

carbon chain

- Position isomerism: The same functional group or

feature occurs at different positions.

- Functional group isomerism: Same molecular formula but different functional

groups.

Boiling Point Trends in Organic Compounds

-Larger molecules generally have stronger dispersion forces.

-Branched-chain isomers usually have lower boiling points than corresponding straight-chain isomers, as the former have a smaller surface area and thus weaker dispersion forces

-Branched molecules generally have less surface contact with neighboring molecules, resulting in weaker dispersion attractions.

-For molecules with similar molar masses, the boiling point order given in the class notes is: Alkanes < Aldehydes < Alcohols < Carboxylic acids.

-Alkanes: Mainly dispersion forces.

-Aldehydes: Dispersion and dipole–dipole forces.

-Alcohols: Dispersion, dipole–dipole forces, and hydrogen bonding. -Carboxylic acids: Strong intermolecular attractions, including hydrogen bonding.

Using IMF to explain properties

Physical properties of halogens:

-form colored gases, are poisonous, form diatomic molecules (color, density and B.P. All increase going down a group)

Understanding properties of liquids:

-Surface Tension: amount of energy required to stretch or increase the surface of a Iiquid by a unit area (because spheres have the smallest SA for their volume, water droplets assume an almost spherical shape)

-Cohesion vs Adhesion Forces: former is attraction between like molecules, latter is attraction between unlike molecules

-Capillary action: Movement of a liquid upward through a narrow tube due to cohesion and adhesion.

- Water in glass: Adhesion > cohesion, producing a concave meniscus.

- Mercury in glass: Cohesion > adhesion, producing a convex

meniscus. Viscosity: A liquid’s resistance to flow.

- Stronger intermolecular forces generally result in higher viscosity.

-Vapor Pressure: Pressure exerted by a vapor when the liquid and vapor are in dynamic equilibrium.

- Dynamic equilibrium: Evaporation and condensation occur at equal rate.

-Volatile liquids: Liquids that evaporate readily.

-Higher temperature → more molecules have enough kinetic energy to escape → higher vapor pressure.

-Stronger intermolecular forces → lower vapor pressure; weaker intermolecular forces →

higher vapor pressure.

Boiling Point:

-A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure.

-Normal boiling point: Boiling temperature at 1 atm

-Higher external pressure → higher boiling point, lower external pressure → lower boiling point.

Phase Changes

Melting: Solid → liquid; absorbs energy.

Freezing: Liquid → solid; releases energy.

Vaporization: Liquid → gas; absorbs energy.

Condensation: Gas → liquid; releases energy.

Sublimation: Solid → gas; absorbs energy.

Deposition: Gas → solid; releases energy.

-During a phase change, temperature remains constant while energy is absorbed or released (the flat part on the phase change diagram)

Phase Diagrams (different from the heating curve, or phase change graph mentioned above):

- A phase diagram shows the conditions under which a substance exists as a solid, liquid, or gas.

X-axis: Temperature.

Y-axis: Pressure.

- Each region represents a phase: solid, liquid, or gas.

- Curves separating regions represent phase-change boundaries.

Triple point: Temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid, and gas coexist in

equilibrium. Critical point: Endpoint of the liquid–gas boundary.

Heating Curve:

-Sloping sections: Temperature increases within a single phase.

- Flat sections: A phase change occurs while temperature remains constant.

Solid warms → melting → liquid warms → vaporization → gas warms.

- Energy is absorbed throughout the heating process.

Structure of Solids

- Crystalline solid: Particles have a regular, repeating arrangement with long-range order.

-Amorphous solid: Particles lack a well-defined arrangement and long-range

order.

- Unit cell: Basic repeating structural unit of a crystalline solid.

Lattice point: Position representing an atom, molecule, or ion in a crystal.

Primitive lattice: A lattice with points only at the corners of the unit cell

- Three common cubic cells: Simple cubic, body-centered cubic, and face-centered cubic.

Types of Crystals:

Ionic crystals:

-Lattice points occupied by cations and anions

-Hard, brittle, and have high melting points.

-Poor conductors of heat and electricity in solid, but molten and (aq) state they can conduct

Examples: NaCl, LiF, MgO, CaCO₃ .

Covalent crystals:

- Lattice points occupied by atoms.

-Held together by covalent bonds.

- Hard and have high melting points(they are covalent network solids)

- Generally poor conductors of electricity, except graphite.

Examples: Diamond and quartz (SiO₂ ).

Molecular crystals

- Lattice points occupied by molecules.

- Held together by intermolecular forces.

- Soft and have low melting points.

- Poor conductors of heat and electricity.

Metallic crystals

- Lattice points occupied by metal atoms.

- Held together by metallic bonds(sea of delocalized electrons with metallic cations that

are attracting each other)

-Range from soft to hard and have low to high melting points.

-Good conductors of heat and electricity.

Examples: Na, Mg, Fe, Cu

## Chapter 3 Stoichiometry

Fundamental knowledge

Note: We have not rigorously defined oxidation states in our course. Knowing this should be enough:

- The oxidation states of all atoms in a species should add up to the charge of the species.

- The common oxidation states of an element show up as the common charges of its monatomic ions.

Thinking about valence electrons and the octet rule might also help with memorization. The following oxidation states are just the most common ones, and other oxidation states can be taken on.

- combustion reaction: rapid reactions that produce a flame (most involve oxygen gas as a reactant)

# 1 Measurement, Significant Figures and Uncertainty

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Everything measured in a laboratory is measured against something else. A **measurement** is a comparison between an unknown quantity and a standard. That definition already tells you why no measurement is perfect: the comparison can only be read as finely as the standard and the instrument allow, and the last digit you write down is always the one you had to estimate.

## Significant digits

**Significant digits** are the valid, reliable digits in a measurement. The last digit in any measurement is an estimated, uncertain digit — it is significant, but it is the one you are least sure of.

Counting them follows a small set of rules:

| Rule | Example |
|---|---|
| All non-zero digits count, and any zeros contained between non-zero digits count | 6 s.f. in $300042$ |
| Exact numbers and constants have infinite significant digits | a counted number of objects, or a defined conversion factor |
| Trailing zeros count if there is a decimal point | 3 s.f. in $200.$ |
| Trailing zeros do not count unless scientific notation is explicitly used | 3 s.f. in $2990$, but 4 s.f. in $2.990 \times 10^{3}$ |

The last two rules are the same rule seen from two sides. A bare trailing zero is ambiguous — you cannot tell whether it was measured or is a placeholder — so the notation has to declare the intent. Writing the decimal point, or writing the number in scientific notation, is that declaration.

## Rounding

These rounding rules apply **only to laboratory and statistical results**, not to ordinary arithmetic:

- If the digit right next to the last significant figure is **less than 5**, do not change the last significant figure.
- If it is **greater than 5**, round the last significant figure up.
- If it is **equal to 5 and is followed by a non-zero digit**, round the last significant figure up.

The Chinese mnemonic for this is **"四舍六入，五成双"** — four and below are discarded, six and above are carried up, and a bare five is rounded so that the retained digit becomes even. Rounding a bare five always upwards would bias a long run of results upwards; sending it to the even digit lets the errors cancel over many measurements.

## Arithmetic with measured numbers

The result of a calculation cannot be more certain than the least certain measurement that went into it. Which property of "least certain" matters depends on the operation:

- **Addition and subtraction:** round the result to have as many **decimal places** as the measured number with the smallest number of decimal places.
- **Multiplication and division:** round the result to have as many **significant figures** as the measured number with the smallest number of significant figures.

## Uncertainty and error

**Uncertainty** is the variation in measured data. Two different things produce it, and they are not fixed the same way.

| | Systematic error | Random error |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A consistent or reproducible error that affects the **accuracy** of a measurement | An unpredictable variation in measurements |
| Caused by | Instrument, environment, or methodology | Human or environmental fluctuations |

Because a systematic error is reproducible, repeating the measurement does not remove it — every repeat is wrong in the same direction. Random error, being unpredictable, does average out over repeats.

Two words that are used loosely in ordinary speech mean different things here:

- **Accuracy** is how close a measurement is to the accepted value.
- **Precision** is the repeatability of the measurement using a given instrument, and is reflected in the number of significant figures.

A measurement can be precise and inaccurate at once — that is exactly the signature of a systematic error.

Two further quantities describe the instrument and the data:

- **Instrument limit of error (ILE):** the maximum amount by which a measurement made by an instrument can deviate from the true value. It is generally the least count of the instrument, or half of the least count.
- **Deviation:** the amount by which a single value differs from the average.

## Representing an experimental result

| Quantity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Absolute uncertainty/error** | The uncertainty $\Delta x$ in the same units as the measurement, reported as $x \pm \Delta x$ |
| **Relative uncertainty** | $\dfrac{\Delta x}{x}$ |
| **Relative error** | $\dfrac{\text{measured value} - \text{expected value}}{\text{expected value}}$ |
| **Percentage uncertainty/error** | The relative uncertainty or relative error expressed as a percentage |

## Error propagation

When measured quantities are combined, their uncertainties combine too, and the rule mirrors the significant-figure rule for the same operation.

**Addition and subtraction** — absolute uncertainties add:

$$\Delta z = \Delta a + \Delta b$$

**Multiplication and division** — relative uncertainties add:

$$\frac{\Delta z}{z} = \frac{\Delta a}{a} + \frac{\Delta b}{b}$$

**Multiplication by an exact number** — multiply the uncertainty by the same exact number:

$$\Delta(ka) = k\,\Delta a$$

**Powers** — for $z = a^{n}$, the relative uncertainty is multiplied by the power:

$$\frac{\Delta z}{z} = |n| \, \frac{\Delta a}{a}$$

Notice that addition and subtraction work in absolute terms while multiplication, division and powers work in relative terms. That is the same split as the significant-figure rules: sums care about decimal places, products care about significant figures.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Measurement** | A comparison between an unknown quantity and a standard |
| **Significant digits** | The valid, reliable digits in a measurement |
| **Uncertainty** | The variation in measured data |
| **Systematic error** | Consistent or reproducible error that affects the accuracy of a measurement; caused by instrument, environment, or methodology |
| **Random error** | An unpredictable variation in measurements; caused by human or environmental fluctuations |
| **Accuracy** | How close a measurement is to the accepted value |
| **Precision** | The repeatability of the measurement using a given instrument, shown by the number of significant figures |
| **Instrument limit of error (ILE)** | The maximum amount by which a measurement made by an instrument can deviate from the true value; generally the least count, or half the least count |
| **Deviation** | The amount by which a single value differs from the average |
| **Absolute uncertainty** | The uncertainty of a measurement expressed in the units of the measurement |
| **Relative uncertainty** | The absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value |
| **Relative error** | (Measured value − expected value) ÷ expected value |

# 6.1 The Wave Nature of Light

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Light is a kind of **electromagnetic radiation**. An electromagnetic wave consists of an electric field and a magnetic field oscillating at right angles to each other.

## Describing a wave

**Frequency** ($\nu$) is the number of waves passing a given point per unit of time. Its unit is the hertz (Hz).

All electromagnetic radiation travels at the same velocity — **the speed of light**:

$$c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$$

Because the speed is fixed for every kind of electromagnetic radiation, wavelength and frequency are not independent. They are locked together by

$$c = \lambda\nu$$

so a longer wavelength must mean a lower frequency, and a shorter wavelength a higher one.

## Colour, wavelength and energy

Different colours of light correspond to different wavelengths and frequencies. Violet has the **shortest wavelength and the highest frequency**; red has the **longest wavelength and the lowest frequency**. Every other visible colour lies between them.

Electromagnetic radiation with higher frequency has higher energy. Combining this with $c = \lambda\nu$ gives the chain that runs through the whole chapter: shorter wavelength → higher frequency → higher energy. Violet light therefore carries more energy per wave than red light.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Electromagnetic radiation** | Radiation, such as light, whose wave consists of electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles |
| **Frequency ($\nu$)** | The number of waves passing a given point per unit of time, measured in hertz (Hz) |
| **Speed of light ($c$)** | The velocity at which all electromagnetic radiation travels, $3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$ |

# 6.2 Quantised Energy and Photons

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Planck explained the behaviour of radiation by assuming that energy does not flow continuously but comes in packets called **quanta**.

## The quantum

The energy of a single quantum depends only on the frequency of the radiation:

$$E = h\nu$$

where $h$ is the **Planck constant**:

$$h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$$

This is the precise form of the statement from the previous section that higher-frequency radiation has higher energy. Energy is not proportional to how bright the light is; it is proportional to frequency, and $h$ is the constant of proportionality.

## The photoelectric effect

Electrons are ejected when light shines on a metal. This is the **photoelectric effect**, and it is the experiment that forces the quantum picture on us.

A **photon** is a particle of electromagnetic radiation with no mass that carries a quantum of energy. Each photon delivers its energy to one electron, all at once — which is why the frequency of the light, not its brightness, decides whether anything happens at all.

Electrons can only be emitted when the frequency exceeds a threshold frequency $\nu_{0}$:

$$\nu > \nu_{0}$$

Below that threshold no photon carries enough energy to free an electron, however many photons arrive. Above it, the energy left over after freeing the electron appears as the electron's motion, so the kinetic energy of the emitted electron is

$$E_{k} = h\nu - h\nu_{0}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Quantum** | A packet of energy; Planck's assumption that energy comes in such packets |
| **Planck constant ($h$)** | The constant relating the energy of a quantum to its frequency, $6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$ |
| **Photoelectric effect** | The ejection of electrons when light shines on a metal |
| **Photon** | A particle of electromagnetic radiation with no mass that carries a quantum of energy |

# 6.3 Line Spectra and the Bohr Model

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two kinds of spectrum

A **continuous spectrum** is one in which one colour fades gradually into the next — the visible spectrum is the standard example. Nothing is missing from it.

An **atomic emission spectrum** is different. The atomic emission spectrum of an element is the set of frequencies of the electromagnetic waves emitted by atoms of that element. It is not continuous: only certain frequencies appear, as separate lines. Any model of the atom has to explain why a heated element emits some frequencies and not others.

## The Bohr model

Bohr assumed that electrons move in **circular orbits** around the nucleus, each orbit designated by a **quantum number** $n$, where $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$

The consequence of that assumption is the important part: energy is only absorbed or emitted to move an electron from one "allowed" energy state to another. There is no in-between.

## Hydrogen's line spectrum

The model accounts for hydrogen's spectrum in three steps:

1. An electron can be **excited** to a higher energy level when it absorbs energy.
2. When the atom is in an **excited state**, the electron can drop from the higher energy level to a lower energy level.
3. The atom then emits a photon corresponding to the **difference between the energy levels** associated with the two orbits.

Because only certain orbits are allowed, only certain differences between orbits exist, so only certain frequencies of radiation can be emitted. That is precisely why the emission spectrum is a set of discrete lines rather than a continuous band — the line spectrum is a direct picture of the allowed energy gaps inside the atom.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Continuous spectrum** | A spectrum in which one colour fades gradually into the next, such as the visible spectrum |
| **Atomic emission spectrum** | The set of frequencies of the electromagnetic waves emitted by atoms of an element |
| **Bohr model** | A model assuming electrons move in circular orbits around the nucleus, each designated by a quantum number $n$, with energy absorbed or emitted only to move an electron between allowed energy states |
| **Quantum number ($n$)** | The number designating an allowed orbit in the Bohr model, $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ |
| **Excited state** | The state of an atom in which an electron has absorbed energy and occupies a higher energy level |

# 6.4 The Wave Behaviour of Matter

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## De Broglie's argument

The photoelectric effect showed that light, long treated as a wave, has material properties. Louis de Broglie ran that argument in reverse: if light can have material properties, then matter should exhibit wave properties.

This is the step that dissolves the strict division between particles and waves. An electron is no longer simply a small ball in orbit, and the next two sections build the model of the atom on that footing.

## The Heisenberg uncertainty principle

The **Heisenberg uncertainty principle** states that the position and the velocity (or momentum) of a moving electron cannot simultaneously be measured and known exactly.

Read against the previous lesson, this is what makes the Bohr picture untenable as a literal description. A circular orbit is a statement about where the electron is *and* how fast it is moving at every instant — exactly the pair of quantities the uncertainty principle says cannot both be known. Whatever replaces the orbit will have to describe the electron in terms of probability rather than position, which is what the quantum mechanical model does.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **De Broglie's theory** | The theory that if light can have material properties, matter should exhibit wave properties |
| **Heisenberg uncertainty principle** | The position and the velocity/momentum of a moving electron cannot simultaneously be measured and known exactly |

# 6.5 Quantum Mechanics and Atomic Orbitals

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The quantum mechanical model

Schrödinger's **quantum mechanical model** replaces Bohr's definite orbits with a description in terms of probability, which is the only kind of description the uncertainty principle permits.

An **atomic orbital** is represented pictorially as a region of space in which there is a high probability of finding an electron. Note carefully what this is and is not: it is not a path the electron travels, and it does not say where the electron is at a given moment. It is a region where the electron is likely to be found.

## Shapes of the orbitals

Each type of orbital has its own characteristic shape:

| Orbital | Shape |
|---|---|
| $s$ | Spherical |
| $p$ | Dumbbell |
| $d$ | Four-leaf clover |
| $f$ | Complex shapes |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Quantum mechanical model** | Schrödinger's model of the atom, describing electrons in terms of probability |
| **Atomic orbital** | A region of space in which there is a high probability of finding an electron |

# 6.6 Representations of Orbitals and Electron Configurations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Counting orbitals

Each kind of orbital exists in a fixed number of orientations, and that number is what limits how many electrons a sublevel can hold:

| Sublevel | Number of orbitals |
|---|---|
| $s$ | 1 |
| $p$ | 3 |
| $d$ | 5 |
| $f$ | 7 |

For an energy level with principal quantum number $n$:

- Number of sublevels in the energy level: $n$
- Total number of orbitals in the energy level: $n^{2}$
- Maximum number of electrons in the energy level: $2n^{2}$

The last of these follows from the one before it together with the Pauli exclusion principle below: $n^{2}$ orbitals, at most two electrons each, gives $2n^{2}$.

## The three filling rules

**Degenerate orbitals** are orbitals with the same energy — the three $p$ orbitals of a sublevel, for instance.

**Aufbau principle:** electrons in different orbitals are filled in the increasing order of energy. That order is

$$1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s < 4d < 5p < 6s < 4f < 5d < 6p < 7s < 5f < 6d < 7p$$

Note that it is not simply the order of the principal quantum number: $4s$ fills before $3d$, and $6s$ before $4f$.

**Pauli exclusion principle:** an atomic orbital may describe at most two electrons, and those two must have opposite spin.

**Hund's rule:** for degenerate orbitals, the lowest energy is attained when the number of electrons with the same spin is maximised. In practice this means electrons spread out singly across degenerate orbitals, all with parallel spin, before any orbital takes a second electron.

## Orbital diagrams

In an **orbital diagram**, each box represents one orbital and half-arrows represent the electrons; the direction of the arrow represents the relative spin of the electron. The diagram is the way to make the Pauli principle and Hund's rule visible — two arrows in a box must point in opposite directions, and a set of degenerate boxes fills with parallel arrows first.

## Abbreviated electron configurations

An **abbreviated electron configuration** (also called a condensed electron configuration, or noble gas notation) represents the electron configuration of the nearest noble-gas element of lower atomic number by that element's chemical symbol in brackets.

This splits the electrons into groups that matter chemically:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Core electrons** | The inner-shell electrons |
| **Outer-shell electrons** | The electrons given after the noble-gas core |
| **Valence electrons** | The electrons involved in chemical bonding |

## Writing a configuration from the periodic table

The periodic table is laid out in the Aufbau order, so it can be read directly as a configuration:

1. Locate the element — which block and group it is in, and which noble gas precedes it.
2. Put together all the orbitals before the element's block.
3. Count the group of the element to determine the number of electrons in the unfilled orbital.

Applying those steps gives a standard pattern for each part of the table:

| Period | Groups | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| 2nd and 3rd | A1–A8 | $[\,]\,ns\,np$ |
| 4th and 5th | A1–A2 | $[\,]\,ns$ |
| 4th and 5th | A3–A8 | $[\,]\,(n-1)d^{10}\,ns\,np$ |
| 6th and 7th | A1–A2 | $[\,]\,ns$ |
| 6th and 7th | A3–A8 | $[\,]\,(n-2)f^{14}\,(n-1)d^{10}\,ns\,np$ |

The extra $d$ and $f$ terms in the later periods are exactly step 2 at work: those sublevels lie before the $p$ block in the Aufbau order, so they are already full by the time you reach groups A3–A8.

## Exceptions

Some elements have electron configurations that differ from what the Aufbau order predicts, because of the extra stability of half-filled and fully filled sublevels:

| Element | Configuration |
|---|---|
| Cr | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{5}4s^{1}$ |
| Mo | $[\mathrm{Kr}]\,4d^{5}5s^{1}$ |
| Cu | $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^{1}$ |
| Ag | $[\mathrm{Kr}]\,4d^{10}5s^{1}$ |
| Au | $[\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^{14}5d^{10}6s^{1}$ |

In every case one $s$ electron is promoted so that the $d$ sublevel becomes exactly half filled (Cr, Mo) or completely filled (Cu, Ag, Au).

## Configurations of ions

- **Metal atoms** lose electrons, forming **cations**.
- **Nonmetal atoms** gain electrons, forming **anions**.
- **Transition metals** lose their outermost-shell electrons first, and only then lose inner $d$-level electrons.

The transition-metal rule is the one most often got wrong. Because $4s$ fills before $3d$ but lies in the outer shell, the $4s$ electrons are the first to go even though they were the first to arrive.

## Excited-state configurations

The electron configuration for an **excited state** shows one or more electrons in a higher energy level than the Aufbau order would put them. Recognising one is a matter of checking the filling order: if a higher orbital is occupied while a lower one is not full, the configuration describes an excited state rather than a ground state.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Degenerate orbitals** | Orbitals with the same energy |
| **Aufbau principle** | Electrons in different orbitals are filled in the increasing order of energy |
| **Pauli exclusion principle** | An atomic orbital may describe at most two electrons, with opposite spin |
| **Hund's rule** | For degenerate orbitals, the lowest energy is attained when the number of electrons with the same spin is maximised |
| **Orbital diagram** | A diagram in which each box represents one orbital and half-arrows represent electrons, the arrow direction showing relative spin |
| **Abbreviated electron configuration** | A configuration in which the nearest noble-gas element of lower atomic number is represented by its chemical symbol in brackets; also called condensed electron configuration or noble gas notation |
| **Core electrons** | The inner-shell electrons |
| **Outer-shell electrons** | The electrons given after the noble-gas core |
| **Valence electrons** | The electrons involved in chemical bonding |
| **Excited-state configuration** | An electron configuration showing one or more electrons in a higher energy level |

# 7.1 Development of the Periodic Table

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Before the table

In the late 1790s, Antoine Lavoisier compiled a list of 23 known elements. By 1870, approximately 70 elements were recognised. The problem the century created was not a shortage of elements but a shortage of order — three times as many substances, with no principle saying which belonged with which.

## Mendeleev's contributions

Mendeleev corrected the atomic masses of several elements, among them Be, In, U, Os, Ir, Pt, Y and Ti. This matters more than it first appears. His table was arranged by atomic mass, so a wrong mass put an element in the wrong place; the arrangement itself was what revealed which masses had to be wrong.

## The modern periodic table

In 1913, Henry Moseley arranged the elements by **atomic number** instead of atomic mass, revealing a clear periodic pattern.

That is the arrangement still used. Atomic number is the count of protons, a whole number fixed for each element, so ordering by it removes the anomalies that ordering by mass produced.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Modern periodic table** | The arrangement of the elements by atomic number rather than atomic mass, introduced by Henry Moseley in 1913, which reveals a clear periodic pattern |

# 7.2 Effective Nuclear Charge

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two pulls on every electron

In multi-electron atoms, electrons are attracted to the nucleus but also repelled by other electrons.

That single sentence is the whole of this section, and it is worth reading slowly, because every trend in the rest of the chapter is a consequence of it. A hydrogen atom has one electron, and that electron feels nothing but the nucleus. Every other atom has at least two, so the net pull an electron experiences is the attraction of the nucleus reduced by the repulsion of the other electrons. That net pull is the **effective nuclear charge**, written $Z_{\text{eff}}$.

## Why it changes across the table

The two influences do not change together as you move about the periodic table, and that is what makes $Z_{\text{eff}}$ vary:

- **Across a period**, atoms' nuclei gain more protons while the added electrons enter the same principal energy level. The attraction grows faster than the repulsion, so $Z_{\text{eff}}$ increases and the nucleus exerts a stronger pull on electrons in that level.
- **Down a group**, $Z_{\text{eff}}$ stays the same for the valence electrons; what changes instead is that those electrons sit in a further principal energy level.

## What it explains

Holding those two statements alongside the distance of the valence electrons from the nucleus is enough to derive the sections that follow — atomic and ionic size (7.3), ionisation energy (7.4), and electron affinity and electronegativity (7.5) all reduce to how tightly the nucleus holds the outer electrons.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Effective nuclear charge ($Z_{\text{eff}}$)** | The net attraction an electron in a multi-electron atom experiences, given that electrons are attracted to the nucleus but also repelled by other electrons |

# 7.3 Sizes of Atoms and Ions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Measuring an atom

An atom has no hard edge, so its size has to be defined by what it does rather than by what it is. The **bonding atomic radius** is defined as one-half of the distance between covalently bonded nuclei.

## Trends in atomic size

- **Across a period, from left to right: smaller radius.** Atoms' nuclei gain more protons, which increases the effective nuclear charge; the stronger pull acts on electrons in the same principal energy level, drawing them inwards.
- **Down a group: larger radius.** Atoms have more principal energy levels, and the larger orbitals mean that the valence electrons are further from the nucleus.

The first of these is the counterintuitive one — an atom with more electrons is *smaller* — and the reason is that the added electrons go into a level that already exists, while the added protons pull on all of them.

## Sizes of ions

Ionic size depends on two things:

- the nuclear charge;
- the number of electron orbitals in which electrons reside.

From those, the rules follow:

- **Cations (positively charged ions) are smaller than their parent atoms.** The outermost electron has been removed and the repulsion between electrons is reduced.
- **Anions (negatively charged ions) are larger than their parent atoms.** An electron has been added and the repulsion is increased.
- **Ionic size increases down a group**, for the same reason atomic size does.
- **In an isoelectronic series** — ions with the same number of electrons — ionic size decreases with increasing nuclear charge. The electron count is held fixed, so nothing is left to vary but the pull of the nucleus, and more protons pull the same electron cloud in tighter.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Bonding atomic radius** | One-half of the distance between covalently bonded nuclei |
| **Cation** | A positively charged ion; smaller than its parent atom |
| **Anion** | A negatively charged ion; larger than its parent atom |
| **Isoelectronic series** | A set of ions with the same number of electrons, in which ionic size decreases as nuclear charge increases |

# 7.4 Ionisation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Ionisation energy

**Ionisation energy** is the amount of energy required to remove an electron — the valence electron first — from the ground state of a gaseous atom or ion. It is the *minimum* energy required to remove an electron, and it is **always positive**, because pulling a negative electron away from a positive nucleus can never release energy.

Electrons can be removed one at a time, giving a first ionisation energy, a second ionisation energy, and so on. **It requires more energy to remove each successive electron**: once the first electron has gone the particle is already positive, so the next electron is held more tightly than the last.

## Trends in first ionisation energy

The **first ionisation energy** is the energy required to remove the first electron.

- **Down a group: less ionisation energy.** $Z_{\text{eff}}$ is the same, but the valence electrons are further away from the nucleus, so they are easier to remove.
- **Across a period: ionisation energy increases**, making the electron harder to remove, because $Z_{\text{eff}}$ increases.

## Exceptions: the discontinuities

The across-a-period increase is not perfectly smooth. Two steps go the wrong way:

| Step | Reason |
|---|---|
| Group 5A to 6A | The electron comes from a doubly occupied orbital, where the two electrons in the same orbital repel each other |
| Group 2A to 3A | The 2A electron is taken from an $s$ orbital, which is more strongly attracted to the nucleus |

Both exceptions come from the same source: the trend argument assumes only $Z_{\text{eff}}$ changes, and at these two points the orbital the electron is being removed *from* changes as well.

## The quantum leap

When all the valence electrons have been removed, so that the next electron must come from the noble gas core, the ionisation energy takes a quantum leap. This is the single most useful diagnostic in the section: find the enormous jump in a table of successive ionisation energies, and the number of electrons removed before it tells you how many valence electrons the element has, and hence its group.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ionisation energy** | The minimum energy required to remove an electron (the valence electron first) from the ground state of a gaseous atom or ion; always positive |
| **First ionisation energy** | The energy required to remove the first electron |

# 7.5 Electron Affinity and Electronegativity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Electron affinity

**Electron affinity** is the energy change when an electron is added to a gaseous atom. Where ionisation energy asks what it costs to take an electron away, electron affinity asks what happens when one is given.

The sign convention is what makes this section awkward, so fix it first: **the more negative the electron affinity, the greater the attraction to the added electron.** A large negative value means the atom wants the electron badly.

**Electron affinities become more exothermic across a period and down a group** — that is, it becomes easier to gain an electron and the value becomes more negative.

## Exceptions

| Group | Reason |
|---|---|
| Group 2A | The added electron goes into a $p$ orbital, so it takes more energy to place it in a higher energy level |
| Group 5A | There is no empty orbital, so the extra electron goes into an already occupied orbital, which creates repulsion |

Both exceptions have the same shape as the ionisation-energy exceptions: the trend assumes the incoming electron always goes into the same sort of place, and in these two groups it does not.

## Electronegativity

**Electronegativity** is the ability of an atom to attract electrons when the atom is in a compound. It is measured on the **Pauling scale**, which runs from 0.7 to 4.0.

- **Down a group, electronegativity decreases.** The valence shell is held less strongly by the nucleus, so it is harder for the atom to attract an electron.
- **Across a period, electronegativity increases.** The attraction from the nucleus is greater, so it is easier for the atom to attract an electron.

Electron affinity is a measured energy change for an isolated gaseous atom; electronegativity describes an atom already bonded inside a compound. They point in the same direction across the table because both are driven by how strongly the nucleus holds the valence shell — and electronegativity is the quantity Chapter 8 uses to decide what kind of bond forms.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Electron affinity** | The energy change when adding an electron to a gaseous atom; the more negative the value, the greater the attraction to the added electron |
| **Electronegativity** | The ability of an atom to attract electrons when the atom is in a compound |
| **Pauling scale** | The scale on which electronegativity is measured, running from 0.7 to 4.0 |

# 7.6 Metals, Nonmetals and Metalloids

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The trend in metallic character

- **Across a period, metallic character decreases.**
- **Down a group, metallic character increases.**

These are the trends of the previous two sections read as chemistry rather than as numbers. Metallic behaviour is the behaviour of an element that gives up electrons readily, so metallic character follows low ionisation energy and low electronegativity — which is why it runs in the opposite direction to both.

## The three classes

| | Metals | Nonmetals | Metalloids |
|---|---|---|---|
| Position | Left and centre of the table | Upper right side of the periodic table | Between the two |
| Appearance | Generally shiny, malleable and ductile | Generally gases, or brittle, dull-looking solids | Physical properties of both |
| Conductivity | Good conductors | Poor conductors | Fairly poor conductors |
| Ions formed | Tend to form cations | Tend to form anions | — |
| Compounds | Compounds formed between metals and nonmetals tend to be ionic | Substances containing only nonmetals are molecular compounds | — |
| Oxides | Metal oxides tend to be basic | Most nonmetal oxides are acidic | — |

**Metalloids** are elements with the physical and chemical properties of both metals and nonmetals. Their intermediate conductivity is the clearest single sign of that: better than a nonmetal, worse than a metal.

## Reading the table

The compound rows are the useful ones for prediction. A metal and a nonmetal differ widely in electronegativity — one holds its valence electrons loosely, the other pulls hard — so electrons transfer and the compound is ionic. Two nonmetals both pull hard, neither gives way, and the result is a molecular compound. The acid–base behaviour of the oxides splits along the same line.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Metals** | Elements that are generally shiny, malleable and ductile, are good conductors, and tend to form cations |
| **Nonmetals** | Elements occupying the upper right side of the periodic table, generally gases or brittle, dull-looking solids, and poor conductors |
| **Metalloids** | Elements with physical and chemical properties of both metals and nonmetals; fairly poor conductors |

# 8.1 Lewis Symbols and the Octet Rule

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why bonds form at all

Coulomb's law governs the formation of a chemical bond, and the logic runs in one direction:

$$\text{formation of chemical bond} \longrightarrow \text{more stable} \longrightarrow \text{less potential energy}$$

A **chemical bond** is the electrostatic attraction force that holds two atoms together. Every kind of bond in this chapter — ionic, covalent, metallic — is that same electrostatic attraction arranged differently.

## The octet rule

The **octet rule** states that atoms tend to have 8 electrons in the outermost shell, a stable octet. An atom can attain that octet in three ways: by **losing** electrons, by **gaining** them, or by **sharing** them.

Those three routes are the three bond types. An atom that loses and an atom that gains produce an ionic bond (8.2); atoms that share produce a covalent bond (8.3). Which route an atom takes is decided by its electronegativity, so Chapter 7 is the input to this chapter.

## Lewis symbols

A **Lewis symbol** is an element's chemical symbol with a dot for each valence electron. It is the smallest possible bookkeeping device for bonding: it shows only the electrons that take part, and it shows immediately how far the atom is from an octet.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chemical bond** | The electrostatic attraction force that holds two atoms together |
| **Octet rule** | Atoms tend to have 8 electrons in the outermost shell (a stable octet), attained through losing, gaining, or sharing electrons |
| **Lewis symbol** | An element's chemical symbol with a dot for each valence electron |
