# 6 The War in the Pacific Theatre, 1941–1945

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## 7 December 1941: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor

The attack **severely crippled the US Pacific fleet**. Because the battleship
fleet in Hawaii was crippled, the United States had to rely on **aircraft
carriers and submarines** instead — which is why the carrier battles that follow
were decisive. Japan's aim was to **destroy the US carrier fleet** so that it
could negotiate for peace.

Between the set-piece battles, Allied forces repeatedly bombed and stormed
Japanese-held territory, targeting tiny islands as well as the jungles of New
Guinea and the Philippines, with the goal of **securing airfields and supply
bases that could serve as launching points for future attacks**.

## May 1942: the Battle of the Coral Sea

Both sides suffered enormous losses, but it was a definite win for the United
States and marked **the first defeat for Japan**. The guide describes it as
ending the peak of Japan.

## June 1942: the Battle of Midway

The **turning point**. The United States prevailed and took the offensive for the
first time, in its **first major victory against Japan**, destroying **four
Japanese aircraft carriers**.

## August 1942: Guadalcanal and the Solomon Islands

The Allies took the **first vital step in driving the Japanese back** in the
Pacific. Its significance is that the United States **prevented Japanese efforts
to disrupt US supply routes to Australia and New Zealand**. **William Douglas
Lansford** took part in this combat.

## March 1943: the island-hopping strategy

**Island hopping** is the practice of **skipping over heavily fortified islands
in order to seize lightly defended locations that could support the next
advance**. It turned the vastness of the Pacific into an American ally, letting
the United States leapfrog across it.

In practice, General **Douglas MacArthur**'s troops first captured **New Guinea**,
but found the heavily defended island of **Rabaul** formidable, so the fleets
pushed westwards to invade less-defended islands first — and eventually captured
Rabaul successfully. It worked because, while MacArthur was island hopping in the
south-west Pacific, there were simultaneous central Pacific campaigns invading
the **Gilbert Islands** in November 1943; with two assaults to face, Japan
crashed out.

## January–February 1944: the Mariana Islands

**Key for the invasion of mainland Japan.** The Marianas were a particularly
valuable asset because they were **close enough to Japan for the new US B-29
bombers to reach the mainland**.

## February–April 1945: Iwo Jima and Okinawa

### Iwo Jima

It was attacked because it was a **strategic air base located between the Mariana
Islands and Japan**.

The Japanese had **carved out underground fortifications**, turning the volcanic
island into a death trap for invading US marines. US planners expected only brief
campaigns; it lasted **over five weeks**. The Japanese commander General
**Kuribayashi** concentrated his forces in northern Iwo Jima, which made the
battle very bloody. Two names capture its brutality: **the meat grinder**, where
850 US marines died, and **bloody gorge**, where the Japanese defenders made their
final stand. The United States eventually took the island.

As a **symbol of nationalism**, on **23 February 1945** US troops reaching **Mount
Suribachi** raised a small American flag, then returned to replace it with a
larger one — producing one of the most notable photographs of the war.

**William Douglas Lansford** also fought here, in the field-intelligence unit;
afterwards he worked as a Hollywood screenwriter and published books on the war
and his experiences. **Howard N. McLaughlin** fought here in the repair section
for heavy equipment, and later joined the front line because of a shortage of
soldiers. In his memoir he wrote of the marines' feelings towards the Japanese:
*they neither liked or hated the Japs. They killed them without anger or mercy.
To them they were part of the forces of evil that had to be destroyed*.

### Okinawa

On **1 April 1945** the US Tenth Army arrived at Okinawa, the **last invasion
before mainland Japan**. Conditions were harsh, with heavy rains and rugged
terrain.

The United States overcame **northern Okinawa easily by 18 April**, but the south
was **difficult** because the Japanese had anchored their defences at **Shuri
Castle** behind a series of well-defended high ridges. On **29 May** the United
States finally smashed down Shuri Castle.

From **26 March**, **kamikaze** pilots deliberately crashed their planes into US
aircraft carriers and other battleships.

| Side | Deaths |
|---|---|
| **American** | 1,200, including the Tenth Army's commander Lieutenant General Simon Buckner |
| **Japanese** | About 90,000 combatants and 150,000 civilians |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Battle of Midway** | The June 1942 turning point and first major US victory, destroying four Japanese carriers |
| **Island hopping** | Skipping heavily fortified islands to seize lightly defended ones that could support the next advance |
| **Mariana Islands** | Islands close enough to Japan for the new B-29 bombers to reach the mainland |
| **The meat grinder** | The name given to the Iwo Jima fighting in which 850 US marines died |
| **Bloody gorge** | Where the Japanese defenders of Iwo Jima made their final stand |
| **Shuri Castle** | The anchor of the Japanese defence in southern Okinawa |
| **Kamikaze** | Japanese pilots who deliberately crashed their planes into US ships |

markdown:
# 7 The End of the War, 1944–1945

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The Allied position throughout was that *the only solution to this war is
Germany's unconditional surrender*.

## The European theatre

Three developments brought the war in Europe to an end.

**1. Operation Overlord (June 1944) and the Battle of the Bulge (December
1944).** D-Day marked the beginning of the Allied effort to liberate western
Europe from Hitler; after pushing eastward the Allies fought the Battle of the
Bulge.

**2. Soviet advance from the east.** After winning at **Stalingrad and Kursk** in
south-west Russia in 1943, the USSR reached Poland by 1945 and **conquered
Berlin**. On the way it **liberated concentration camps such as Auschwitz**, which
Allied soldiers found spine-chilling.

**3. The link-up on the Elbe.** On **25 April 1945** American and Soviet troops
converged on the **Elbe River near Torgau**, and both sides knew the end of the war
was days away.

> The guide dates this meeting to April 1944. Its own sequence places it after
> the December 1944 Bulge and the 1945 fall of Berlin, so 1945 is the year the
> guide's own account requires.

### Why Hitler lost so badly

Rather than surrendering when there was clearly no turning back, he **pulled
grandfathers and children into the war** under the order to *fight to the last
man*. German soldiers, however, surrendered. When he finally recognised his
failure he **took his own life**, after which a German general signed the
**unconditional surrender** with the Allies.

**8 May 1945** was **V-E Day** — Victory in Europe Day — when the Allies
celebrated, and it is the date the war in Europe formally ended.

The guide heads this section "officially ended on May 2nd 1945" and then gives 8
May as V-E Day; the two do not agree. **2 May** is the day the Berlin garrison
surrendered, not the end of the war in Europe — take 8 May as the end date.

## The Pacific theatre

In May 1945 the Allies remained sceptical, because **Japan had never declared
surrender** and might attack again. Five events followed in quick succession:

- **6 August** — the United States dropped an atomic bomb on **Hiroshima**,
  killing **140,000 people**
- The **USSR declared war on Japan** and the Red Army took **Manchuria**. Japan
  now faced more enemies, which contributed to its surrender
- **9 August** — the United States dropped an atomic bomb on **Nagasaki**, killing
  **70,000 people**
- **14 August** — Japan surrendered at the **Potsdam Conference**. This was
  **V-J Day for Americans**, and celebration erupted across the United States
- **2 September** — the official time for celebration, late because this was the
  day the formal surrender documents were signed aboard the **USS Missouri** in
  Tokyo Bay: fireworks, confetti, parades, and American flags hung up in New York's
  Times Square

In **Honolulu**, veterans and their girlfriends crowded onto trucks and drove
around. **15 August** was **Britain's V-J Day**, later than the American one
because the Americans wanted to join it.

## The brutality of the war

*It was too much death to contemplate, too much savagery and suffering.* The
total was **65 million deaths worldwide**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Unconditional surrender** | The Allied condition for ending the war, requiring no negotiated terms |
| **V-E Day** | Victory in Europe Day, 8 May 1945 |
| **V-J Day** | Victory over Japan Day: 14 August for Americans, 15 August for Britain |
| **Potsdam Conference** | Where Japan surrendered on 14 August |
| **USS Missouri** | The ship in Tokyo Bay where the formal surrender documents were signed on 2 September |

# 8 The Holocaust, 1933–1945

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

The Holocaust was the **systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six
million European Jews by the Nazi German regime and its allies and
collaborators**. It began in **1933** when Hitler came to power and ended in
**1945** when the Allies defeated the Axis. It is also known as **the Shoah**,
meaning *catastrophe*.

## The target

**Antisemitism** is prejudice against, or hatred of, Jewish people. It was an
old and widespread prejudice dating back to the **Middle Ages (500–1400)**, when
Christians blamed Jews for the death of Jesus. The Nazis then **blamed Jews for
Germany's defeat in the First World War (1914–1918)**, saw Jews as a **separate,
inferior and dangerous race**, and had aimed since the First World War for a
**pure Aryan race**.

The Nazi definition was **racial rather than religious**: it included people who
identified as Christians and people who did not practise Judaism at all.

> The guide's own wording of this definition is damaged, and reads as though the
> Nazis defined Jews *as* Christians. Its sense is that the racial definition
> reached people who were Christian or non-practising — which is why conversion
> offered no protection.

## Practices of persecution

As Germany annexed much of Europe and the USSR, Nazi influence produced
religious and ethnic persecution and execution across Europe. **Persecution** is
hostility and ill-treatment on the basis of beliefs or ethnicity.

- **1935 Nuremberg race laws** — outlawed Jewish–German marriages and stripped
  citizenship
- **Antisemitic propaganda**, boycotts of Jewish-owned businesses, and public
  humiliation through **badges** worn for identification
- **Violence** — for example **Kristallnacht**, concerted violence by Nazis
  against Jews throughout Germany and Austria
- **Ghettos, deportation and isolation**
- **Internment** — imprisoning people
- **Confiscation of Jewish property** and **forced labour**
- Prohibiting sexual relations between Jews and *German blooded people*

Hitler was the main leader, alongside Nazi leaders including **Hermann Göring,
Heinrich Himmler, Reinhard Heydrich and Adolf Eichmann**, other Axis powers, and
local institutions and bureaucracies.

## The Final Solution to the Jewish Question

Finalised at the **Wannsee Conference in January 1942**, the Final Solution was
the **deliberate and systematic mass murder of Jews** — the last stage of the
Holocaust, taking place from 1941 to 1945. **Liquidation** is the process of
dissolving ghetto administrative structures.

Two methods were used.

**1. Mass shooting**, on the outskirts of villages, towns and cities, on an
unprecedented scale and without shame: massacres were **conducted in daylight in
front of residents**. The German units involved included the **Einsatzgruppen**
(special task forces of the SS and police), Order Police battalions and Waffen-SS
units, with the German military providing logistical support.

**2. Gas poisoning**, at killing centres and with mobile gas vans using carbon
monoxide exhaust. This took the name **euthanasia** or *mercy death*, the Nazis
disguising mass murder by telling victims they were to be given showers.

### Killing centres

From late 1941 the Nazis built killing centres in German-occupied Poland, also
called **extermination camps** or **death camps**. Five operated: **Chelmno,
Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau**. They murdered Jews using
poisonous gas. The Nazis disguised their intentions when deporting Jews by
calling the deportations **resettlement actions**. Conditions were inhumane, and
some stronger Jews were sent to forced labour instead.

### Ghettos

**Ghettos** were areas of cities or towns where German occupiers forced Jews to
live in **overcrowded and unsanitary conditions**, enclosed by walls with guards
ensuring nobody escaped. Their purpose was as **holding sites prior to
deportation or murder**; the original purpose was to **isolate and control large
local Jewish populations** in occupied eastern Europe. The first were created in
German-occupied Poland, in **Warsaw and Lodz**.

Jews there were exploited through **forced labour in factories and workshops**,
with minimal food, extreme temperatures, and physical torture and attacks by
Nazis.

Jews in the ghettos **maintained a sense of dignity and community**, and
practised both spiritual and physical resistance: spiritually through the
**Shabbat archive**, and in **armed resistance** through the **Warsaw ghetto
uprising of 1943**.

## Who carried it out

The organisations were the **Nazi Party**, the **SA** (stormtroopers) and the
**SS** (*Schutzstaffel*, Protection Squadron). The German military, national
railway and healthcare systems, the German civil service and criminal justice
systems, and companies and banks all assisted with the Final Solution.

Some Germans cheered as Jews were beaten, and took their Jewish neighbours'
property. Other Axis powers and **Vichy France**, German-backed local
bureaucracies, and local police forces deported Jews. Some citizens denounced
Jews to German authorities and exposed their hiding places, then took their
valuables.

The motives given for German citizens are **enthusiasm, fear and self-interest**,
though **most individuals were bystanders**. Many helped because Nazi propaganda
reinforced longstanding local antisemitic prejudices; the *jew hunters* acted
either from ideological alignment with the Nazis or for **monetary rewards**.

## Other victims

The Nazis targeted other groups as threats to the health, unity and security of
the German people:

1. **Political opponents** — officials and members of other political parties,
   and those merely suspected of opposing the regime; sent to concentration camps
   or arrested if they refused military service
2. **Germans practising *dangerous activities*** — men accused of homosexuality,
   and *asocials* (beggars, prostitutes, alcoholics); also sent to concentration camps
3. **Black people**
4. **People with disabilities**
5. **Minorities** including Roma, Poles and Soviet prisoners of war
6. **Communists, Socialists and Jehovah's Witnesses**

## The end, and after

When the war ended, after the strategic and systematic bombing of Hitler's
occupied territories, he lost power and took his own life. The USSR and the
Americans **liberated surviving prisoners and survivors of death marches**.

But prejudice did not end with the war: some survivors, though physically alive,
**faced ongoing antisemitism and displacement** in their new lives.

### Survivors

Most Jews who survived within Germany did so through **help from others**, both
Jewish and non-Jewish, who found hiding places, procured **false papers**
protecting Christian identities, and provided food and supplies — and through
**luck**.

Most survivors overall were those who **emigrated from Germany** once they saw the
signs, escaping to the United States or Britain. This was very difficult, because
**no country wanted them** — antisemitism had spread beyond Germany's borders.

### Consequences

Survivors confronted the trauma of having lost entire families. Some had PTSD
from the war; some were isolated; deportations still occurred to a limited extent
in Hungary. Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators had **completely
devastated thousands of Jewish communities across Europe**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **The Holocaust** | The systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews by the Nazi regime and its allies and collaborators |
| **The Shoah** | The other name for the Holocaust, meaning catastrophe |
| **Antisemitism** | Prejudice against or hatred of Jewish people |
| **Persecution** | Hostility and ill-treatment on the basis of beliefs or ethnicity |
| **Nuremberg race laws** | The 1935 laws outlawing Jewish–German marriages and removing citizenship |
| **Kristallnacht** | Concerted Nazi violence against Jews throughout Germany and Austria |
| **Internment** | Imprisoning people |
| **Wannsee Conference** | The January 1942 conference at which the Final Solution was finalised |
| **The Final Solution** | The deliberate and systematic mass murder of Jews, 1941–1945 |
| **Liquidation** | The process of dissolving ghetto administrative structures |
| **Einsatzgruppen** | Special task forces of the SS and police that carried out mass shootings |
| **Euthanasia** | The Nazi euphemism for gas poisoning, presented as mercy death |
| **Killing centres** | Extermination or death camps in German-occupied Poland: Chelmno, Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, Auschwitz-Birkenau |
| **Resettlement actions** | The Nazi euphemism disguising deportations to killing centres |
| **Ghettos** | Walled areas where occupiers forced Jews to live in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions as holding sites before deportation or murder |
| **Warsaw ghetto uprising** | The 1943 armed resistance by Jews in the Warsaw ghetto |
| **SS** | The Schutzstaffel or Protection Squadron |
| **SA** | The Nazi stormtroopers |

# 9 The Cold War, 1945–1991

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

The Cold War was a period of **geopolitical tension between the United States and
the USSR and their respective allies**, the **Western Bloc** and the **Eastern
Bloc** — an intense rivalry between two global superpowers, lasting from the end
of the Second World War in **1945** until the **collapse of the USSR in 1991**.

It was an **ideological war**:

| | United States | USSR |
|---|---|---|
| **Ideology** | Capitalism, democracy, individual freedoms | Communism, state-controlled economy, one-party rule |

It **did not involve direct military conflict**.

## Why it stayed cold

Two reasons are given, and they are the whole explanation for the name. The
Second World War had only just ended and **neither side had recovered from it**;
and both sides held **nuclear weapons that neither would use**, because of
**Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)**.

Instead the two powers **competed for influence in Europe, Asia, Africa and Latin
America**, and both **built massive military forces and developed nuclear weapons
that threatened global destruction**.

## The Yalta Conference, February 1945

Its purpose was to **agree a post-war settlement and decide what to do with
Germany**. The figures present were Prime Minister **Winston Churchill**
(Britain), President **Franklin Delano Roosevelt** (United States) and Premier
**Joseph Stalin** (USSR).

Four outcomes followed.

**1. Germany divided into four zones of occupation**, with the USSR, Britain, the
United States and France each controlling one. France was included because
Churchill and Roosevelt forced a role for it.

| Zone | Controlled by |
|---|---|
| **North-west** | United Kingdom |
| **North-east** | USSR |
| **South-east** | United States |
| **South-west** | France |

**2. Berlin divided into four zones** of occupation, among the same countries.

**3. The Declaration on Liberated Europe** — countries freed from Nazi control
could hold **free, democratic elections** to choose their own governments. Stalin
was offered a **sphere of influence in eastern Europe** where communist ideals
would dominate.

**4. The United Nations** — the Allies agreed to set up an organisation dedicated
to **international cooperation and the prevention of war**.

All the leaders committed to **pursuing and putting on trial suspected Nazi war
criminals**, to prevent Nazis from doing further harm.

> The guide labels the first of these outcomes a *Potsdam excerpt* while listing
> it under Yalta. Both conferences are named in the source and it is worth
> keeping the distinction in mind.

## Konrad Adenauer's memoir

**Konrad Adenauer**, the first prime minister of West Germany, records why the
settlement failed in practice:

- The **Potsdam Conference** required Germany to be treated as **a single economic
  unit**, and this **failed**
- The powers agreed that every decision needed **consensus from the Control
  Council** — France, the USSR, the United Kingdom and the United States — and this
  **also failed**, because they refused to listen to one another
- The **four occupation zones drew further apart economically**, hindering
  economic stability after the war, since **each zone pursued its own policy**

The three points are one argument: a rule requiring unanimity among rivals
produced no decisions, and with no joint decisions each zone went its own way.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Cold War** | The 1945–1991 geopolitical tension between the United States and the USSR and their allies |
| **Western Bloc** | The United States and its allies |
| **Eastern Bloc** | The USSR and its allies |
| **Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)** | The condition in which both sides hold nuclear weapons neither will use |
| **Yalta Conference** | The February 1945 meeting agreeing the post-war settlement and the division of Germany |
| **Declaration on Liberated Europe** | The agreement that countries freed from Nazi control could hold free, democratic elections |
| **Sphere of influence** | The area of dominance Stalin was offered in eastern Europe |
| **United Nations** | The organisation the Allies agreed to set up, dedicated to international cooperation and preventing war |
| **Control Council** | The four-power body whose required consensus prevented decisions being made |

# S1M-1 Semester 1 Midterm review: Scientific Revolution, Enlightenment, American Revolution, Fren

## Semester 1 Midterm review: Scientific Revolution, Enlightenment, American Revolution, Fren

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm History H review guide (PA). Writers: James Gao 10(6). Editor: Aman Zhu 10(5). Range: Scientific Revolution, Enlightenment, American Revolution, French Revolution. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**The Scientific Revolution**

**Background and Origin**

The Scientific Revolution was a sweeping intellectual and cultural transformation that took place roughly from the mid1500s to the early 1700s. It emerged first in Europe, even though the Islamic world had led the globe in science from 800 to 1400 and China had unmatched technological achievements.

**Scientists**

**Copernicus** proposed heliocentrism, challenging the Earthcentered view of the Church.

**Kepler** proved planets move in elliptical orbits.

**Galileo** used the telescope to gather empirical evidence that undermined traditional cosmic beliefs, but he was condemned by the Church.

**Newton** unified physics with universal laws of motion and gravitation, portraying the universe as a selfregulating machine governed by natural laws.

**Key idea**

Knowledge comes from evidence, reason and experiment — not from tradition, religion or ancient authority.

**Science & Religion**

There was serious conflict with the Catholic Church, yet early scientists remained religious. Over time, science and religion were treated as separate realms.

**Legacy**

It reshaped European views of humanity and the cosmos, laid the intellectual groundwork for the Enlightenment, and eventually became a global marker of modernity.

**Enlightenment**

**Background** **and Origin**

The Enlightenment first emerged in the late 1600s, growing directly out of the Scientific Revolution. Discoveries by **Isaac Newton, Galileo Galilei and other scholars** proved that the natural world could be explained through reason, logic and empirical observation, rather than religion or ancient tradition. This rational way of thinking was soon applied to human society, law and politics.

The movement began in England, where thinkers such as **John Locke** rejected the divine right of kings and built the early theoretical framework for liberal government and individual rights. To summarize, the Enlightenment used reason and observation, inspired by the scientific revolution, to build new theories of government.

**Enlightenment Philosophers**

**Thomas Hobbes**

**Main idea**: people need an all-powerful ruler to avoid chaos.

**State of nature:** no laws, and people pursue self-interest. Life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short."

**Social contract:** people give up their freedom to a sovereign. The agreement is only among the people, not with the king.

**Best government:** an absolute monarchy. Once power is given, people have no right to revolt.

**John Locke**

**Main idea:** government exists to protect natural rights, and people can revolt if it fails. (Two Treatises of Government)

**Natural rights:** life, liberty, and property are inalienable, meaning they cannot be taken away or given up.

**Social contract:** an agreement between the people and the ruler.

**Right to revolt:** if a ruler violates natural rights, the contract is broken and people can set up a new government. This influenced the Declaration of Independence.

**Government:** limited ("govern lightly"), with a supreme legislature. Property is the most important right, and only male property owners should vote.

**Montesquieu**

**Main idea:** divide government into separate branches so none becomes too powerful. (The Spirit of the Laws)

**Three branches:** legislative, executive, and judicial, each checking the others.

Uniting these powers, as in the absolute monarchy of France, leads to despotism.

He admired England's system but misread it, since power there was mostly in Parliament. Americans later used his theory with others as the basis of the U.S. Constitution.

**Jean-Jacques Rousseau**

**Main idea:** all power belongs to the people, who express it through the general will. (The Social Contract)

**State of nature:** people are naturally good, and society corrupts them. Property created inequality and war.

**Old social contract:** a fraud by the rich and powerful against the common people.

**True social contract:** people give all their rights to the whole community, which is the sovereign.

**General will:** everyone votes directly on laws for the public good (**direct democracy**). There are no representatives and no separation of powers.

**Immanuel Kant**

**Main idea:** enlightenment means thinking for yourself, and it requires freedom to reason publicly.

**Self-incurred immaturity:** being unable to use your own understanding because you lack the courage to try.

**Why people stay immature:** laziness, cowardice, and guardians (such as priests and officials) who do the thinking for them.xxx

Revolution does not change how people think. Enlightenment comes slowly through freedom.

**Atlantic Revolutions (1770s1840s)**

A wave of revolutionary movements across the Atlantic world, inspired by Enlightenment ideas. ScientificRevolutioninspired faith in human progress, and anger over unfair taxation, political inequality, and old hierarchical systems. Includes American, French, Haitian, and LatinAmerican revolutions.

**The American Revolution**

**Causes**

British taxed colonists after the Seven Years’ War; colonists argued no taxation without representation**.**

Enlightenment influence: John Locke’s naturalrights & socialcontract theory.

Resentment of British control over colonial political and economic life.

**Major Events**

1776: Declaration of Independence (Jefferson; Lockeinspired: life, liberty, pursuit of happiness)

War against Britain; France provided military support

1783: Treaty of Paris → US independence

**The French Revolution**

**Four Main stages**

Stage 1: National Assembly (17891791) – Early Moderate Revolution

Stage 2: Radical Revolution (17921794) – Reign of Terror

Stage 3: The Directory (17951799)

Stage 4: Age of Napoleon (17991815)

**Causes**

**Social:** **The Three Estates System**

1st Estate (Clergy): ~1% population; owned 10% land, paid almost no taxes

2nd Estate (Nobility): ~2% population; owned 25% land, taxexempt

3rd Estate (Commoners: peasants, urban workers, bourgeoisie): 97% of people, owned 65% land, paid nearly all taxes. Deep resentment of unfair hierarchy.

Enlightenment influence

Ideas of reason, natural rights, equality challenged the old social order.

**Economic**

**Massive national debt: Seven** Years’ War, French support for American Revolution, costly Palace of Versailles, lavish royal spending.

**Bad harvests (17881789):** bread prices skyrocketed. Bread was the main food for poor Parisians; hunger fueled popular anger.

**Unfairness:** King Louis XVI tried to raise taxes, but only the Third Estate bore the burden.

**Political: Absolute Monarchy**

King Louis XVI held total power: he made laws, set taxes, used lettres de cachet to jail people without trial, censored speech/press.

EstatesGeneral (representative body) had not met since 1614. This meant many reformative ideas and reformations were suppressed and unable to be proposed.

**Trigger Event**

May 1789: Louis XVI calls the EstatesGeneral to fix France’s financial crisis. Each estate got only one vote → First + Second Estate always outvoted Third Estate. Nothing was changed and the members of the third estate got angry.

**National Assembly (17891791)**

**Tennis Court Oath (June 20,1789):** Third Estate broke away, created the National Assembly. Locked out of their meeting hall, they swore they would not disband until they wrote a constitution limiting royal power.

**Storming of the Bastille (July 14, 1789):** Paris revolutionaries attacked the Bastille fortress, a symbol of royal tyranny. This date is France’s national holiday. Marked the start of popular uprising.

**August Decrees (Aug 4,1789):** Abolished feudal privileges of clergy and nobility.

**Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen (Aug 26,1789):** Enlightenmentinspired document, states Men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Rights: liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression, free speech, innocent until proven guilty.

**Women’s March on Versailles (Oct 1789):** Hungry Parisian women marched to Versailles, forced King Louis XVI and MarieAntoinette to move to Paris. Royal family now under popular watch and are

**Constitution of 1791:** Created a limited constitutional monarchy: King kept executive power, lawmaking power went to elected National Assembly. Judicial branch elected by people.

**Monarchy escapes:** King and Queen try to flee Paris to Varennes (Northeastern France), but are found and taken back. Monarchy loses trust and evokes public hate.

**Radical Revolution (17921794)**

**War begins (April 1792):** European monarchs (Austria, Prussia) feared revolution would spread and threatened France. France declared war on them.

**Fall of monarchy** **and** **Radicals took power** **(January 1793):** Louis XVI executed by guillotine. France became a republic without a king.

**Committee of Public Safety (17931794)**: Led by Maximilien Robespierre. Purpose: defend France from foreign armies and internal counterrevolutionary enemies.

**Reign of Terror (17931794)**

Suspended many individual rights; spies hunted “enemies of the revolution”.

Thousands executed by guillotine. Most victims were peasants & urban workingclass people, not just nobles or clergy.

Attacked Catholic Church power in France.

End of Terror: Thermidorian Reaction (July 1794) Members of the National Convention arrested and executed Robespierre. The Reign of Terror ended.

**Reasons of execution:** People feared Robespierre’s terror and that they might be on the list of execution. Another reason was because Robespierre hosted a ceremony declaring a new god instead of Catholicism where he dressed up as a godly servant in front of the whole of Paris. People believed he went nuts.

Achievements: Defended France from foreign invasion.

Limits: Mass humanrights abuses; fear and bloodshed tore French society apart.

Note: September Massacres – Parisians killed thousands of suspected counterrevolutionary prisoners; newspapers (Marat) helped spread radical calls for violence.

**The Directory (17951799)**

New Constitution of 1795 set up the Directory: 5man executive group.

Goal: Avoid oneperson tyranny (reaction against Robespierre).

Weaknesses: Corruption, unstable politics, coups, still fighting foreign wars, unable to solve economic problems.

People grew frustrated with Directory failures.

**Age of Napoleon (17991815)**

**Coronation (Dec 1804):** Napoleon crowned himself **Emperor of France**. Revolution’s antimonarchy ideal was reversed.

**Napoleonic Wars (18031815):** Napoleon’s armies conquered much of Europe, spreading revolutionary legal ideas across the continent. But constant war drained France’s resources.

**Invasion of Russia (1812):** Catastrophic defeat for Napoleon.

**Defeat &Exile (1814):** Napoleon defeated; exiled to island of Elba. Bourbon royal family restored: Louis XVIII became French king (constitutional monarchy, not absolute).

**Return & downfall (1815):** Napoleon escaped Elba, returned to power → defeated finally at **Battle of Waterloo**. Exiled to remote SaintHelena, where he died.

**Congress of Vienna (18141815)** European leaders met after Napoleon’s fall. The goals were to restore old preNapoleon borders, create “balance of power” to prevent future largescale European war.

Coup of 1799 Popular military general Napoleon Bonaparte overthrew the weak Directory. He became First Consul (neardictator).

Napoleonic Code unified French law, preserved many revolutionary gains: equality before law, end of feudalism, property rights.

Negative affect: Rolled back women’s rights; men held full authority over family.

**Overall Significance:** **Failures**

Revolution began fighting for liberty & equality but turned to mass violence in the Terror.

Women’s rights were mostly ignored; later rolled back by Napoleon.

The revolution aimed to reform social systems to benefit the third estate and the lower class, but instead the ones affected most negatively were arguably the commoners and peasants.

After decades of revolution and war, a monarchy returned to France.

**Overall Significance:** **Successes**

Permanently ended feudalism in France.

Spread Enlightenment ideals: liberty, legal equality, popular sovereignty across Europe.

**Test structure**

**UWA Friday 11/6**

DBQ chart (similar to what you did for the Catholic Church and Scientific Revolution) - 30% of the midterm grade

**Midterm** **Wednesday** **11/11,**

MCQs - about 20, approximately 40% of midterm grade

SAQ - 2 sets of ABC (6 prompts total) - roughly 30%

**Final** **Note**

Some classes in Block A may differ in the UWA Date, so check with your teacher and take into account that this is only for reference.

For further info, you could reference the video made by oversimplified on YouTube. He is a great creator and you could watch his vid on the French revolution.

# S1M-1 Semester 1 Midterm review: 17.1, 17.3, 18

## Semester 1 Midterm review: 17.1, 17.3, 18

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm History S+ review guide (PA). Writers: Vivienne 10-3. Editor: Jenny Chen 10-7. Range: 17.1, 17.3, 18. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 17.1

The Enlightenment was rooted in reason and natural law, building on breakthroughs of the Scientific Revolution to rethink society, politics, and economics.

Hobbes believed human nature was selfish and brutal. Under the social contract, people give up freedom to a strong absolute government to maintain peace and order. Locke took a more optimistic view: people are reasonable and born with natural rights to life, liberty, and property. Governments exist to protect these rights, and citizens may overthrow a government that violates them.

Key philosophic ideas include:

- Montesquieu’s separation of powers, which splits government into branches to create checks and balances

- Voltaire’s defense of free speech and religious tolerance, alongside criticism of corruption and prejudice

- Diderot’s Encyclopedia, a large collection of writings designed to spread Enlightenment thought and push for education and free expression

- Rousseau’s argument that people are naturally good, and legitimate government should follow the “general will” of the community

Wollstonecraft challenged the limits placed on women, arguing that equal education would allow women to fully take part in public life.

New economic ideas emerged with the rise of laissez-faire. Adam Smith argued that free markets, shaped by supply and demand, function best with little government interference.

Overall, Enlightenment ideas challenged absolute monarchy and traditional religious authority, and became major influences on later revolutions and modern democratic systems.

## 17.3

Britain’s Rise & Colonial Conflict

- Britain became a global power by controlling trade routes, building colonies, and winning European wars.

- The French and Indian War left Britain with massive war debt. Parliament passed taxes (Sugar Act, Stamp Act) on the colonies to pay this debt.

- Colonists’ main protest: no taxation without representation — they had no representatives in Parliament. Parliament repealed the Stamp Act but claimed total authority over the colonies.

Key escalating events:

- Boston Massacre: British soldiers fired on colonial protesters

- Boston Tea Party: Colonists dumped British tea to protest tea taxes

- Parliament passed harsh punishment laws, uniting the colonies against Britain

- Lexington and Concord (April 1775): First shots of the American Revolution.

- Common Sense (Thomas Paine): Enlightenment-inspired pamphlet arguing the colonies should separate from Britain.

Declaration of Independence

- Written primarily by Thomas Jefferson; adopted July 4, 1776

- Core Enlightenment ideas (from Locke):

- Natural rights: life, liberty, pursuit of happiness

- Popular sovereignty: government power comes from the people’s consent

- People have the right to alter or abolish unjust government

American Revolution: War Advantages & Turning Points

- Colonists’ disadvantages: Fewer trained soldiers, limited money, no formal army, many Loyalists (colonists loyal to Britain)

- Colonists’ strengths:

- Fought on familiar home geography

- Strong leadership from George Washington (persisted through hardships like Valley Forge)

- Turning point: Battle of Saratoga (1777) → convinced France to ally with America, sending supplies, troops, warships

- End of war: British surrender at Yorktown; Treaty of Paris (1783) formally recognized U.S. independence

U.S. Constitution & Bill of Rights

- Articles of Confederation: America’s first government, too weak to rule effectively

- Constitutional Convention (1787, Philadelphia): Delegates (Washington, Madison, Franklin) rewrote the government framework, drawing on Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau

- Constitution structure:

- Federal republic: power divided between national (federal) government and state governments

- Separation of powers: 3 branches (legislative, executive, judicial)

- Checks and balances: each branch can limit the others to prevent too much power

- Bill of Rights (first 10 amendments, protects natural rights):

- 1st: freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly, petition

- 2nd: right to bear arms

- 3rd: no forced quartering of troops

- 4th: protection from unreasonable searches/seizures

- 5–8th: due process, fair trial, limits on punishment

- 9th: rights are not limited only to those listed

- 10th: powers not given to federal government belong to states or people

Impact: The Constitution became the nation’s supreme law and a symbol of freedom, inspiring reformers in Europe and Latin America

18.1-18.3 French Revolution

Causes & the Old Regime

France under the ancient régime had three rigid estates:

- First Estate: clergy, owned large land, paid almost no direct taxes

- Second Estate: nobility, held top government/military positions, tax exemptions

- Third Estate: everyone else (bourgeoisie, peasants, urban workers). Paid nearly all taxes, faced high bread prices and hunger. The bourgeoisie resented being locked out of political power.

Economic crisis: Years of deficit spending from wars and lavish royal costs. Bad harvests drove food prices up, leaving poor families starving. Louis XVI called the Estates-General (not summoned for 175 years) to fix the financial crisis.

- Voting rules favored the First and Second Estates (one vote per estate).

- Third Estate broke away, declared itself the National Assembly, and took the Tennis Court Oath: they would not disband until France had a constitution.

- July 14, 1789: Parisians stormed the Bastille, marking the start of the French Revolution.

Early Moderate Phase (1789–1791)

Peasant unrest spread, sparking the Great Fear: rumors of noble plots made peasants attack manor records and destroy feudal obligations. The National Assembly responded:

- Abolished feudalism and old noble privileges

- Issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen: natural rights to liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression; inspired by Locke and the American Revolution

- Olympe de Gouges wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Citizen,

challenging the document’s exclusion of women

- Women’s March on Versailles (Oct 1789): Thousands of women marched to Versailles over bread shortages; forced Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette to move to Paris

- Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1790): put the Catholic Church under state control; many clergy and devout Catholics rejected it

- Constitution of 1791: Created a limited constitutional monarchy. Voting rights limited to tax-paying male citizens. Louis XVI tried to flee France but was captured; this destroyed trust in the monarchy. European rulers feared revolution spreading and threatened intervention.

Radical Phase (1792–1794)

War began against Austria and Prussia. Working-class city supporters called sans-culottes pushed for a republic. The Jacobins, a radical political club, allied with them.

- 1792: National Convention abolished the monarchy and set up the French Republic. Louis XVI was tried and executed for treason.

- Committee of Public Safety was formed to defend the revolution from foreign war and internal rebellion. Led by Robespierre.

- Reign of Terror (1793–1794): Suspected enemies of the revolution were arrested and executed, often by the guillotine. Robespierre argued terror was necessary to protect the revolution and achieve a “republic of virtue.”

- After thousands of deaths, Convention members turned against Robespierre; he was executed in July 1794, ending the Terror.

The Directory & Lasting Changes

Post-Terror, the Constitution of 1795 created the Directory: a five-man executive and two- house legislature. It was weak, corrupt, and unstable, facing food riots and royalist threats.

- Rise of Napoleon Bonaparte: a popular military hero who eventually seized power. Long-term changes from the revolution:

- End of feudal privileges, noble titles, and the old social order

- Rise of nationalism: strong loyalty to the nation, not a monarch

- New symbols: tricolor flag, “La Marseillaise” as national anthem

- Social reforms: state-run schools, abolition of slavery in French colonies, religious tolerance

Napoleon’s Rise to Power

- Napoleon Bonaparte was born in 1769 on Corsica, an island in the Mediterranean.

- He trained in the French military and quickly rose through the ranks during the French Revolution.

- His successes as a general made him popular with the French people and the army.

- In 1799, Napoleon took part in the Coup of 18 Brumaire, overthrew the Directory, and seized power.

- He first became First Consul, then in 1804 crowned himself Emperor Napoleon I.

Napoleon’s Reforms in France

- Napoleon centralized the government and made administration more efficient.

- He reformed the legal system with the Napoleonic Code, which gave France a clear set of uniform laws.

- The code protected some revolutionary gains, such as equality before the law and property rights.

- He reorganized education and established state-run secondary schools.

- He restored relations with the Catholic Church through the Concordat of 1801.

- He also supported economic recovery, improved roads and canals, and encouraged industry.

Napoleon Builds an Empire

- Napoleon conquered much of Europe through a series of military victories.

- By 1812, his empire included or controlled:

- Belgium

- the Netherlands

- Switzerland

- much of Italy

- large parts of Germany and Spain

- He placed family members and loyal supporters on the thrones of conquered countries.

- He spread some revolutionary ideas, including legal equality and reforms against feudalism.

- But he also forced conquered peoples to accept French rule and pay taxes.

Challenges to Napoleon’s Empire

- Nationalism became a major enemy. People in conquered countries resented French domination and wanted their own independent nations.

- Napoleon tried to make Europe submit to France through the Continental System, a blockade designed to hurt Britain.

- The blockade failed because Britain was too powerful at sea, and European countries resisted French control.

- Spain and Austria rebelled against Napoleon.

- The Peninsular War in Spain drained French resources.

- In 1812, Napoleon invaded Russia. The Russians used scorched-earth tactics and a harsh winter destroyed most of his army.

Napoleon’s Fall

- After the Russian disaster, Napoleon’s weakened position encouraged his enemies to unite.

- European powers formed coalitions against him and defeated France.

- In 1814, Napoleon abdicated and was exiled to the island of Elba.

- He returned briefly in 1815 in what is called the Hundred Days.

- His final defeat came at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.

- He was then exiled to Saint Helena, where he died in 1821.

Congress of Vienna

- After Napoleon’s defeat, European leaders met at the Congress of Vienna in 1814– 1815.

- Their goals were to:

- restore stability to Europe

- strengthen countries around France

- bring back old royal families

- prevent one nation from becoming too powerful

- The Congress redrew the map of Europe and created a balance of power.

- It succeeded in avoiding a large general war for many years, but it also ignored many demands for national independence.

Main Themes

- Napoleon brought order and important reforms to France, but his power depended on military success.

- His empire spread revolutionary ideas while also imposing foreign rule.

- Nationalism and the cost of constant warfare helped destroy his empire.

- The Congress of Vienna tried to restore the old order and keep Europe balanced.

# 1.1 The Emergence of Homo Sapiens and the Neolithic Revolution

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Orienting yourself in time

Before the detail, fix the large landmarks of the period this course covers. Everything in the early chapters happens either before or between these dates.

| Date | Development |
|---|---|
| 3000 BCE | Beginnings of the first civilisations |
| 1000–500 BCE | Assyrians and Persians |
| 400 BCE | Alexander the Great — a short-lived empire; the Romans rule; the Indians are part of the Mauryan Empire |
| Last few centuries BCE | The Qin and Han dynasties of China |

## The emergence of Homo sapiens

**Homo sapiens** originated around 250,000 years ago. Between 200,000 and 150,000 years ago the species settled and developed in Africa, and only around 70,000 years ago did populations move out of Africa. The Neanderthals became extinct around 30,000 BCE.

## The hunter-gatherers of the Palaeolithic Age

**Palaeolithic** means "stone", and the age takes its name from the tools that define it. In Palaeolithic societies both men and women found food; the division of labour that later ages take for granted is not yet in place. Two capacities mark the period out: the use of fire and the use of tools. The age also leaves the first great body of art — paintings of large animals, of which Chauvet is the standard example.

## The Neolithic Revolution

Around 10,000 BCE the end of the ice age led to the **Neolithic Revolution**. *Neolithic* means "new stone", and the name is literal: a new type of polished stone axe appears. The revolution itself, however, is agricultural rather than merely technological. It consists of the growth of crops and the domestication of animals, and because a community that grows its own food no longer needs to follow it, people settled down and populations increased.

Between these two ages sits the **Mesolithic Age**, the "Middle Stone Age", the transition from food gathering to food production.

Systematic agriculture developed between 8000 and 5000 BCE. In the Middle East this meant wheat and barley among crops, and pigs, cattle, goats and sheep among animals. By 4000 BCE agriculture was well developed in central Europe.

## The first towns

Two old towns in the Middle East show what settlement produced. **Jericho** has been occupied since 8000 BCE and was surrounded by mudbrick walls. At **Catal Huyuk** people walked on the rooftops.

Settlement allowed people to build houses, store food and engage in trade. The goods that follow are the physical signature of the Neolithic: pottery, woven baskets, stone tools, and **obsidian**, a volcanic glass that is easily flaked and therefore valuable for tool-making.

Settled agricultural life also led to **patriarchy** — a society dominated by men.

## Invention and the Bronze Age

Between 4000 and 3000 BCE came inventions that greatly changed life: writing, and metal, with bronze appearing in western Asia. The **Bronze Age** runs from 3000 to 1200 BCE.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Homo sapiens** | The human species, originating around 250,000 years ago, settling and developing in Africa 200,000–150,000 years ago and moving out of Africa 70,000 years ago |
| **Palaeolithic** | "Stone"; the age of hunter-gatherers who used fire and tools and painted large animals |
| **Mesolithic Age** | The "Middle Stone Age", the transition from food gathering to food production |
| **Neolithic** | "New stone"; the age of polished stone axes, crop growing and animal domestication |
| **Neolithic Revolution** | The development of agriculture after the end of the ice age around 10,000 BCE, which made people settle down and increased population |
| **Obsidian** | Volcanic glass that is easily flaked |
| **Patriarchy** | Society dominated by men |
| **Bronze Age** | 3000–1200 BCE, following the appearance of metal in western Asia |

# 1.2 The Emergence of Civilisation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What makes a civilisation

A **civilisation** is a complex culture in which large numbers of people share a variety of common elements. The guide gives seven of them, and it is worth treating the list as a checklist: if you are asked whether a society counts as a civilisation, these are the boxes to tick.

| # | Element |
|---|---|
| 1 | An urban focus |
| 2 | Political and military structures |
| 3 | A social structure based on economy |
| 4 | Complexity in material life — agriculture, trade, luxury items |
| 5 | Religion |
| 6 | Writing |
| 7 | Artistic and intellectual activity |

## Early civilisations around the world

The first civilisations are not confined to one region, and they do not all appear at once. Three examples fix the spread.

| Civilisation | Date |
|---|---|
| Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro | 3000–1500 BCE |
| The Shang dynasty in China | 1570–1045 BCE |
| The city of Caral, Peru | 2600 BCE |

## Why did early civilisations develop?

Two causes are given, and they answer different halves of the question.

The first is economic. A **food surplus** — more food than the producers themselves need — frees people from producing food, and that leads to **job specialisation**. This is the material precondition for several of the seven elements above: without specialists there are no full-time priests, soldiers, scribes or artists.

The second is religion, which provides unity among humans. Where surplus makes a complex society possible, religion is what holds that complex society together.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Civilisation** | A complex culture in which large numbers of people share a variety of common elements: urban focus, political/military structures, a social structure based on economy, complexity in material life, religion, writing, and artistic/intellectual activity |
| **Food surplus** | Surplus food production, which leads to job specialisation |
| **Job specialisation** | The division of work into distinct occupations, made possible by a food surplus |

# 1.3 Civilisation in Mesopotamia

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The land

**Mesopotamia** is the valley between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Its agriculture depended on irrigation and on the control of the river flow, so the management of water is the practical foundation of everything that follows: the cities, the priesthoods and the kings all rest on a river that has to be harnessed.

## The city-states of ancient Mesopotamia

The **Sumerians** were the first Mesopotamian civilisation. By 3000 BCE there were independent cities, of which Ur is the standard example. Walls surrounded the cities and dwellings were built of sun-dried brick.

At the centre of each city stood a **ziggurat**, a temple dedicated to the chief god or goddess, built atop a massive tower. The priest or priestess held political power, and Sumerian government was therefore a **theocracy** — government by divine authority — in which the king was an agent from God.

## Empires in ancient Mesopotamia

The city-states did not stay independent. Two empires follow.

The **Akkadians** lived north of the Sumerians and were a Semitic people. In 2340 BCE **Sargon**, leader of the Akkadians, overthrew the Sumerians. Akkadian power was based on the military, and an attack from a neighbour brought the empire to an end.

**Hammurabi's empire**, centred on Babylon, begins in 1792 BCE. Hammurabi was known as the "Sun of Babylon". The empire fell after his death, but he is remembered above all for **Hammurabi's Code**.

## The culture of Mesopotamia

The great literary survival is the **Epic of Gilgamesh**, about the legendary king of Uruk. Mesopotamian religion was **polytheistic**, and it included **divination**: relieving anxiety by finding out the gods' intentions.

From 3000 BCE the Sumerians used the **cuneiform** system of writing. They were also strong in mathematics and astronomy.

## An exam note

Section 1.4 will not be tested.

## Keywords

|---|---|
| **Mesopotamia** | The valley between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers |
| **Sumerians** | The first Mesopotamian civilisation, with independent walled cities such as Ur by 3000 BCE |
| **Ziggurat** | A temple dedicated to the chief god or goddess, built atop a massive tower |
| **Theocracy** | Government by divine authority, with the king as an agent from God |
| **Sargon** | Leader of the Akkadians who overthrew Sumerian power in 2340 BCE |
| **Hammurabi** | Ruler of Babylon from 1792 BCE, the "Sun of Babylon", author of Hammurabi's Code |
| **Epic of Gilgamesh** | The Mesopotamian epic about the legendary king of Uruk |
| **Divination** | Relieving anxiety by finding out the gods' intentions |
| **Cuneiform** | The writing system used by the Sumerians from 3000 BCE |

# 1.5 New Centres of Civilisation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Nomadic peoples: the impact of the Indo-Europeans

### The Hittites

From around 1750 BCE the **Hittites** were established in Asia Minor, or Anatolia. Their distinguishing technology was iron, and they transformed Mesopotamian cultures. The Hittite state ends in 1190 BCE.

### The Phoenicians

The Phoenicians are remembered for one thing above all: the invention of the alphabet. Politically they were defeated by the Assyrians and then the Persians, but the alphabet outlived them and, as a later section shows, passed through the Greeks to much of the world.

## The Hebrews

The Hebrews were the "Children of Israel", and their defining religious feature is **monotheism**. They moved to Egypt, where they were enslaved by the pharaohs.

### The kings

| Ruler | Achievement |
|---|---|
| Saul | The beginning of the united kingdom of Israel; after his death, anarchy |
| David | Saul's lieutenant; established control over all of Canaan |
| Solomon | David's son; strengthened royal power |

### The Kingdom of Judah

Judah was forced to pay tribute to Assyria and gained independence only after Assyria's decline. That independence did not last: the **Chaldeans** defeated Assyria and then conquered Judah. In 586 BCE Jerusalem was destroyed and the upper class was taken to Babylon for captivity. When the Persians destroyed the Chaldeans, the Jews were allowed to come back. Judah then remained under Persian control until Alexander the Great.

### Hebrew religion

Three ideas structure it:

- **The Covenant**, between Yahweh and the people
- **The Law**, that is, obedience to God
- **The prophets**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Hittites** | An Indo-European people in Asia Minor/Anatolia from 1750 BCE who made use of iron and transformed Mesopotamian cultures; ended 1190 BCE |
| **Phoenicians** | The people credited with the invention of the alphabet, later defeated by the Assyrians and Persians |
| **Monotheism** | Belief in one God, the defining feature of Hebrew religion |
| **Chaldeans** | The people who defeated Assyria and conquered Judah, destroying Jerusalem in 586 BCE |
| **The Covenant** | The agreement between Yahweh and the people |
| **The Law** | Obedience to God |

# 1.6 The Rise of New Empires

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Assyrian Empire

The Assyrians emerged in Assyria, on the Upper Tigris, and were Semitic-speaking. Under **Ashurbanipal** the empire was overextended; by his reign Babylon was in rebellion and Assyria began to disintegrate. Overextension is the point to hold on to — the same military reach that built the empire is what made it impossible to hold.

Assyrian power rested on terror and warfare, which produced excellence in the military. Religion was the cohesive force in society. Ethnicity was not important; language was the marker of identity. The empire also lived on trade and agriculture, and it assimilated much of Sumerian and Babylonian culture.

## The Persian Empire

### Neo-Babylon

In 539 BCE the Neo-Babylonian state falls. **Nebuchadnezzar** had rebuilt Babylon after its collapse.

### The rise of Persia

The Persians came from southwestern Iran, and the **Achaemenid** dynasty unified them.

| Ruler | Achievement |
|---|---|
| Cyrus the Great | From 550 BCE extended Persian control over the Medes |
| Cambyses | Cyrus's son; invaded Egypt |
| Darius | Built the largest empire the world had ever seen |

### Governing the empire

The Medes became the first **satrapy**, or province, and Babylonia was likewise made into a province under a **satrap**, or governor. Existing government officials kept their positions — a policy that explains how so large an empire could be absorbed so quickly, since conquest did not require rebuilding local administration from nothing.

### Zoroastrianism

From around 660 BCE **Zoroaster** taught a monotheistic religion whose God is **Ahuramazda**.

| **Achaemenid dynasty** | The dynasty that unified the Persians of southwestern Iran |
| **Cyrus the Great** | Persian ruler who from 550 BCE extended Persian control over the Medes |
| **Satrapy** | A province of the Persian Empire; the Medes were the first |
| **Satrap** | The governor of a satrapy |
| **Darius** | Persian ruler who built the largest empire the world had ever seen |
| **Zoroastrianism** | The monotheistic religion taught by Zoroaster from around 660 BCE, whose God is Ahuramazda |

# 2.1 Classical Greece

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Geography decides politics

Greek geography dictated many of the decisions and characteristics of Greek civilisation. The terrain is mountainous, with no fertile land for agriculture, so the Greeks relied on trade. Distance and mountains also made some areas hard to control, and that difficulty shaped politics directly: it is why Greece produced independent city-states rather than a single unified kingdom.

## Daily life

### Gender roles

Men worked as artisans, farmers and merchants in the morning, and in the afternoon exercised and attended assemblies. Women cooked and wove at home; poorer women worked in the markets, selling food and cloth.

The upper class attended **symposiums**, where public affairs, philosophy and literature were discussed. Entertainment at them included dancers, singers, magicians, acrobats and alcohol.

### Slavery

Around one third of the population was enslaved. The enslaved were prisoners of war, foreigners and debtors. They did heavy work and mining, though some were teachers or servants.

## Athens

Athens began as an aristocracy.

### Education

The sons of free men were required to be educated. The main texts were the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*, and the curriculum covered arithmetic, geometry, drawing, music, gymnastics and rhetoric. At eighteen they were required to serve in the military for two years.

### Architecture and the arts

Greek builders started using stone around the sixth century BCE; before that wood was the main material. The guide distinguishes three column types: **Ionic** (flat tops), **Doric** (curly tops) and **Corinthian** (very fancy).

Sculptors used idealised forms. **Phidias** created the statues for the Parthenon and the statue of Zeus at Olympus.

### Reform: why Athens changed

Athens had many social problems that forced change — above all poverty and debt. The three reformers below are best read as a sequence, each one finishing what the last began.

**Draco and the archons.** An **archon** was the leader of the aristocratic government and the supreme judge. Draco created a strict code of law to curb crimes, so strict that the word **draconian** now means excessively harsh or severe, especially of laws or their application. He also extended voting rights to anyone with armour.

**Solon**, elected archon in 594 BCE, continued solving the problems Draco had tried to solve. He cancelled or reduced debts and eliminated slavery for debt, and he eliminated the "helot" class except for foreigners and women.

**Cleisthenes** finished what the previous archons had started, and his reforms were the ones that empowered common people. He redesigned the electoral districts so that they were not divided by wealth, and he created the **Council of Five Hundred**: five hundred people chosen by chance to help run the government. Because places were allotted rather than elected, most people could participate at least once, and any free man could now become powerful.

He also began **ostracism**: if six thousand people wrote someone's name on an **ostrakon**, a piece of broken pottery, that person was banished for ten years. Finally he expanded the Court of Appeal juries, with 1,501 jurors sitting at once — a number large enough to protect against corruption.

## Influences on and of Greece

Greece both borrowed and lent. The civilisations of the Near East and Egypt influenced Greek culture. In the other direction, Greek religion and its features were adopted into Roman culture, and the Greek alphabet — which itself came from the Phoenicians — was adopted by many other civilisations.

## Sparta

Sparta was founded by the descendants of the Dorians, who invaded Greece around 1200 BCE, and was located on the Peloponnesus. It invaded its neighbours and enslaved many of them, so that between 65 and 85 per cent of the population were enslaved **helots**, who farmed the large estates. **Citizen** in Sparta meant the land-owning leisure class: by definition, citizens owned helots and did not have to work.

Education began at around seven years old, in a military camp for boys with no weapons or armour, designed to create faithful citizens.

### Gender roles

Spartan women had more freedom than other Greek women but had no place in government. They were expected to exercise and be strong so as to give birth to strong babies.

### Government

| Body | Composition and role |
|---|---|
| The two kings | Little power, almost figureheads; led the army and religious services |
| The assembly | Males over thirty; held the most power |
| The council of elders | Twenty-eight men over sixty; similar to a supreme court |

### The limits of Sparta

Despite Sparta's popularity and its reputation as an advanced state with an all-powerful army, it was behind on the arts, science and similar fields, and was very conservative. The reason is given plainly: the Spartans were afraid of change and of outside influence.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Symposium** | A gathering of the upper class at which public affairs, philosophy and literature were discussed |
| **Archon** | The leader of the aristocratic government and supreme judge |
| **Draconian** | Excessively harsh or severe, especially of laws or their application |
| **Council of Five Hundred** | Cleisthenes' body of five hundred people chosen by chance to help run the government |
| **Ostracism** | Banishment for ten years if six thousand people wrote a person's name on an ostrakon |
| **Ostrakon** | A piece of broken pottery used for writing a name in an ostracism vote |
| **Helot** | An enslaved farm worker in Sparta, making up 65–85 per cent of the population |
| **Citizen (Sparta)** | The land-owning leisure class, who owned helots and did not have to work |
| **Phidias** | Sculptor who created the statues for the Parthenon and the statue of Zeus at Olympus |

# 2.2 The Founding of Rome and the Roman Republic

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Origin myths

Rome told two stories about its own beginning.

**Aeneas** was the son of the goddess Venus and a mortal man, a Trojan hero fighting for the Greeks, who founded Rome.

**Romulus and Remus** were the twin sons of Mars. The boys were set adrift on the Tiber, found by a she-wolf and then raised by a shepherd's family. Romulus killed Remus.

## The Roman conquest of Italy

At the beginning of the Republic, Rome was surrounded by enemies, including the Latin communities. The conquest of Italy runs as follows.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 338 BCE | Rome crushed the Latin states in Latium |
| The next fifty years | Successful struggles with the hill people of central Italy, then direct contact with the Greek communities |
| 267 BCE | Rome completed the conquest of southern Italy by defeating the Greek cities |
| 264 BCE | Rome crushed the Etruscan states in the north and had conquered most of Italy |

In 338 BCE the Romans also devised the **Roman Confederation**. Some people, the Latins, were given full Roman citizenship; the remaining communities were made allies. Allies were free to run their local affairs but were required to provide soldiers for Rome, and loyal allies could improve their status and even become Roman citizens. The arrangement therefore turned conquest into recruitment: every victory enlarged the pool of soldiers available for the next one.

## The Roman state

After the overthrow of the monarchy, Roman nobles were eager to maintain their position of power, and established a republican form of government.

### Magistrates

**Consuls** and **praetors** were the chief executive officers of the Roman Republic. Two consuls were chosen annually; they administered the government and led the army into battle. The office of praetor was created in 336 BCE and was in charge of civil law, but a praetor could also lead armies and govern Rome when the consuls were away.

### Senate and assemblies

The **Roman Senate** came to hold an especially important position. Formally it could only advise the magistrates, but this advice was not taken lightly, and by the third century BCE it had virtually the force of law.

The **Centuriate Assembly** elected the chief magistrates and passed laws. Its structure mattered more than its function: the wealthiest citizens always had a majority in it.

The **Council of the Plebs** came into being in 471 BCE.

## Social divisions

| | Patricians | Plebeians |
|---|---|---|
| Who they were | Descendants of the original senators appointed during the period of the kings; great landowners; an aristocratic governing class | The larger group of non-patrician landowners, less wealthy landholders, artisans, merchants and small farmers |
| Citizenship | Citizens | Citizens |
| Voting | Could vote | Could vote |
| Office | Only they could be consuls, magistrates and senators; controlled the centuriate assembly | Could not hold governmental office |

Intermarriage between the two orders was forbidden.

## The struggle of the orders

In the fifth century BCE the plebeians began to seek equality, and won it in stages.

- The **Council of the Plebs**, a popular assembly for plebeians only, was created in 471 BCE.
- The **tribunes of the plebs** were given power to protect plebeians against arrest by patrician magistrates.
- Intermarriage was allowed.
- In 287 BCE the plebeians could pass laws.

The outcome was not the levelling that might be expected. Because intermarriage was now permitted, a select number of patrician and plebeian families formed a new senatorial aristocracy that came to dominate the political offices. The struggle of the orders replaced one narrow governing class with another.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Aeneas** | Son of the goddess Venus and a mortal man; a Trojan hero fighting for the Greeks who founded Rome |
| **Romulus and Remus** | Twin sons of Mars, set adrift on the Tiber, found by a she-wolf and raised by a shepherd's family; Romulus killed Remus |
| **Roman Confederation** | The 338 BCE arrangement giving some Latins full Roman citizenship and making the remaining communities allies who ran their own affairs but supplied soldiers |
| **Consuls** | Two chief executive officers chosen annually who administered the government and led the army |
| **Praetor** | Office created in 336 BCE, in charge of civil law, able also to lead armies and govern Rome in the consuls' absence |
| **Roman Senate** | Body that could only advise the magistrates but whose advice had virtually the force of law by the third century BCE |
| **Centuriate Assembly** | Assembly in which the wealthiest citizens always had a majority; elected chief magistrates and passed laws |
| **Patricians** | Descendants of the original senators; great landowners and the aristocratic governing class |
| **Plebeians** | The larger group of non-patrician landowners, artisans, merchants and small farmers |
| **Council of the Plebs** | Popular assembly for plebeians only, created in 471 BCE |
| **Tribunes of the plebs** | Officers given power to protect plebeians against arrest by patrician magistrates |

markdown:
# 2.3 The Roman Conquest of the Mediterranean

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Carthage

Carthage was founded around 800 BCE on the coast of North Africa by the Phoenicians, and flourished. By the third century BCE it held northern Africa, southern Spain, Sardinia, Corsica and western Sicily, and controlled western Mediterranean trade. It was therefore not a distant rival but the power that owned the sea Rome had just reached.

## The Punic Wars

### The First Punic War (264–146 BCE)

The Romans decided to intervene in a struggle between two Sicilian cities and sent an army to Sicily. The Carthaginians considered Sicily part of their territory, so war began. To fight a naval power the Romans developed a navy. Carthage gave up all rights to Sicily, and Sicily became the first Roman province; Corsica, Sardinia and Sicily all became part of Rome.

Afterwards the Carthaginian general **Hannibal Barca** swore to restore his nation's honour.

### The Second Punic War (218–201 BCE)

The Romans encouraged one of Carthage's Spanish allies to revolt against Carthage. Hannibal crossed the Alps with an army of thirty to forty thousand men and terrorised the Romans for fifteen years. At the **Battle of Cannae** in 216 BCE the Romans lost 400,000 men and were on the brink of disaster.

Rome recovered by changing method rather than by winning a bigger battle.

- The Romans began to reconquer the Italian cities that had gone over to Hannibal's side.
- **Fabius Maximus**, as dictator, avoided pitched battles and attacked supply lines — the **Fabian strategy**.
- **Scipio Africanus the Elder** learned from Hannibal's own tactics and pushed the Carthaginians out of Spain by 206 BCE.
- The Romans then took the war directly to Carthage, forcing the Carthaginians to recall Hannibal from Italy.

At the **Battle of Zama** in 202 BCE the Romans crushed Hannibal's forces and Carthage lost Spain. Rome became the dominant power in the western Mediterranean.

### The Third Punic War (149–146 BCE)

In 146 BCE Carthage was destroyed. It burned for ten days, fifty thousand people in the area were sold into slavery, and Carthage became a Roman province called Africa.

## The nature of Roman imperialism

Roman expansion is best divided into three stages:

1. The conquest of Italy
2. The conflict with Carthage and expansion into the western Mediterranean
3. Involvement with, and domination of, the Hellenistic kingdoms

## The Roman army

The army was built of four legions, each made up of four to five thousand men. Each legion had about three hundred cavalry, and the rest was infantry. Soldiers were recruited from citizens between eighteen and forty-six.

The terms of service changed over time, and the change matters for what comes later. At first soldiers were unpaid, provided their own weapons and could join if they wanted — service rested on loyalty. Later they received professional training and a stipend. Later still they received the spoils of victory.

## Other wars

| War | Dates | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Jugurthine Wars | 112–106 BCE | Sulla and Marius add parts of Africa to Rome |
| Social War | 91–87 BCE | Italian cities revolt, desiring citizenship, since the Roman military relied heavily on their populations |
| Mithridatic War | 88–63 BCE | Sulla and Pompey add much of Anatolia to Rome |
| Three Servile Wars | 135–132, 104–100, 73–71 BCE | Slave rebellions in Sicily and southern Italy, including Spartacus |

## The results of conquest

Conquest made Rome rich and destabilised it at the same time.

The gap between rich and poor widened. More land meant that patricians could buy more land at a cheaper price and acquire slaves to work it, while plebeians got less land and moved to the cities unemployed. Country life changed accordingly, dominated by the **latifundia**, massive farming estates worked by many slaves, sustained by an influx of enslaved people.

Culturally, a new Hellenised urban culture appeared: Roman literature mimicked Greek modes and Romans adopted Greek-style baths. There were greater opportunities for Roman aristocrats, politically and materially.

There was also a cost that is easy to miss: the loss of enemies meant the loss of patriotism and of Roman frugality.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Carthage** | City founded around 800 BCE by the Phoenicians on the North African coast, controlling western Mediterranean trade by the third century BCE |
| **Hannibal Barca** | Carthaginian general who swore to restore national honour and crossed the Alps with 30,000–40,000 men |
| **Battle of Cannae** | 216 BCE battle in which the Romans lost 400,000 men and were on the brink of disaster |
| **Fabian strategy** | Fabius Maximus's method of avoiding pitched battles and attacking supply lines |
| **Scipio Africanus the Elder** | General who learned from Hannibal's tactics and pushed the Carthaginians out of Spain by 206 BCE |
| **Battle of Zama** | 202 BCE battle in which the Romans crushed Hannibal's forces; Carthage lost Spain |
| **Legion** | Roman army unit of 4,000–5,000 men, about 300 of them cavalry and the rest infantry |
| **Latifundia** | Massive farming estates worked by many slaves |
